knowledge: This book is written for people who have the resolve to take on responsibility. Products often fail to grow not because of poor specifications or insufficient technical skill, but because it remains ambiguous who ultimately takes responsibility.

責任 (responsibility) means making the final decision amid uncertainty and never running away from explaining business outcomes. 引き受ける (taking it on) means, when failure occurs, not blaming the market or other departments, but personally standing in the line of fire and taking the blame.

If that responsibility is not fulfilled and the product is defeated, the person must have the resolve to impose penalties on themselves such as demotion or resignation, and not flee heavy consequences involving the product’s survival, colleagues’ livelihoods, and market defeat.

The primary audience is product owners: product managers (PM), business owners, and anyone whose role is accountable for product value and business success. Specialists who work with them (engineers, designers, marketers, sales, PR, legal, etc.) should also read it, because understanding what the product owner holds, decides, and delegates is a shortcut to maximizing specialist results.
This is a book to use, not merely to read. It is designed to be opened, closed, and returned to in the middle of actual work, not only to be read straight through from the beginning.

Reading approach for the book: start from the chapter matching the challenge you currently face; move back and forth among chapters related to your role or phase; use the book as a discussion starter with teams and specialists.

Each chapter can be read independently, yet all chapters are connected by a single underlying philosophy. Progressing through the book reveals how ideas from one chapter relate to others, enabling a three-dimensional understanding of those relationships.
The book (Chapters 1–12) is designed as one large tree. Product development knowledge is structured as roots, trunk, and branches/leaves; if any part is missing, the tree cannot grow healthily.

Roots: the fundamental philosophy that underpins all product development. This is not skills or methods, but core values that emerge from a person’s philosophy and way of living. Covered in Chapter 7 (Experience Design and Communication Design) and the final chapter (Reunion with Product Management).

Trunk: basic education and fundamental techniques needed to advance a business in the modern era. Corresponds to Chapter 2 (Vision and Business Development), Chapter 3 (Management Planning and Budget Management), Chapter 4 (HR Strategy and People Management), and Chapter 5 (Project Management and Agile).

Branches and leaves: highly specialized applied knowledge and tasks that rest on foundational knowledge. From a product owner’s perspective much of this is delegated to experts; without solid roots and trunk, work becomes disjointed and loses consistency. Corresponds to Chapter 6 (Technology and Engineering), Chapter 8 (GTM Strategy and Marketing), Chapter 10 (PR and Branding), and Chapter 11 (Legal and IP Strategy).

Early chapters dig into the essence of product management and what it means to take responsibility; the middle of the book addresses specialists such as designers, engineers, marketers, sales, legal, and PR.
The book's single unifying question across all chapters is: who takes final responsibility for this judgment/decision? (この判断の最終責任を、誰が引き受けるのか？)

Later sections of the book specifically unpack how to divide roles with specialists and what the product owner must hold onto; they also cover organization theory in the AI era, redefining the product owner as a mini-CEO, and what a product development organization that continues to win looks like.
Chapters 1–11 each end with a 'learning resources' (学びのリソース) section recommending further reading.

Author 蜂須賀大貴 (Hachisuka Daiki) has worked product development across startups, mega-ventures, and enterprise new businesses, as both a PM in the field and a product owner making decisions, experiencing both growth and failure (including products that succeeded and products that were withdrawn).
Core thesis: product failures were typically not caused by insufficient skills or frameworks. The real problems were simpler and about unclear responsibility and stance.

Typical failure patterns: (1) it was ambiguous who decided the market; (2) it was unclear who held customer understanding through to the end; (3) it was unknown who decided 'we will not do this'; (4) it was ambiguous who would take responsibility for failure.
The book exists to put into language what a product owner / プロダクト責任者 should take on, based on field discomfort, regret, and successful experience.
The book is about stance (姿勢), not job titles. PM, CPO, VPoP, CTO, or any other title is irrelevant; what matters is the attitude of the person who takes product responsibility (プロダクト責任者).

Four defining stances of a product leader: (1) do not run away from customer value; (2) do not postpone decisions; (3) even when delegating, do not abandon responsibility; (4) when failing, take responsibility instead of making excuses.

The intended residue after reading is not perfect mastery but lingering questions: What should I hold onto vs. what should I delegate? Where are the responsibility gaps in the current organization? Can I see customer value and business results at the same time? When making the next decision, can I commit (腹を括る)?
If those questions stay with the reader in daily work, the book has done its job.

The book’s opening inquiry is: What is responsibility in product development, and what does it mean to take it on? The preface (序章) will unpack an “OS” for fighting through that pressure without fleeing it.

A product manager (プロダクト責任者) needs a thinking OS (operating system) that lets them correctly use knowledge across strategy, organization, technology, engineering, marketing, sales, PR, and legal work. Individual skills and frameworks should be learned only after this OS is in place.
Even an excellent application (strategy) will not function correctly if the OS (the foundation of thinking) is outdated or full of bugs.

The universal OS for product managers—independent of product phase or market—is three foundational abilities (3つの基礎体力): (1) logical thinking (ロジカルシンキング / 論理的思考力), (2) the ability to move back and forth between the concrete and the abstract (具体と抽象を行き来する力 / 概念化能力), and (3) decision-making literacy (意思決定リテラシー / 判断の軸).

Product owners (プロダクト責任者) need three interconnected abilities: decision-making literacy (意思決定リテラシー / 判断の軸), the ability to move between the concrete and the abstract (具体と抽象を行き来する力 / 概念化能力), and logical thinking (ロジカルシンキング / 論理的思考力).

These three skills are not independent; they operate as a linked process. Logical thinking captures the structure of facts, interpretation, and action; moving between concrete and abstract raises resolution; decision-making literacy then determines the next action.
This combined thinking process is presented as the condition for leaders who keep producing results under uncertainty.

Logical thinking is defined as the ability to grasp things in terms of action and structure and to organize them in relation to purpose—not as sounding smart or defeating others in argument. It is the power to impose order on chaotic situations.

When trouble occurs, the recommended approach is not emotional handling (e.g., “push through with fighting spirit” or “scold the person in charge”) but immediately posing structural questions and organizing the events.
When diagnosing trouble, first identify the layer: is it a strategy mistake, a tactics mistake, or an operations (front-line) error?
Examine structural placement along the timeline: which process defect actually triggered the problem?
Confirm context: what purpose was this function originally meant to achieve?
List other variables that must be considered (technical constraints, legal risk, user psychology, etc.).
Language these factors as a tree and organize them MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) so the leverage point—the place whose fix stops recurrence—becomes visible.
Leaders who lack this bird’s-eye ability treat every event as both urgent and important and are trapped in endless whack-a-mole.

The skill is analogous to engineering debugging: do not patch surface symptoms one by one; locate the root bug in the overall system structure and distinguish where shortcuts are acceptable versus where they are forbidden.
Logical thinking is therefore indispensable for finding that structural leverage.
The ability to move freely between the concrete and the abstract is tightly coupled with logical thinking and is decisive for innovation and new-value creation.

One use of that ability is to extract structure from individual events and turn it into a reproducible mechanism (an asset); the other is to extract the skeleton of an existing idea and generate entirely new value.
The text then begins discussing the first of these—systematizing on-site events into reusable mechanisms.

Incoming product signals are always concrete (e.g., “User A cancelled,” “a request came for feature B”). Handling them only at that concrete level yields only symptomatic treatment (対症療法). You must abstract once, extract the essence, and transfer it to other concrete situations.
The ability to move back and forth between the concrete and the abstract is the dividing line between a mediocre product owner and an excellent one (プロダクト責任者).

Example (PIVOT, a business video media company): Introducing a “PIVOT Miles” points program looked like a mismatch. Highly business-literate users were not expected to get excited about drugstore-style “point collecting,” so the idea would normally be rejected as off-target.

Do not stop at the first concrete judgment. Abstract the points system: it is not merely “points for discounts” but essentially feedback/recognition for users’ learning behavior and contributions, and incentive design for continuation.

Raise the abstraction further and look for incentive structures that high-income users (PIVOT’s typical audience) actually prefer: airline mileage programs, American Express-style status cards, or point systems on doctor-oriented platforms.
Redefining the same idea as “miles” or “status” rather than mere points can make it resonate with that user layer.

Reusable process: Concrete (own idea) → Abstract (extract essence) → Another concrete (success cases from other industries) → Re-concretize (apply to your own product). This loop can turn an initially weak-looking idea into a meaningful, powerful measure.
Consciously training the skill of going between concrete and abstract is a thinking method that directly connects to results.

Decision-making literacy (意思決定リテラシー) is a coined term meaning the minimum knowledge and judgment axes needed to guarantee decision quality in each specialized domain; it functions as a foundational OS especially for product managers (PMs).
A product owner/PM is the final decision-maker, yet it is impossible to possess expert-level knowledge across every domain (engineering, design, marketing, sales, PR, legal, etc.).

You do not need to become an expert in every area. What is required is not the specialized skills themselves but a judgment axis that lets you engage experts as equals and evaluate risk versus return.

Four types of questions a non-expert decision-maker should be able to pose to specialists: (1) What to ask (identifying the issues)—specialized knowledge, cases, and the expert’s unique judgment criteria; (2) What to decide (defining the decision)—what is optimal when applied to the company’s own situation and how far to go considering the whole; (3) Where the risks are (avoiding fatal damage)—existing violations, time-consuming requirements such as licenses that conflict with the project schedule; (4) What to delegate versus what to hold (boundary of authority)—materials needed for the decision and the respective roles in decision-making.

In a for-profit business, financial/accounting knowledge cannot be avoided. Core items include the structures of P/L (profit-and-loss statement), B/S (balance sheet) and C/F (cash-flow statement), the meaning of gross profit, and the distinction between CAPEX (investment) and OPEX (operating expense). These are not merely accounting specialists’ knowledge but basic literacy for understanding management and for knowing when to accelerate or brake the business.

A product owner (プロダクト責任者) cannot abdicate responsibility by fully outsourcing legal or engineering work to specialists; even without knowing statutes, they must know which laws are fundamental to the business model, and even without writing code they must understand how accumulating technical debt affects the business.

The product owner is both the product’s final line of defense and its front line; they cannot escape the daily judgments required of them. Decision-making literacy (意思決定リテラシー) is what supports those last judgments.

Delegating (任せる) means keeping outcome responsibility yourself while giving ownership to experts. Dumping/throwing everything (丸投げ) means handing over both outcome responsibility and thinking, thereby isolating the experts.
Dumping makes the locus of responsibility unclear and almost certainly causes the business to fail.
Properly delegating to experts requires request skills (依頼のスキル) and questioning skills (質問のスキル).

Request skills consist of the requester holding specific information; without that information, the expert’s thinking is constrained, and the more excellent the expert the harder they become to work with.
Later chapters cover collaborating with specialists (engineers, designers, marketers, CFO, legal, etc.); the distinction between delegating and dumping is the common premise for all of them.

When handing off work, six elements must be aligned first: 背景 (background/premise story of why the initiative is needed now in the market or business), 目的 (purpose: whose problem will ultimately be solved), 判断基準 (decision axis for what to prioritize vs. discard among options), 期待値 (expected role and output quality from specialists), 期限 (deadline plus the reason that date was set), and リスクと不確実性 (visible concerns plus unverified black boxes).

Handing off work without those elements reliably produces ブラックボックス化 (black-boxing), quality degradation, 属人化 (work becoming person-dependent), and inability to explain; the ball then drops at role boundaries so no one can take responsibility.

To delegate, the product owner must personally hold five criteria (図表0-2) before specialists’ thinking can expand; giving only a concrete request without background and context is the worst anti-pattern.
Criterion 1 目的 (Why): even if the work looks irrational, medium-to-long-term or investment-like implications often justify it; the product owner must therefore state the why forcefully.

Criterion 2 制約条件 (constraints of cost, schedule, legal, and technical debt): strong will otherwise becomes blind push-forward that misses failure risk; constraints must sit behind passion so judgment stays calm.
Criterion 3 成功指標 (KPI/KGI): without quantitative metrics it is impossible to know which axis to improve on.
A product that continues without a guiding principle (目指す指針) loses sight of the value it provides and ends up being for nobody.
Options (代替案): Always consider alternatives together with risks. That way, when a risk is encountered, you can keep moving forward calmly without pausing to think.
Risk / Worst Case (リスク): By thinking through conceivable scenarios in advance as much as possible, you can respond with composure (平常心) when that situation actually arises.
Framework for delegating (任せるための前提 / Diagram 0-2) consists of five elements: Purpose (目的), Constraints (制約条件), Success metrics (成功指標), Alternatives (代替案), and Risk (リスク).

Questioning skill when working with experts means being able to ask specifically: 'Why that approach?' — i.e., the logic, based on the expert’s knowledge, for judging that method as optimal for your company.
Questioning skill also includes asking 'What other options were there?' — learning the alternatives that were considered and then rejected, in order to understand the decision-making.
When working with experts, check validity and breadth of perspective using structured questions that raise decision quality, not mere inquiries.
Ask what risks a choice creates: future technical debt and business trade-offs that may follow the decision.
Ask the worst-case scenario: recovery possibility if it fails, and how fatal the damage to the business would be.
Ask how it could be even better: if current constraints were removed, what the expert would see as the most ideal state.
Without decision literacy, experts quickly detect that you do not understand; output quality drops, discussion stays shallow, and the business is hurt.
A product owner who asks high-quality questions is easier for experts to work with, which clearly improves output quality.
Expert advice is usually correct within its domain, but business success is not determined by domain correctness alone.
A product owner judges with two lenses: domain correctness × business correctness. Experts supply only one side.
The product owner must decide whether advice is correct in the business context. Final responsibility always stays with you; do not let go of the wheel no matter how many excellent experts you have.
A culture of delegation requires resolving information asymmetry so that delegation becomes reproducible and decision speed rises.
Resolve information asymmetry by having the product owner keep learning from experts, and by having experts understand the product background.
In regular meetings (定例), prepare only the information needed as judgment material so decisions can be made from a complete, uncluttered state.
Use documentation to structure discussions and make debate more organized and productive.
The ability to delegate (任せる力) is career-defining for a product owner (プロダクト責任者).
As an organization grows, the product owner must shift from a hands-on, personally executing role to a role that raises the quality of decision-making.
The more people one delegates to, the heavier and more complex the product owner's remaining decisions become.
Only a product owner who possesses the ability to delegate can gather strong specialists and fully unlock their latent potential.

Effective delegation means: assign work, continue to watch over it afterward, and course-correct at the right moments—this is a viewpoint extremely close to management and is the foundation for growing an organization.
Delegation is not mere transfer of authority; it is leadership itself for building a reproducible organization.
This material appears in the preface/introduction (序章) of a work framed as the 'OS' (operating system) of the product owner.

Core principle of market selection: 'Choosing a winnable market determines everything.' Even superior strategy, tactics, or a strong team will fail if the market itself is not winnable, because outcomes are governed by market 'wind direction' (conditions and shifts).

BlackBerry case study: BlackBerry dominated the business-phone battlefield of 'efficient email via physical keyboard.' The iPhone created a new battlefield of 'intuitive touch operation plus app extensibility,' after which the contest was decided regardless of BlackBerry's team quality. A complete change in market wind cannot be resisted.

Practical implication: Daily business success similarly depends first on whether the chosen battlefield (market) is advantageous. The decisive skill is discerning which field to fight in, not merely assembling a strong team.
Definition of a winnable market (product development / business): A market that satisfies any one (or more) of three specified conditions (illustrated in Figure 1-1 on the source page).

Three conditions for a winnable market (勝てる市場の3つの条件): (1) Growing market — the overall market is in a growth phase so one can ride an upward escalator; it should be a new or redefined market. (2) Absence of an overwhelming No.1 — multiple players already exist but no dominant leader yet. (3) Exclusive/monopolistic position (MOAT) — the company can occupy a unique standing via proprietary technology or assets, with potential for platformization.

Selecting the opposite type of market starts one at a strategic disadvantage: markets that are shrinking or in long-term stagnation; mature markets or those with unique ecosystems and extremely high entry barriers; or markets already monopolized by an overly strong player.

A stagnant or mature market can still be chosen deliberately if the plan is to change industry customs or create innovation via digital power (e.g., DX or AI-driven business transformation); such a choice is viable only because the market situation has been correctly read.

The three conditions form an interrelated framework for market selection in Chapter 1 (市場選び), visualized as Chart 1-1 with growing market (up escalator), no overwhelming No.1, and exclusive position (MOAT).
Market selection determines business growth, product success, and personal career trajectory; it is equivalent to choosing the difficulty level of the game you are about to play.
First-time business leaders should start in lower-difficulty markets to accumulate success, then gradually expand horizontally into higher-difficulty markets (the standard approach).

Serial entrepreneurs (second-time operators) increasingly jump directly into the highest-difficulty markets, often by bringing experienced serial entrepreneurs as partners, because market speed does not allow a leisurely approach.
The first and greatest challenge is knowing one's own capabilities (身の程) and deciding which difficulty level to take on.

The only way to find a winnable market is to accumulate sufficient input through information gathering: constantly keep antennas up, observe trends in each market, discern what is new and where the wind is blowing, catch new markets at the moment they emerge, compare them to past markets, and forecast how they will unfold.
Market-selection information gathering means looking beyond one's current industry and adjacent fields with a broader view of trends.

Information-gathering basic 1: Always overview widely and deeply (常に・広く・深く). Capture overall business movements via sources such as the Nikkei, observe daily stock prices and market changes to see which domains currently have tailwinds and which companies are attracting attention. Overseas information is equally essential: follow advanced foreign cases to grasp technologies and models not yet in Japan, enabling time-machine management (replicating overseas successes in Japan).
After a market is somewhat narrowed, shift from broad awareness to currently needed, narrow, and deep information: industry-specific problems and internal circumstances that news does not cover.

Ways to raise information density: attend industry-association events and conferences and speak directly with insiders; use AI research tools (e.g. DeepResearch) to produce detailed reports on a domain or company; hear operators’ unfiltered language via business media.
Superficial knowledge becomes conviction about market choice only after it is grounded in those raw voices.
Markets are living systems that change daily; stock-price movement is a symbol of that continuous motion.

Intermittent, one-shot research (e.g. “this week we do market research”) cannot capture the whole picture; habitually connect always-on wide-and-shallow intake to currently needed narrow-and-deep inquiry.
Mental model: understand the market like a river’s flow—upstream and downstream ecosystems together, while accounting for weather and wind.
Information gathering is war preparation (戦支度): to build a product organization and create value, you must first become a professional in that market.
Neglecting research leads to getting stuck; hard-to-exit markets and long wars that kill motivation are risks that should have been avoided at the market-selection stage.
Do not spare time selecting a winnable market; keep researching until you are personally convinced—that is preparation for a long campaign.
Once candidates are reasonably narrowed, the next step is to judge whether you yourself should fight in that market.
Long-term business battles cannot be endured even when the market is growing and winning conditions are in place, unless one can put genuine personal feeling and commitment into the work.
Choosing a market or battlefield is not merely searching for a place that looks profitable; it is the process of finding the intersection where one's own passion overlaps with market potential.
Direction becomes clear when organized on two axes: source of passion (情熱の源泉) and market understanding (市場理解).
The vertical axis, source of passion, has two directions: past experience and accumulated strengths (過去の経験／強み), versus future vision and aspiration for the world one wants to create (未来のビジョン／志).

Lack of an original personal experience does not disqualify someone from a market; one path uses built-up track record as a weapon, while another uses strong future empathy or a conviction of 'this is how it ought to be' as driving force.

The horizontal axis, market understanding, splits into the present position of issues waiting to be solved now (市場の現在地) versus future prediction of signs that will become a large wave in coming years (市場の未来予測).

The four quadrants formed by these axes are: (1) cultivated skills that can be used immediately in the current market, labeled demonstrating expertise (専門性の発揮); (2) leveraging existing strengths while waiting for a future wave, labeled building first-mover advantage (先行優位の構築); (3) desire to solve existing problems or 'un-' (dissatisfaction, injustice, inconvenience) in the present market, labeled pursuit of social significance (社会的意義の追求); (4) creating a new culture or world in an anticipated future, labeled pioneering unexplored domains (未踏領域の開拓).

The 2x2 framework (図表1-2) therefore maps personal history versus future aspiration against current problems versus emerging signs, producing four distinct strategic postures for choosing where to compete.
Four strategic domains for competing/winning in a market are formed by combining past experience vs. future vision with current market vs. future market prediction.
Domain: 【専門性の発揮】(Demonstrating Expertise) = past experience × current market position. This is the highest-certainty area where you can immediately deploy your existing skills.
Domain: 【先行優位の構築】(Building First-Mover Advantage) = past experience × future market prediction. A strategic area that leverages existing strengths while waiting for the next large incoming 'wave'.
Domain: 【社会的意義の追求】(Pursuing Social Significance) = future vision × current market. The area of resolving present 'dissatisfactions/injustices' (「不」) through one's own sense of mission.
Domain: 【未踏領域の開拓】(Pioneering Uncharted Territory) = future vision × future market prediction. A value-creation area that presents new culture and values that do not yet exist in concrete form.

What matters is not which of the four domains is 'correct,' but being conscious of which domain you are currently trying to win in; this dramatically changes the resolution of skills you should polish and messages you should communicate.

Cross-check the four domains and write out merits, demerits, and why you personally should operate in that market; this clarifies whether it is 'a battlefield you should win' or 'a battlefield someone else should take on.'
Business is a marathon, not a sprint. The source that makes you still want to continue when it becomes painful is original experience (原体験) and/or company vision.

To develop strong problem awareness and passion, first excavate your original experiences (原体験): past events that strongly moved your heart, including happy moments, frustrating moments, or even small lingering memories.
Original experiences (原体験) do not have to be positive.

Author example of original experience: childhood as a TV kid whose worries disappeared while laughing or crying at video/media; this later became the desire to do work that brightens people through media.
Deeper origin for wanting to 'deliver emotion to people': high-school brass-band club experience involving 150 people.

原体験 (original/formative experience) is a core personal event that shapes one's identity and supplies lasting motivation; it need not be positive—negative experiences and emotional wounds can generate equally strong passion.

A high-school band-leader experience of filling a hall and seeing audiences cry demonstrated that even amateur performance can move hearts, becoming the driving force for wanting work that gives people 感動 (emotional impact).

The career choice of media over pure music followed the intuition that adding video to music could brighten more people, combined with conviction that technology would transform media experiences, crystallizing into the unshakable mission: create products that use media to brighten a dark world even a little.

Possessing a clearly felt original experience supplies the stamina to keep competing in a chosen market and the perseverance to endure difficult periods, because one can feel that “that event is shaping who I am now.”
No one truly lacks an original experience; it is merely unverbalized. Proceeding with a venture without having language for it is exhausting, because the source of one’s action-fuel remains unknown.
Vision Quest (ビジョンクエスト) is a workshop method for surfacing original experience: a retreat-style session (e.g., on a coast) in which one spends a dedicated hour facing oneself with only paper and pen.

Vision-quest practical rules: (1) bring only paper and pen; leave all phones, PCs and other concentration-disrupting electronics behind; (2) begin with a visual-field expansion exercise—close the eyes, breathe deeply, then expand awareness from a single point outward, analogous to an athlete’s focus drill of moving the thumbs forward and back.

An eye-expansion exercise: alternately move the thumbs, then move only the eyes to the left and right extremes to consciously become aware of the limits of one's visual field; returning the gaze afterward should make the world appear slightly wider, serving as a starting point for broader perspective.

A one-hour solitary beach reflection exercise: ask 'Why am I here?', 'What do I want to accomplish?', and 'What accumulation of choices made me who I am now?', writing down everything that arises—career choices, school selections, life turning points—as fragments of the reasons one is here now.

Daily busyness often causes people to lose sight of why they do their work; tracing the past always surfaces turning points that shaped the self, and the feeling 'because of that event, I am here now' identifies one's original experience (原体験).

Original experience is a unique personal asset that no one else can imitate; even events that appear small to others matter most if they are what actually drives the person, and re-examining them clarifies markets one can wholeheartedly immerse in and fields one can sustain.

A second method for finding whether one can be serious about a market is deriving passion from corporate vision: a sense of mission held as personal philosophy beyond original experience, such as wanting to eliminate food loss, war, or educational inequality.

Vision-type motivation need not come from one's own lived experience; it can arise from a documentary, events seen or heard overseas, or beliefs inherited from parents or others, and it continually reminds one why one exists in that market while serving as the philosophical axis for leading a team over long-term business operations.

Neither original experience (原体験) nor corporate vision is inherently more correct; both function as supporting pillars that sustain the self. Selecting a winnable market is only the first step; without a genuine reason to persist, the effort will not last.

In the course of building a business, painful situations will inevitably arise. What enables one to endure them is not strategy held in the head, but motivation that wells up from the bottom of the heart—whether that motive is original experience or corporate vision. A market lacking such motive requires pausing to reconsider.

If a strong original experience for the current market cannot be recalled, dig into the question “Why am I drawn to this problem?” Reverse-engineering original experiences related to the market’s issues is also effective. Ultimately, choosing a market one can approach with genuine passion is the final decision of the battlefield.
Once feelings are settled, one can resolve to fight even in a red-ocean or oligopolistic market. Conversely, even a blue-ocean market is not one’s battlefield if heartfelt commitment is absent.
Those already running a business should re-examine the question “Why am I in this market?” The source of long-term fighting energy lies in that inquiry.

In real product-development settings, especially when a PM joins a team mid-stream, the market to compete in has often already been decided by management or founders, creating a different practical landscape from the ideal of freely choosing a market.

The initial battlefield (market/domain) is typically already set by founders based on intense personal experience or by strategic decisions of the management team. They have already raised the flag of 'we will solve this problem in this domain,' and an early product (MVP) may already exist.

A product owner's role is not merely to fight using given resources inside a predetermined battlefield. They are accountable for the ultimate business results, so they must have the courage to verify even management's initial settings (market definition) without treating them as sacred, and to propose course corrections when needed.

Management's initial hypothesis is only a hypothesis based on the landscape visible at that time. The product owner is on the front line that actually puts the product into the market and touches the raw reality of customer reactions.

Field-only truths include: the problem exists but is not painful enough that customers will pay to solve it; and a different player than the assumed competitor is actually the biggest obstacle. Facing those truths requires flexibly re-examining the relationship between market and solution (the product as solution).
Two approaches exist for revising market-solution fit: a market-in perspective and a product-out perspective.

Market-in perspective (マーケットイン的視点): remake the solution to fit the market's problem. If the target customer's pain is real but the current product does not fully heal it, keep the market definition and pivot the product's features or value proposition (バリュー・プロポジション).

Market-in example: for the genuine pain of 'complexity of restaurant shift management,' a multifunctional PC management tool failed to stick in the field; the team pivoted to a simple product based on the smartphone chat UI employees already used daily.
Many startups' search for PMF (Product Market Fit) is itself the process of fundamentally remaking a product from the ground up so that it can spread rapidly once fit is found.
The product-out perspective is an approach that searches for the market in which one's own solution (strengths) will shine most brightly, rather than starting from a pre-chosen market.
A company's original experience, unique technology, or assets may be valued more highly in a completely different market than the one originally assumed; this is not uncommon.

Example: image-recognition technology developed for one industry can find explosive demand in the inspection processes of an entirely different industry. The guiding question is: 'This is our weapon. Where is the battlefield where this weapon can win most decisively?'
Initial market selection may have been the job of the management team, but there is no guarantee that that market definition remains the correct one for the present or the future.

A product leader must deeply understand and respect the vision and passion of management, yet must not follow it blindly; they must continually ask, with on-the-ground reality: 'Can we really win in this market with this solution?'

The product leader's work is to move back and forth between the problem (issue) and the solution, hunting for the sweet spot where the business can actually win. This dynamic market-selection process is a core responsibility of the product owner.

Once a winnable market has been chosen and the team is ready to commit with conviction, the next stage is to advance the business using the product as the weapon. The most important factor at this point is team composition and role division.
The degree of a product leader's success depends not only on individual capability but heavily on relationships with those around them, especially the management team and business owners.
Designing the team and clarifying responsibility boundaries is the first step toward making a product-development organization function healthily.
Section 1-4 focuses on sharing roles with management and business owners so that product and business leadership can operate in complementary rather than conflicting ways.

The first step for an organization to function healthily is to clarify the relationship among three parties: executives (経営陣), business leaders (事業責任者), and those who carry the product management function (プロダクトマネジメント機能).
PM should not be treated merely as a job title, but as a role that owns responsibility for what to build (What / 何を作るか) and why to build it (Why / なぜ作るか).

In the business launch phase, role boundaries among executives, business leaders, and PM do not need to be sharply separated; the entrepreneur or business leader who owns the product should personally take on the PM role.
The person who chose the market based on strong personal original experience (原体験) and vision is best able to breathe life into the first product by directly reflecting that passion in it.
This is especially important for BtoC (consumer) products, where the founder’s own experience of being stuck or inconvenienced is a key source of product direction.

Ideal launch-phase relationship (図表1-3): executives concentrate on decision-making and ownership and stand at the front of hypothesis validation; business leaders concentrate on business promotion and management and work with PM to make the management vision concrete; PM concentrates on practical execution, project management, and supporting hypothesis validation.
Ambiguous current state to avoid: mixed decision-making and execution, overlapping roles, unclear independent responsibilities, and lack of efficiency and clarity about who decides and who executes.
After the launch phase, authority should be gradually delegated to the PM so that decision-making, business promotion, and execution can proceed smoothly with clear roles.

For B2C products, starting from personal issues the founder themselves experienced makes it easier to gain empathy and easier to communicate as a story. For B2B products, verify whether the founder's hypothesis actually matches market pain; the founder themselves should meet potential clients to confirm that a burning need (a problem they desperately want solved) truly exists.
In the launch/startup phase, the executive team must take strong ownership and stand at the front of hypothesis validation. Beside them, the PM supports the practical side of project management.

The most important job of a PM in the launch phase is to install the founder's vision (and the contents of the founder's mind) into themselves: thoroughly understand the founder's way of thinking, thinking rhythm, judgment criteria, and values to the point of being able to explain them as a substitute for the founder.

If this resonance/sync is shallow, product development direction easily drifts and misalignment arises in team communication. When the PM can deeply understand the meaning of the founder's words and even explain the background, the PM can function as the founder's right hand, as the team's driver and translator.
The quality of synchronization in this phase becomes a watershed that later determines how much authority the PM can hold.

When there are multiple executives (e.g., CTO for technology, CFO for finance, CMO for marketing), division of labor according to strengths is needed. The PM stands between them as a hub that pursues overall optimization, understands across domains, and adjusts so the product does not contradict overall strategy.

If the launch-phase team gathered on a relationship basis and specialties are not clear, the PM has no choice but to become the person who picks up dropped balls: complementing executives' areas of strength, picking up unaddressed issues, and not letting overall progress stop. The ideal image of a PM in the launch phase is to move as the shadow of the executive team.

In a company's growth phase, when an organization of a certain size that already has existing businesses launches a new business, the most important factor is how much the management team is willing to bet (commit) on the new venture.

Management involvement in new business typically follows two patterns. Pattern 1: The executive personally takes charge as the new-business leader, returning to 'startup mode' with a strong vision and original lived experience, just as they did when launching the first product. Existing businesses are delegated to a COO or other business leaders so that exploration (new) and exploitation (existing) can be pursued in parallel.
Example of Pattern 1: CyberAgent President Fujita Jin left most existing businesses to other executives and personally directed the launch of the video-streaming service ABEMA as producer.

Pattern 2: Management concentrates on growing the existing businesses and appoints a dedicated business-unit leader. The leader may be an external hire with prior business-development experience or an internal person who possesses entrepreneurial qualities.
Figure 1-4 (Expertise and Roles) contrasts roles whose expertise is clearly defined (e.g., PM, CFO, CMO, CTO) with roles whose expertise is unclear (complementary / gap-filling positions).
A person or role that 'fills every gap' is described as an existence that occupies all remaining interstices when specialized C-suite and PM functions are already assigned.

Product managers (PMs) always embody the vision of executives while acting as on-the-ground practitioners, regardless of whether management is deeply involved or a dedicated business owner is in place.
When executives are deeply involved in operations, the PM supports execution in a COO-like capacity. When a business owner exists, the PM takes on more CEO-like strategy and decision-making.
To grow as a product leader, one must constantly recognize which of the two roles is currently required and flexibly switch stance.

CEO-type product leader: A decision-making principal who makes management judgments spanning market, organization, finance, legal, and development. Applies when serving as a new-business owner or when granted substantial authority by executives. Requires company-wide optimization, not merely a product-centric view.

COO-type product leader: An execution owner who translates the vision of executives or business owners into the field. Integrates a broad range of operational work—business planning, staffing, marketing, and more—beyond product development. Must convert ideals into reality as a translator of vision.
In both cases, management concentrates on resource allocation and decision-making while delegating authority to the responsible person.

A true promoter with a management perspective (経営視座を持つ真の推進者) is a PM who can constructively share roles with executives and business leaders, making a clear judgment of how far to take on personally versus from where to leave work to specialists.
Clear role-sharing between PM, executives, and business owners enables later authority delegation (権限移譲) and, in turn, organizational self-running / autonomy (組織の自走化).
From later chapters of the book, each domain is explained in terms of 'areas the responsible person should hold' versus 'areas to leave to specialists.'
Product success or failure is determined by the team's overall capability, not by any individual.
At the outset of product work, clarify three roles: who raises the flag (誰が旗を掲げ), who draws the strategy (誰が戦略を描き), and who fights on the front line (誰が前線で戦うのか).

The prototype of a winning product-development organization is a team in which executives, business leaders, and product leaders understand each other's strengths and roles and can move in the same direction.
Initiative (イニシアティブ) is not gathering opinions and making the final decision; it is the power to first show one's own will and indicate direction. It is not doing everything yourself.
While building team relationships and dividing roles, taking on everything yourself is a foolish strategy (愚策).
What matters is discerning the parts where you should wave the flag versus the parts where you follow as a follower (フォロワー).
First identify flag-waving areas = areas in which you hold initiative. How far that covers (management / business / product) depends on team composition and company phase.
If you are in a position close to CEO, take initiative across all layers: management, business, and product.
If management members are already clearly waving the management flag, the range you should hold may be limited to the product organization.

Product organizations span a very wide range of domains, including development organization building, personnel planning, resource allocation, budget creation, architecture design (infrastructure, server-side, frontend structure and language characteristics), and product management. The scope of one's initiative changes depending on how far one interferes in each of these areas.
The essential skill is exercising leadership and initiative while simultaneously earning the team's trust. Self-centered, tyrannical decision-making that tosses people around is incorrect.

Depending on the company's phase, consensus-based decision-making is not always sufficient; there are situations that require the leader to make the decision themselves and sometimes push through opposition. Even when the leader believes they are advancing with a clear vision, it can appear forceful to others.

Leaders must look at themselves objectively while building team trust. A core practice is fulfilling accountability: explaining the background and context of decisions as carefully as possible so that members can more easily act in the same direction as the leader's vision.

Management information asymmetry is a structural reality: leaders often make decisions based on a vantage point closer to management or on information that cannot yet be disclosed to members. This can cause members to perceive the decision as hasty and based on incomplete information.

This perception can be resolved through repeated explanations and accumulated trust over time. A single muddy or incomplete explanation destroys trust. However, a person who has consistently and sincerely kept promises with the team and stakeholders can say 'I cannot explain this now, but we will proceed in this direction' and the team will follow.
Reliably fulfilling small promises accumulates a sense of security that “if I follow this person, I won’t go wrong.” That repetition ultimately connects to the power to take initiative.
Initiative is not the power to give orders, but directional leadership.
A product manager must decide which domains to hold personally and which to delegate.

Vision, market, and customer problems are domains a PM should always hold. If a product leader cannot articulate vision, lacks market understanding, and does not recognize customer problems, that is simply a capability gap.

This is not limited to a small launch-phase team. Even when a product organization grows to 50 or 100 people, the person with the product-owner title must remain the most knowledgeable person on vision, market, and customer problems.
If you feel you are no longer in that position, it is time to have the resolve to hand the role to someone else.
Technical selection and architecture design should be understood by the product owner, but if a CTO or tech lead exists, that domain should be entrusted to specialists.
The product owner should focus on “why to build” and “what to build,” and does not need to carry “how to build” alone.
Appropriate division of labor creates a foundation for discussion between the product owner and engineers, which produces a stronger product.
The product owner should still grasp data structures and the types and meaning of collected data, because that knowledge expands available options.
For design and UX, the product owner holds direction (customer understanding and experience principles), while concrete UI and experience design should be left to designers.
For marketing and sales, be particular about strategy and KPI design, and leave execution of tactics to specialists.

Management planning, budget management, and HR planning should involve the PM in the launch phase, but after the growth phase they should be transferred to executives and back-office specialists so that organization design can happen at a higher level.

To decide how far you should do work yourself, in high-uncertainty domains you should first try doing it yourself. Hands-on work builds intuition (勘所) and helps you understand what a capable specialist in that domain looks like. Only after you can delegate with reproducibility should you transfer the work.

Delegating to experts in a high-uncertainty area before you have personal intuition is unhealthy, because you never develop the ability to evaluate experts’ proposals. Early advice is fine; the point is to gain experience and a judgment axis, which later raises team performance.

Two domains where a leader should keep initiative: (1) their own specialty—e.g. a product owner must know vision, market, and customer problems better than anyone and must never hand these over no matter how large the organization grows; (2) high-uncertainty areas they do not yet know well—paradoxically, these are exactly where they should first get hands-on, with expert advice, so they can later set conditions and make judgments that let specialists thrive.

Recommended tool: a Product Owner Involvement Level Map (プロダクト責任者の関与レベルマップ). Vertical axis = hierarchy (strategy / tactics / measures); horizontal axis = phase (startup / growth / expansion). For each cell, map whether you hold it yourself, hold it jointly, or delegate. Example: in UI/UX, the product owner is strongly involved at the strategy level in the startup phase, and involvement shifts toward the measure level by the expansion phase.

Having initiative as a PM does not mean doing everything yourself; it means first showing direction and creating conditions in which others can act. This requires fulfilling accountability, accumulating trust, and keeping small daily promises.
A PM should understand vision, market, and customer problems better than anyone else, and in uncertain domains personally experience the work in order to sharpen their own judgment criteria.

PMs should delegate what should be delegated and create an environment in which specialists can thrive. Consciously managing the gradient between domains where one takes initiative and domains one delegates is a sign of PM maturity and the leadership needed to build a winning product-development organization.
Mapping domains of ownership makes it clear to the whole team what the PM holds and what is delegated (e.g., delegating design authority to the design organization).

Product owner involvement-level map (図表1-6) by company stage: Startup (立ち上げ期) — Strategy: hold yourself; Tactics: hold yourself; Measures/施策: jointly hold. Growth (成長期) — Strategy: jointly hold; Tactics: jointly hold; Measures: delegate. Expansion (拡大期) — Strategy: jointly hold; Tactics: delegate; Measures: delegate.

Chapter summary of market-selection failure patterns begins with six patterns. Pattern 1: Choosing a market on passion alone — over-relying on personal origin stories (原体験), setting aside the judgment of whether a winnable market actually exists, and pushing forward on feeling rather than evidence.

A common startup failure pattern is lacking monetization points and customers with sufficiently serious problems, so business funding (原資) is insufficient: the problem exists, but solving it still does not make a viable business. This contradiction often surfaces after Series A–B (growth and expansion phase).

Strong original lived experience (原体験) easily gathers trust and investor support in the seed stage (business-problem exploration period) because of excitement about a new opportunity. Without accompanying economic growth potential (伸びしろ), however, capital and the team are eventually exhausted and the venture stalls.
Key conclusion: markets that generate emotional empathy but lack economic growth potential tend to burn out easily.

Another failure pattern is choosing an overcrowded (競合過多) market because it is currently booming, chasing first-mover advantage (先行者優位). The generative-AI dawn (e.g., GPT-3 era) is a representative example.

In such markets, weak differentiation leads to price-and-feature competition. Low barriers cause a flood of similar products, inflating marketing costs. Early user acquisition can still fail if quality and experience are unfinished, because later polished products or well-capitalized incumbents absorb the market.

Over the past 20 years Big Tech has repeatedly flipped markets by injecting later, highly polished products that embed into daily life, backed by massive capital and delivery power. Winning a red ocean on speed alone is therefore high-difficulty.

Challenging a red ocean is nevertheless a necessary passage for growth. Starting in a niche, locking in customer value, and then attracting large-company entry is itself evidence that a real market has been created.

To win after large players enter, differentiation factors (MOAT) must be designed in advance, and sustainable competitive advantage (持続的な競争優位性) must be built in experience, delivery/provision, or revenue structure—preferably in more than one of these.

A third failure pattern is launching in a premature market: the market is not yet mature and customers do not even recognize the problem. Metaphorically this is doing a business ten years too early (e.g., the early smartphone era).
Proposing advanced mobile experiences before they are widespread only raises enlightenment (education) costs if communication infrastructure and cultural literacy are not yet in place.
iPhone succeeded because of preceding market maturity: 3G proliferation and the new phone experience pioneered by BlackBerry.

Customers can typically imagine only one step ahead (early adopters bear that risk); two steps ahead has few acceptors. A wise strategy is to nurture the idea while first building a half-step-ahead preceding market.

Pitfall: selecting a market that has no real customers. Internal teams decide 'this would be convenient' without customer interviews or market research, producing products for imaginary users. This is the product-out trap (thinking 'how do we sell what we already made').

A common failure mode is the 'desk chimera' (机上のキメラ): stitching together company-convenient features into a fictional customer persona that barely exists. After launch this forces a pivot and redevelopment under technical debt. Especially common in large-company new-business units; startups more often avoid it because they must grow via customer/market validation.

Pitfall of unbalanced thinking when choosing a market: (1) neglecting information gathering and deciding by gut feel, looking only at domestic data and missing overseas de-facto standards (typical of inactive product managers); (2) over-analysis that delays decisions, thick documents, missed GO timing, and competitors pulling ahead (typical of unthinking product managers).
Inactive product managers and unthinking product managers are equally dangerous. Rhythmically cycle information collection + hypothesis validation with decision-making + learning.

Failure pattern 6: Overconfidence (慢心) causes a company to lose a winnable market. An initial success in correctly identifying a market becomes a curse: re-verification is neglected, strategy is not updated for environmental change, and defending the once-successful market becomes an end in itself.
Customer experience continues to update (example: AI utilization) while the provider’s product cannot change, so customer defection proceeds quietly rather than as a sudden collapse.

Recent example: SaaS vendors postpone AI embedding and integration; customers’ operations become AI-premised and the vendor misses the wave. A winnable market is chosen yet not won, largely because of an unwillingness to follow change.
All listed failure patterns begin from not inspecting premises (前提を点検しない).

Premises that must be continually checked: (1) Is the market actually growing, in both quantity and quality? (2) Where is the customer’s burning need (バーニングニーズ)—whose pain, at which moment? (3) What market advantage (MOAT) can the firm actually build—experience, provided value, revenue structure, data, operational assets? (4) Is that MOAT designed so that it strengthens over time?
Initiative and authority-delegation design is essential. In high-uncertainty areas, do the work yourself first to grasp the knack; once reproducibility appears, delegate appropriately.
Fulfilling accountability and stacking small promises builds the foundation that lets a team accept strong decision-making.
Knowing where the traps sit raises the odds of avoiding them and lets a team put a product into the market with greater conviction about the next move.
When choosing a market, do not run on passion alone; examine economic viability and whether there is a sound economic line (経済性の筋) that can sustain the business.
In a red ocean (highly competitive existing market), compete by designing a market advantage or economic moat (MOAT / 市場優位性) rather than undifferentiated rivalry.
Assess timing carefully and create or enter the market from half a step ahead (半歩先), rather than lagging or leaping too far ahead of demand.
Avoid building in a customer vacuum (顧客不在); go outside and validate with real customers instead of assuming demand internally.
Decision-making should be a reciprocating cycle: think then move, move then think (考えて動き、動いて考える), refining judgment through repeated action and reflection.
Do not rest after hitting a successful market; continuously update strategy rather than treating a win as permanent.
Chapter 1 of this material is titled Market Selection (市場選び) and frames these principles as the core of choosing where to compete.
Product owners/product managers are expected to be multi-skilled professionals who span broad domains such as engineering, business, and UX.

LIFE SHIFT (Linda Gratton and Andrew Scott, 2016) frames careers on a time axis under a 100-year-life premise; it is useful as a self-understanding tool for drawing the boundary between which specialties to deepen oneself and which to delegate to others (initiative vs. authority transfer).
The book helps synchronize one’s personal life strategy with the market strategy one should pursue.
Blue Ocean Strategy (W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, 2015 new edition) argues not how to win in existing (red ocean) markets, but how to design new markets that make competition itself irrelevant.

For product leaders, Blue Ocean thinking prevents falling into mere feature comparison or price competition, and trains strategic thinking about how to build a ‘win without fighting’ structure into the product.

Zero to One (Peter Thiel and Blake Masters, 2014) is built on the idea ‘Don’t compete—monopolize,’ and examines how to build overwhelming advantage from three angles: market structure, technology, and time axis.

Zero to One supplies a judgment framework for avoiding the failure of jumping into overcrowded markets, and for designing entry timing and differentiation strategy (MOAT) so that one’s own product can monopolize a market.

Marty Cagan’s INSPIRED is a practical bible for product management covering vision, market, customer understanding, team formation, and delivery; leaders should read it mainly for its strong-style philosophy.

Core idea from INSPIRED on responsibility: you can delegate correctly only because you grasp and can execute everything yourself; this warns against easy dumping of work and forces a product owner to re-examine how far they must keep the initiative.
Kazuto Ataka’s 『イシューからはじめよ』 teaches how to distinguish the essential question (イシュー) that must be solved from countless market problems that are merely noise.
For a product owner, market selection is the ability to set the right question (問いの設定力): raising the precision of what to let go and what to focus on (選択と集中).
That issue-first thinking is described as a thinking OS that should be installed so the owner can see what is worth thinking about.
Daniel Pink’s Motivation 3.0 explains spontaneous action through three internal conditions: autonomy (自律), mastery (熟達), and purpose (目的).

For product leaders managing specialized engineers and designers, people management is not primarily external rewards such as pay and titles, but designing intrinsic motivation and creating a state of trusting people enough to let them run on their own.
These three books together frame a product owner’s work as: owning the full scope of responsibility, choosing the right market/issue, and enabling a self-propelled team.
Chapter 2 covers the product owner's role in setting vision and driving business development after a market is chosen; the first step of strategy is answering Why me / Why now (なぜ自分 / なぜ今).

Why me / Why now are two axes: whether you can win if you yourself pursue the opportunity, and whether you can win if you pursue it now. These personal questions are the starting point of all strategy formulation.

People often associate strategy with frameworks or numerical models, but the initial strategy begins from extremely personal questions. Articulating Why me / Why now is the work of making strategy one's own.
When Why me / Why now is shared with the team, strategy stops being a mere document and becomes a shared will, forming the skeleton of a strong organization.
Even excellent ideas or attractive markets will cause the vision to fall apart if thinking on Why me / Why now is weak.
Example: An industry-wide shock such as logistics' 2024 problem is not necessarily a place to compete if the person has no interest or knowledge of logistics.

Example: Discovering innovative technology in R&D does not justify hasty commercialization if the current phase still requires deepening research rather than practical application; rushing leads to failure.
Therefore it is essential to carefully discern both 'why I should do it (Why me)' and 'why it is needed now (Why now)'.
Why me (自分がやるべき必然性) is the necessity or inevitability of why you yourself, rather than someone else, should undertake a particular business theme.

Three perspectives for considering Why me: (1) connection to original experience (原体験との接続), (2) connection to unique assets (独自の資産との接続), and (3) connection to ideology (思想との接続). These three overlapping create the necessity of you taking it on.

Original experience connection: whether the business theme connects to past pain, challenges, strong emotion, or attachment. Example: many medical-tech entrepreneurs have original experiences of a close person's illness or nursing; the reason it must be you often lives here.

Unique assets connection: assets mean network, technology, experience, and domain knowledge (not financial assets). Even if many people pursue the same theme, almost no one can pursue it with the same structure; this non-substitutability (非代替性) is the core of Why me.

Ideology connection: even if original experience and unique assets are in place, you cannot finish the run if they contradict the social change you want to create. Articulating how you want to improve the world through the product attracts the team and generates user empathy.
Verbalization of Why me is aided by storytelling in the sequence: past (original experience) → present (strengths/assets) → future.
Diagram 2-1 (Why me構成要素) places Why me at the center of the three connections: original experience, unique assets, and ideology.
Speak of the desired future (the world you want to realize) as one coherent story/line. The clearer this story is, the less the team wavers and the more consistent decision-making becomes.

Why now is the necessity of pursuing the venture at this particular timing. Starting too early yields neither empathy nor monetization; starting too late lets pioneers capture the market. Discern the rationality and alignment of the external environment with timing.
Why now has three main components: (1) changes in technology, institutions, and infrastructure; (2) changes in society and culture; (3) changes in competitive environment and industrial structure.

Technology/institution/infrastructure component: Check whether conditions for realization are now in place due to new technology, regulatory/institutional development, or infrastructure spread. If technology leads but institutions lag, the business will not launch; if institutions are ready but technology is immature, ROI is thin. Examples such as ride-sharing, Web3, and generative AI show that a market window opens the moment they exceed the critical point of social implementation.

Society/culture component: Check whether the business fits trends in values, work styles, and consumption behavior. Even the same 'attendance management' product requires completely different experiences under a Showa-era labor view (assuming 24-hour operation) versus a Reiwa-era view (where side jobs and remote work are normal). Read social nuances and identify unfulfilled pain.

Competitive environment/industrial structure component: Identify what breakthrough can be opened in a market where existing players are saturated or rigid. Cases of new players defeating established firms via AI/DX are increasing; overseas entrants (e.g., Netflix as a 'black ship' in video streaming) can transform local markets. Capturing the seams of industrial structure is essential.

Thinking about Why now means discerning which position you occupy on the wave of change. Being too early (before the wave) or too late (after it has passed) are both too late. Preparation and judgment are required to get on the board at the rising moment.

Why now is composed of three elements: (1) changes in technology, institutions, and infrastructure; (2) changes in society and culture; (3) changes in the competitive environment and industrial structure.

Why me and Why now are each insufficient on their own. Even if the personal reason to act is strong, the venture will not last without market tailwinds. Conversely, even if timing is perfect, you cannot win unless you can stand as unique (唯一無二) in that market. Combining both axes produces the core of business strategy: Why this business.

Once the two axes are verbalized, judgment criteria for market selection, product design, and team composition stay consistent. The same compass then guides daily priorities, investment allocation, and whether to pivot.

Why me / Why now comparison (図表2-3): Starting point — Why me: original experience, strengths, and philosophy; Why now: changes in technology, society, and industry. Meaning — Why me: the necessity that you specifically must do it; Why now: the necessity that it must be done now. Effect — Why me: raises the team’s conviction; Why now: gains empathy from outside stakeholders.

Carefully articulating Why me and Why now naturally surfaces why the business exists; that purpose becomes the vision. Vision is not a top-down slogan; it emerges by refining questions. Products wrapped in this purpose context carry energy that goes beyond short-term KPIs.

Example purpose statements: wanting to reduce the number of people who share the same pain through one's own original experience; wanting to define the next generation's way of working precisely because social structural change is happening now.

When you can answer Why me and Why now in your own words, strategy design has already begun. From there, design the structure for talking about the vision: who empathizes, how they empathize, and how they act.

Business development in this book is not merely creating new products or features. It is combining the market issues already identified with the company's strengths (Why me / Why now) to design and construct a business mechanism that sustainably generates value and profit.

The first requirement for business development is collecting seeds of business ideas. Ideas here are not flashes of inspiration or random thoughts; they are crystallizations of thinking born from experience and knowledge. Product managers' ideation power is determined by how many business fragments they hold from observation and accumulation, and how they reconstruct them.

Observe successful cases not only in one's own industry but in other industries and overseas markets; analyze their factors, abstract them, and cycle through reinterpretation. Do not imitate success cases. Structurally understand why they worked and translate that into your own company's context. This translation ability is the largest differentiator of product-manager skill.
成功事例を溜めるには、観察と整理を日常の習慣にする3つのステップが推奨される（図表2-4）。
ステップ1：毎日1プロダクト、1事業を観察する。日々のニュースやトレンドを追う中で、少なくとも1日ひとつは気になるプロダクトを実際に触る。UI・UX・導線・価格などを観察し、「なぜこの体験が成功しているのか」「どんな顧客価値を提供しているのか」を考える。この観察思考を続けるだけで、発想の引き出しが驚くほど増える。
ステップ2：事業モデルを分解してストックする。そのプロダクトのビジネスモデルを自分なりに分解し、メモツールやスプレッドシートに記録する。慣れるまでは書き出すことが大切。頭の中で整理するよりも、一度外に出すことで構造化され、記憶にも定着する。価格設計、顧客獲得の導線、マネタイズモデルなど、共通構造を見つける感覚を養う。
ステップ3：成功要因を「どのレイヤー」で捉えるかを言語化する。その事例の成功は「顧客課題の解決」なのか、「テクノロジー活用」なのか、「収益構造の革新」なのか。どのレイヤーが鍵だったのかを明確に言語化する。これを続けていくと、成功の共通点や、自分が関心を持つ業界のパターンが見えてくる。成功を理解しているつもりから、構造として理解している状態へ移行できる。
Accumulating the habit of case analysis enables instant judgment of which existing pattern a new business most closely resembles.
Business is never reinventing the wheel; most new value is created by borrowing predecessors' wisdom, changing it slightly, and shifting it slightly. A stock of wisdom is therefore a prerequisite.
Idea accumulation need not be solitary: teams should share learning and convert success cases into knowledge assets so ideas become collective creativity rather than personal.

Practical team mechanisms include: operating a tagged case database (e.g., Notion or Miro) covering UX, business models, and organizational structures; holding monthly 5-minute product-observation sharing sessions with discussion; and building a hypothesis catalog that multiplies stocked cases by the company's own strengths to list the next experiments to run.

The next critical skill after accumulation is reconstituting success cases as reusable templates fitted to one's own context. This requires both translation ability and redesign/editing ability—the capacity to combine an understood case with the company's strengths.

People who find other-company cases uninspiring or inapplicable usually treat them as someone else's story. The corrective is to observe subjectively, asking 'If I were the person responsible for this business, how would I think?'

Observation becomes strategy-applicable learning when divided into three explicit perspectives (referenced as Figure 2-5). Absorbing cases as lived experience rather than as documents determines the depth of learning for a product owner.
Three perspectives for turning other companies' case studies into learning: (1) observe through tactile/hands-on experience, (2) observe through structure, (3) observe through philosophy/thought.
Hand-feel observation (手触りで観る): actually experience the product as a user. Using it for several days makes the UX design philosophy become naturally visible.

Structural observation (構造で観る): analyze why the company was able to grow using numbers, time axes, and organizational structure. Tracing the evolution from business launch to the present enables understanding of the growth mechanism.
Philosophical observation (思想で観る): relive the vision, decision-making, and failure stories spoken by founders and executives. Mentally simulate 'If I were this founder, how would I have judged?'
When redesigning success cases one approaches the problem of imitation; imitation has good and bad forms.
Bad imitation is superficial copying. Merely imitating design or features without understanding the underlying philosophy will not produce results.

Example of bad imitation: even if one imitates the gig/part-time matching (スキマバイト) market and only raises matching accuracy, Timee's (タイミー) essential strengths cannot be reproduced. Timee's value lies in its sales organization going directly into customer stores and building trust through on-site DX support; imitating the product surface cannot reproduce that core.
Good imitation means redesigning the mechanisms, philosophy, and context so as to raise reproducibility.

Imitation that starts as copying can produce originality once a company's own context accumulates; especially useful is imitation from other industries (structural hybridization as a seed of innovation).
Example: a SaaS company adopting LTV design and gamification from the game industry to raise product stickiness (users stay and use habitually rather than churn).
Example: a D2C brand learning SaaS-style subscription design to increase repeat purchases.
Good imitation is not mere copying: it must stay consistent with 'Why me' and 'Why now', deciding what can be transferred and what must be discarded.

When transferring practices, consider not only technical feasibility but also downsides and industry-specific constraints; a monetization structure that works elsewhere can harm customer experience in one's own market, and simple copying can infringe business-model patents.
What is required is editorial skill: reconstruct by combining the borrowed element with the company's own strengths.
A product leader is an editor of the business: take worldwide success cases as raw material and recompose them in the context of the company's strategy, market, and philosophy.
Leaders who drive a business must run the cycle observe → abstract → implement with high accuracy and continuity.

Good imitation: redesign mechanisms, philosophy, and context and localize them to the company; the object is underlying principles, structure, and essential strengths; the result is higher reproducibility and eventual originality as own context accumulates.
Bad imitation: superficial copy of visible design or features; the core is not reproduced and results are hard to achieve.
In the startup or new-business launch phase, the boundary between PM (Product Manager) and BizDev (business development) often becomes ambiguous, producing three frequent misconceptions.

Misconception 1 — PM becomes BizDev-ized and loses the customer perspective: rushing growth leads to prioritizing market or company convenience and over-weighting sales/revenue design; deep exploration of customer problems and continuity of value delivery thin out, causing PMF opportunities to be missed.

Misconception 2 — BizDev invades the PM domain via external pressure: stacking short-term requests such as “if we build this feature it will sell” turns the product into a collection of individually optimized pieces; long-term UX improvement is postponed and a chimeric, hard-to-use product results.

Misconception 3 — diffusion of responsibility produces middle-management-ization: neither party states final accountability, so decisions delay; the field waits for dual approvals and stalls under contradictory instructions. The countermeasure is to document responsibility demarcation points and decision-making authority in writing.
PM and BizDev possess essentially different thinking axes for realizing a vision, even though both ultimately aim to maximize business value.

PM approach (customer-origin): starts by sincerely facing customer problems and continuously delivering value; polishing a sustainable experience maximizes user value, after which business results follow.

BizDev approach (market/revenue-origin): starts by exploring market opportunities, designing the revenue structure, and formulating growth strategy; it captures the joint between the company’s strengths and market structure in order to create business results.
PM and BizDev are complementary rather than competitive; they climb the same mountain of business-value maximization by different routes.

PM and BizDev work as a pair (二人三脚): PM polishes the product and maximizes customer value through continuous value delivery, while BizDev opens markets and maximizes business value via revenue structure and expansion strategy. Together they simultaneously raise customer-provided value and the company's own business value.
Designing the overlap between PM and BizDev roles and clarifying decision-making responsibility points is the watershed (分水嶺) that determines whether an organization grows.

PM creates differentiation by deepening customer experience; BizDev creates growth opportunities by expanding market structure. Both share the same summit of business success. Understanding which axis each role stands on (rather than treating them as superior/inferior) prevents confusion inside the team.

Ideal collaboration does not fragment roles but designs overlap while assuming some misalignment of focus. Under a shared North Star Metric (NSM / ノーススターメトリクス), each party's contribution route is made explicit.
SaaS example of shared NSM: ARR and retention (continuation) as common goals.

Comparison of PM vs BizDev (図表2-7): Goal for both is maximizing business value, but PM approaches it via maximizing user/customer value first, while BizDev approaches it via maximizing the company's own business value first.
PM looks at: customers, experience, data, specifications. BizDev looks at: market, revenue, partners, contracts.
Time horizon: PM is middle-to-long (product growth); BizDev is short-to-middle (revenue and expansion).
Success metrics: PM uses PMF, NPS, retention rate, UX improvement. BizDev uses ARR, sales, market share, ROI.
Deliverables: PM produces product, features, and experience. BizDev produces business model, revenue scheme, and partnerships.

When ARR and retention rate are the goals, PM contributes via experience improvement and retention-rate improvement, while BizDev contributes via market development and channel/partnerships (see collaboration design around NSM/KPI trees).
Visualizing NSM (North Star Metric) and KPI trees reduces daily confusion about priorities and investment allocation.

PM should provide BizDev with: evidence of customer value (qualitative and quantitative); results of customer interviews and hypothesis validation; and high-resolution customer segments needed for GTM (Go-to-Market). Showing why something is valuable with verified facts strengthens business judgment.
