A dual-axis leader must integrate three viewpoints (Figure 4-2): the business perspective (PM-like viewpoint), the people perspective (People Management), and the technology/organization perspective (EM-like viewpoint).

Leaders need to integrate three perspectives—business, technology, and people—because each in isolation is insufficient: business alone yields unrealistic plans (“pie in the sky”), technology alone yields craftsman temperament, and people alone yields kindness without growth.
Dual-axis leaders (二軸リーダー) who can cross and integrate these three perspectives are required for effective organizations.
A dual-axis leader who can translate between business language and technology language makes conversations with executives, CFOs, and BizDev far smoother.

Technical debt should be framed as an investment in profit improvement: not mere code cleanup or engineer convenience, but reduced future maintenance cost, faster time-to-market for new features, and improved mid-to-long-term gross profit.

UX improvement should be framed as LTV improvement: not just making screens easier to use, but lower churn (churn rate), reduced user frustration, greater attachment, and higher lifetime value per user.

Architecture rebuild should be framed as optimization of development “fuel efficiency”: not a technical ego desire for modern systems, but reduced infrastructure cost, higher output per engineer, and lower barriers to hiring engineers—as a multi-layered business strategy.

Dual-axis leaders fundamentally resolve PM–EM conflict by creating a structure in which one person holds final judgment rather than pushing responsibility, thereby unifying decision axes (e.g., when to pay down technical debt relative to engineering load in business growth).
Engineering leaders must continuously manage trade-offs such as whether to chip away at issues in daily development or dedicate concentrated time solely to rearchitecture.
A core trade-off is balancing engineers’ desire to resolve technical debt or try new frameworks against the business’s implementation priority ranking.
Another trade-off is short-term revenue-generating customer requests that diverge from the product vision versus realizing a mid-to-long-term worldview and roadmap.
Organizational load management requires weighing temporary overtime for important feature releases against the risk that such load becomes the organizational norm.
A coherent story spanning business strategy → technology roadmap → team structure → why the candidate joins significantly raises hiring and development quality.
Closing the loop of hiring → onboarding → training → evaluation → business strategy without misalignment creates organizational reproducibility and dramatically faster growth.
Two-axis leaders (those who simultaneously see business phase and organizational phase while balancing offense and defense) are scarce.
Required skill: ability to understand technical structure at the level of principles so one can participate in technology selection.

Required skill: financial and management literacy (P&L, cash flow, gross margin, ROI) so technical investment and debt repayment can be translated for executives not as mere cost but as future profit generation (“fuel-efficiency improvement”).
Required skill: strategy-building power—articulating why now (market change plus company strengths: Why me / Why now).
Leaders need people-management capability (hiring, development, culture): place talent by working backward from strategy, guarantee psychological safety, and promote members' autonomous growth.
Decision-making transparency: verbalize not only the conclusion but the background and constraints that led to the judgment, thereby accumulating team trust.

Ability to explain priority-setting criteria: confront QCDS (Quality, Cost, Delivery, Scope) trade-offs and logically explain, from a business-results viewpoint, what will not be done (what will be sacrificed).

Phase-specific strategic flexibility: update fighting style and one's own role (the boundary of authority delegation) according to the growth stage of the business/organization (e.g., 0-to-1 versus growth phase).

A leader who carries both business and organization cannot personally execute everything; they need people to whom they can 'entrust their back'—people who can be trusted with judgment and who share the same decision-making criteria.
In product-development organizations the conventional HR model (HR owning hiring, onboarding, evaluation, and exit end-to-end) does not function as it does for most other job families.
Structural reasons include a long-standing complete seller's market for engineers and PMs, and the fact that senior talent can individually multiply business impact by 10x or 100x.

In competitive tech hiring, companies fight over a small high-end talent pool. Strong engineers and PMs can receive ~100 scout emails per day simply by setting their job-site status to 'open to conversation.'

To win such candidates, three things are required: (1) communication grounded in technical and product context, (2) the ability to articulate the product vision and the company’s longer-term plans, and (3) a high-quality candidate experience across interviews, selection, and offers.

At this talent tier, companies that fully outsource recruiting to HR typically fall out of the candidate’s consideration set. Strong business or compensation is not enough if the message never reaches or never lands.

This pressure produced DevHR / TechHR: people with engineer, designer, or PM experience who also own recruiting, development, and org-building inside (or tightly with) the product organization. Forms vary—embedded in product vs. partnering with HR—but the role exists because generic HR cannot carry the technical and product conversation.
Product-development leaders must deliberately design three things: how much to leave to whom, what they themselves keep, and which decision criteria must be shared.

The needed profile is not a specialist clone of the boss but a complementary partner with cross-domain capability. Alignment on values, strategy, and product philosophy is the premise; together they define a level of trust closer to 'can be entrusted' than mere 'delegation.'

HR staff alone often cannot fully handle engineering talent and product-development culture because most HR professionals lack engineering experience and therefore struggle to understand technical context.

Engineers, PMs, and designers grow up in a distinct professional ecosystem unlike other occupations: contribution to tech communities is valued, people routinely attend conferences and study sessions at night, and outputs such as talks, OSS contributions, and blogs function as career credentials.

These behaviors can look mysterious to other professions, but they are rational: technology advances faster than textbooks and commercial books, and web search often yields only abstract information rather than usable know-how.

Study groups and communities therefore developed as venues for sharing battle-tested knowledge, exchanging anti-patterns and failure stories so the industry as a whole avoids reinventing the wheel, and meeting peers beyond the boundaries of one’s job.

In Tokyo, dozens to hundreds of such events occur even on weekdays; they produce not only learning but also everyday communication with community peers, referral hiring that bypasses job boards, and mutual understanding strong enough that people want to work together.
Those community relationships feed directly into hiring and career decisions.

HR people who treat events as recruiting venues and only pitch, scatter business cards, and hand out pamphlets violate the spirit of mutual learning and mutual aid, and are often shunned by the community.
The atmosphere of these communities can only be felt by people who have actually participated and contributed.
Understanding the (tech/product) ecosystem is a prerequisite for recruitment activities.
DevHR / TechHR refers to HR professionals who come from an engineering background or have a strong understanding of engineering.

Roles of DevHR/TechHR include: technical recruitment (requirements definition through scouting and interview design); design and operation of evaluation systems for engineers and PMs; system design for productivity improvement (focus time, review culture, tool introduction, etc.); connecting technology roadmaps with recruitment plans; talent allocation design by product phase; and recruitment/technical PR (tech blogs, hosting study sessions, supporting conference talks, etc.).

A new problem arises if DevHR/TechHR becomes too independent: it can become disconnected from company-wide HR, producing perceived unfairness such as rising engineer salary levels, preferential-looking career paths, and higher work flexibility only in the product organization.
Product-organization uniqueness is necessary, but overall balance and accountability are also required; therefore the product owner/leader is important as a bridge between DevHR/TechHR and core HR.
The team that owns recruitment and HR strategy for a product development organization needs the multiplication (combination) of three specializations.
HR alone cannot move a technical organization; management alone cannot create reproducibility in hiring and development; engineering alone cannot arrange organizational sustainability.
A product-development HR strategy team that people can fully trust (背中を預けられる) is formed only by combining three specializations: HR expertise, engineering expertise, and management expertise.

HR expertise includes recruitment-process design: designing the full funnel from awareness and recall through casual-interview applications, multiple interviews, offer, and joining, plus communication design among all people involved.
HR expertise includes evaluation and grade systems: promotion/demotion requirements defined in alignment with the organization’s expectations of each individual.
HR expertise includes labor and compliance: preventing excessive labor load on a subset of talent (overtime bias) and preventing/handling daily communication errors including harassment.
HR expertise includes compensation and offer design: pay structures that match both organizational and individual expectations, plus the end-to-end experience design up to the actual offer.

Management expertise includes aligning strategy with organizational structure: designing expansion or contraction of organizations and teams according to company/business scale and executing reverse-calculated actions.

Management expertise includes role definition and responsibility-range design: assigning roles to teams and individuals (including leaders) according to their talents, defining the domains they should own, and then aligning expectations with each person.

Team building and onboarding design involves defining and executing actions needed to build team relationships, sometimes promoting autonomous movement within the team, and designing/executing so that new members fit into the team.

Performance management means creating conditions where high performers can work comfortably while also handling mentoring or reassignment of low performers, so that overall organizational performance stays high through design and execution.
Engineering understanding for this role includes grasping the company's tech stack, architecture, and data flows, plus current trends and popular languages/frameworks in the hiring market.

Required talent differs by product phase: 0-to-1 business launch, existing business that has reached PMF and is scaling, new-business launch, or a combination of these; people who thrive in one phase may not in another.
It is important to understand the technical-debt and productivity issues that engineers discuss daily.
Unlike other professions, engineering has a distinctive community culture; mutual sharing, public output, and interaction are useful for catching up on technology.
In practice few people master all three specializations at a high level, so a realistic structure is three complementary key people: the product owner, DevHR/TechHR, and the HR leader.
Those three must communicate continuously while covering four points, the first of which is respecting each other's expertise.

Product leaders must clearly define what kind of DevHR/TechHR they want to rely on, what they expect from HR, and which parts of organization design they want to co-create, then actively search for such partners.
If practical work can be entrusted to capable DevHR/TechHR plus HR staff, the product leader can concentrate more on how to grow the business.

The needed right-hand person is not a mere recruiter or general HR staffer: they understand the ecosystem of a product-development organization, rest on both HR expertise and management expertise, grasp technical structure, and can connect strategy with organization.
Finding and developing such a partner is one of the most important jobs of a future product leader.

Connecting engineering and HR requires translating each side’s language, keeping legal/regulatory and institutional-design constraints in mind as non-negotiable conditions, and keeping employer branding consistent from the candidate’s viewpoint.
This coordination is extremely high-difficulty; many companies have ended up with distorted organization design because it failed.
Chapter summary presents six failure patterns of talent strategy and people management.

Failure pattern 1 (most common): shallow definition of hiring requirements produces mismatch. What looks like merely poor verbalization actually exposes an underlying deficiency in organizational strategy itself.
A typical sub-pattern is that strategy and hiring requirements are not linked, so the company ends up hiring people who merely ‘look excellent’ rather than people who fit the real strategy.

Hiring failures often stem from inability to hire the right people because job descriptions (ジョブディスクリプション) are too abstract: required abilities, roles, and expected outcomes are vague, causing interviewer evaluation criteria to vary widely.

A common hiring mistake is over-seeking a 'jack-of-all-trades' (万能型) candidate by confusing currently needed capabilities with those required for a later business phase; demanding someone who can do everything results in no candidate fitting.
Vague or fuzzy hiring requirements and roles mean that even highly capable candidates fail to mesh with the position.

Mismatch between business phase and hired talent is a major failure pattern: hiring someone because they 'might thrive in the future' can destroy the current organization; over-emphasizing diversity can also produce phase mismatch.
In the startup/launch phase, hiring people suited to a growth phase often backfires: they avoid hands-on work, focus only on systematization, collide with the existing organization, and resign.
When the need is to repay technical debt, hiring people who only want to do new development means they avoid essential problems, leaving the team exhausted.

Placing people whose only experience is at large corporations into a chaotic environment with undeveloped processes leaves them unable to self-start; they become isolated and turn into organizational debt.

Even high-ability people should not be hired if their values or behavioral standards do not fit the culture: a 'brilliant jerk' (ブリリアント・ジャーク) who delivers results but disrupts cooperation will destroy organizational culture.
Leaders whose decision-making criteria or sense of speed do not match the organization generate friction and can cause the team to collapse.
Neglecting non-skill areas such as learning attitude, sincerity/honesty, and ownership worsens workplace atmosphere and slows the speed of the entire organization.
An insufficient or poorly designed recruitment process directly leads to hiring mistakes.

Common recruitment-process failures include: conducting only formal interviews without deep questioning; interviewers having unaligned expectations so they repeat the same questions; not using case studies or assignments, so reproducible thinking cannot be verified; non-unified evaluation criteria that let interviewer bias dominate; and rushing so that the team compromises on a merely ‘better-than-nothing’ candidate instead of the person actually wanted.
Inserting personal emotion into decisions produces systematic judgment errors in hiring and people management.
Atmosphere hiring (selecting someone because they ‘click’ or the conversation is lively) is described as the most dangerous emotional-hiring pattern.
High expressed motivation or ‘heat/passion’ does not guarantee subsequent performance or success.
Emotional loyalty to existing members—failing to demote, reassign, or otherwise act on under-performers, or giving them roles above their actual contribution—reduces organizational productivity.
Inability to let go of people who should leave commonly occurs when evaluation systems and expected roles are vague, so the criteria for termination remain unclear.

Post-hire evaluation itself becomes distorted: over-raising expectations before the person joins prevents calm assessment; managers continue hoping ‘they will grow soon’ even when no progress is visible.
When hiring standards keep being lowered, the capability level of the entire organization can decline as a result.
A compounded failure pattern occurs when a hiring mistake is noticed but emotion (情) prevents corrective action; at that stage it is no longer merely a hiring failure but an organizational failure.

Typical symptoms of this compounded pattern include: repeated reassignment cycles described as an 'prayer rotation' (お祈りローテーション); a sharp drop in team productivity; high performers becoming exhausted from caring for mismatched hires and then quitting; collapse of organizational culture and a ruined employer/hiring brand.

Hiring and HR failures occur with high probability when multiple root causes compound: (1) hiring requirements are not connected to strategy; (2) the structure of talent—ability × will × fit/compatibility—is not understood and people are judged by skills alone; (3) hiring proceeds without understanding the organization's phase; (4) evaluation and expectations are vague, so HR and the front line use different standards; (5) product owners/leaders abdicate hiring by dumping it on others; (6) information asymmetry creates illusions and insufficient understanding of candidates; (7) leaders are poor at painful decisions such as termination or rejection.

Prevention requires putting the book's practices into action: reverse-engineer hiring requirements from strategy; define required capabilities clearly according to organizational phase; and place strong weight on culture and values fit.
Hiring (採用) is continuous decision-making, just like business strategy; the lower the quality of those decisions, the more the organization collapses.
To avoid hiring mismatches and emotion-driven judgments, managers must understand strategy, structure, and psychology, then judge calmly.
Confirm reproducible thinking by using case studies and deep questions.
Build mechanisms that separate emotion (情) from facts when making judgments.
Resolve information asymmetry in hiring and evaluation.
Develop managers who can make painful decisions when necessary.
Chapter 4 topic: 人事戦略とピープルマネジメント (HR strategy and people management).
For product owners, hiring is the highest-leverage investment, yet interviewers frequently fail due to personal bias or vague intuition that a candidate 'seems talented.'

People should be evaluated three-dimensionally across layers such as skills, thinking characteristics, and guts (胆力) rather than surface resumes; systematic profiling can reveal a person's essential energy and potential toxicity (mines).

A legendary coach of Google and Apple CEOs taught how to unite highly specialized top talent by combining strict commitment to business goals with deep personal care that creates psychological safety, thereby maximizing engineer and designer performance and psychologically bonding the team.

Community-style organizations (exemplified by GitHub and Ubuntu) can be built so members act autonomously and human synergies continually emerge, generating passionate belonging and spontaneous collaboration.
Organizations can be upgraded from a traditional 'managing' model to a co-creating community in which members contribute of their own accord.
A small elite team can deliver maximum value; the belief that adding more people automatically increases development speed is an illusion to be rejected.
Constraint management (制約のマネジメント) means discarding wasteful meetings, excess features, and an obsession with scale in order to concentrate only on truly important core value.
Personnel load and burn rate (燃焼速度) should be optimized so that healthy logistics (兵站) can be maintained over time.
These ideas form a strong antithesis to conventional scaling-and-staffing thinking and are associated with the practices of Basecamp (formerly 37signals).
The recommended source is the complete edition of “小さなチーム、大きな仕事” by Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson (Hayakawa, 2012).
Chapter 4 of the surrounding text addresses personnel strategy and people management.
Chapter 5 covers project management and agile as closely related topics for driving tactics and executing strategy. The author treats them as foundational to turning strategy into execution.

The author's first encounter with project management came when moving from engineer to team lead, working with external SI vendors. Communication broke down via a 'telephone game,' decision-making became dispersed, and the Why (purpose) of what was being built failed to propagate. This caused deliverable direction to drift and quality to decline.
Those failures prompted ongoing study of what kinds of communication and relationships allow a project to proceed correctly.
Agile and Scrum entered the author's life in the same period (study groups, speaking, community organizing) and became formative elements of their professional identity.

In this book, Agile is defined not as a mere system-development process but as 'a way of thinking and a structure for maximizing the speed of strategy execution by rapidly repeating hypotheses and adaptations under high uncertainty.'

Scrum is presented as one concrete framework (mechanism) for practicing that Agile thinking in the field: the team repeatedly plans, executes, and retrospects in short timeboxes (sprints) in order to maximize product value.
Project management (プロジェクトマネジメント) refers to a project's rules and role assignments; it is a foundational, unavoidable skill for a product owner (プロダクト責任者).

Product management is a perpetual activity that continues as long as the product exists and ends only when the product itself ends. Project management is time-boxed work to deliver outcomes for a specific period and purpose. Neither is hierarchically above the other; they mutually encompass each other.

It is common for specific projects to run in service of one product's growth. Conversely, a single project (e.g., exhibition preparation or year-end sales) can contain multiple instances of product management.
Project management is required for all work and cuts across time management, quality management, stakeholder management, and the other domains treated in the book.

Projects are living things: unexpected events are normal, so priority design that anticipates them is essential. Visualizing 'where we are heading' (e.g., with an Inception Deck; see section 5-2) is an effective practice.

Calling a product manager 'PdM' is Japan-specific. Strong SI culture had already established 'PM' for project manager, so PdM arose to distinguish the roles. Globally, Product Manager is written PM and project-progress roles are often Program Manager (PgM); at Google, PM and PgM sit side by side, splitting project execution from value delivery.

Japan's 'PM = project manager' usage differs from the global terminology system. The author uses 'product manager = PM' in this book because consistency of terms is directly tied to consistency of decision-making.
Even an excellent strategy is meaningless unless it is applied in the field with high reproducibility.
In product development organizations, strategy failing to translate into execution is the greatest cause of organizational collapse and product stagnation.
Product leaders must therefore build a bridge between strategy and the field.
Strategy is the decision of which battlefield to fight on and which winning path (勝ち筋) to choose.
Execution is the work of making concrete what the team should do today.

Common gaps between strategy and execution include: strategy that is too abstract for the field to own; goals without descending priorities; daily tasks causing the overall strategy to be forgotten; KPI meanings not being shared; and field voices not being reflected, causing divergence from strategy.
These gaps indicate missing infrastructure for operating strategy.
Product development is high-complexity intellectual collaboration; no mechanism automatically translates strategy into action, so a foundation for converting strategy into daily behavior is required.
There are three layers for translating strategy into execution.
Layer 1 is verbalization of strategy (clarifying Why/What). When strategy is clear, the field can judge autonomously.

Example of verbalized strategy: which market (startup industry); which customers (lone, struggling one-person information-systems departments); what value to deliver (account creation/deletion accompanying large volumes of joining and leaving).
A product roadmap is not merely a feature-implementation schedule; it is a statement of priorities and intent that connects vision and strategy to daily development tasks (the backlog).
The roadmap is drawn once customer problems are visible and a strategy exists for whose problems to solve and in what order.
A roadmap is not fixed after it is drawn; it is a living document that is continually updated in response to market change and customer feedback.
Agile organizations must distinguish what must not change from what should change.

Example quarterly theme: complete API integration with 30 major SaaS products used by startups and establish the foundation for automatic account provisioning (automatic issuance and deletion) at join/leave.
Example milestone: in month 1, focus on SaaS with the highest usage frequency among domestic startups.

Hierarchy for translating strategy into execution: (1) verbalizing strategy (clarifying Why/What), (2) structuring strategy (roadmap and placement on a time axis), (3) execution foundation (agile operations and ceremonies).
Investment focus for integration: increase as far as possible the types of software that can be linked, chosen from those managed by the information-systems department.

SaaS integration rollout timeline: after selecting the top 30 services and completing API specification and integration-requirements research, month 2 implements integrations with the top 15 (Google Workspace, Slack, Notion, etc.) plus beta tests with some customers; month 3 finishes the remaining 15, polishes the UI, and does production release to all users.

Desired outcome of the identity/provisioning product: the information-systems team can finish onboarding/offboarding account issuance and deletion across many SaaS products in one click instead of logging into each service, driving simple operational hours nearly to zero and removing security risk from forgotten leaver accounts.

KPIs for the 30 new SaaS connectors: monthly active companies using the new integration features; monthly count of automatic account issuance/deletion executions via the integrations; error rate at integration-setup time (target below a stated percentage).
KPOs (qualitative success measures): high usability scores from beta customers on “ease of setup”; UX that lets users finish connector configuration without opening the help pages.
Execution foundation (実行基盤) is the set of daily-operating mechanisms (especially Agile ceremonies) that let a team move forward without hesitation.

Sprint planning example: convert work into a short, concrete goal such as “this sprint implement Google Workspace and Slack automatic account provisioning (issue/delete) and complete test-environment verification.”

Sprint review: at sprint end, demo the implemented connectors to PM or Customer Success and collect feedback against real customer use cases (e.g., “when offboarding is executed, is the Slack account immediately suspended?”).

Retrospective example: capture process lessons such as “vendor A’s API docs were outdated and investigation overran estimates; next time insert a technical-verification task before development starts.”

Priority-setting rules for choosing the next SaaS integration use explicit criteria: number of requests from existing customers (impact/scope), API availability and development difficulty (cost), and security/governance importance, to rank the backlog.

Definition of Done is a team-agreed standard of releasable quality, not merely writing code. Examples include: code review passed, automated tests cleared, successful staging integration tests for account issuance/deletion, and a draft of the user-facing help page created.

Daily Scrum is a fixed-time ~15-minute daily sync to share progress and blockers so work does not stall. Example updates: yesterday Slack API integration was implemented; today Notion integration starts; the team is blocked by Notion API limits and wants expert input.
High-performing organizations share decision-making literacy: strategy-originated prioritization, transparency of decisions, shared understanding of KPIs, and acceleration of feedback loops.
The essence of Agile is increasing learning speed: field learning is reflected back into strategy, and the strategy itself is continuously updated.

Agile is not merely a cycling technique. It is a structure that maximizes strategy execution speed and adaptability under uncertainty. Fixing a plan in an uncertain environment only drives toward a future in which failure is already determined.

Customer understanding deepens during development; markets constantly change; LLM models can become obsolete in 1–3 months. Therefore strategy must be updated through team learning. Teams must verify in small cycles and keep learning while holding both successes and failures at the same time.
Strategy and execution are connected by people: the PM reads market change; the EM balances technical and organizational constraints (the designer role is introduced as the next actor in that chain).

In product organizations, designers maximize customer experience while engineers embody (realize) value. Strategy execution is a collaboration of knowledge across functions; the product owner’s role is to design this ecosystem.

The product ecosystem to design includes: shared recognition (共通認識) that company/business goals are common; a common language (共通言語) so KPIs and goals are expressed in the same words; trust (信頼) that others will professionally complete their work at high quality; and psychological safety (心理的安全性) so people can constructively discuss views that differ from their own.

Project management is the skeleton that connects strategy and the field. It verbalizes strategy, structures it, drops it into an execution foundation, and continues learning in an agile way. When this flow is in place, the product gains a pulse; organizations with a stable pulse continuously create value.
In project management that turns strategy into execution, the most important task is to balance QCDS and make priorities explicit.

QCDS: Quality (quality, completeness, reliability); Cost (budget, effort, people, and all investable resources); Delivery (deadlines, speed, time until value reaches the customer); Scope (range of features and requirements—how far to go).

Modern software development assumes continuous updates rather than one-time delivery. This makes it possible to design where the first version sits and what will be recovered later, so the entire QCDS set (including scope) can be treated as adjustable levers.
The Inception Deck is used to set QCDS priorities in strategy-to-execution project management.
QCDS (Quality, Cost, Delivery, Scope) cannot all be maximized at the same time; treating “satisfy all of QCDS” as obvious is unrealistic.
Leaving “everything is important / everything is priority” unaddressed makes the team rigid: a no-failure atmosphere forms and unsustainable working styles become the norm.

A state started for short-term results can quietly become permanent and turn into a death march; the best people leave first, quality itself then fails, and an organization that has lost sustainability ultimately cannot produce anything.
Setting priority means deciding what to sacrifice. If that choice stays vague, the project cannot move forward.
Projects always run under constraints; Q, C, D, and S are always in a trade-off relationship.
Priority must be an explicit decision, not intuition. It has to be shared as a common reference so every member can return to it when judgment is unclear.
The “right” QCDS mix changes by phase and timing.

QCDS always shifts during a project. Not all constraints are visible at kickoff; premises often change (budget cuts, policy changes, competitors shipping a better product faster than expected, customers revealing strong value in existing features, or sudden feasibility from technology such as AI).
Launch phase may reasonably prioritize cost and delivery while sacrificing quality and scope to some degree.
Around product–market fit, not lowering quality may be prioritized in order to win customer trust.
In the growth phase, adding and removing scope becomes more important. Even for the same product, priority order changes with the period.
Because these variables can arrive at unknown times, the team needs a judgment axis so it does not freeze when change happens.
An Inception Deck is an effective tool for agreeing on QCDS (Quality, Cost, Delivery, Scope) priorities with the team and stakeholders.

An Inception Deck is a consensus-building document created at the start of an agile product development project and updated as the project progresses; it can be viewed as a modern update of the traditional project charter.
The Inception Deck covers two main areas: Why (why the work is being done) and How (how it will be done).

Why-related elements of the Inception Deck include: (1) Why are we here?, (2) Elevator pitch, (3) Package design, (4) Not-to-do list, (5) Find the neighbors, (6) Draw the solution, (7) Problems that keep you up at night, (8) Determine the period, (9) Trade-off slider, and (10) How much of what is needed.
The recommended starting procedure for Why-related elements is to begin with the question “Why are we here?”—clarifying why team members have gathered and why they are advancing this project.
The Inception Deck is used to verbalize why a project exists and to set shared policy so the team faces the same direction.

Create an elevator pitch so the project can be explained to someone unfamiliar with it in 15–30 seconds. Package design, analogized to product packaging on a shelf, aims for an expression that conveys project value at a glance. The process refines a long explanation into a short, intuitive one.
An explicit not-to-do list defines what the project will not do, eliminating scope ambiguity. “Find the neighbors” means identifying involved stakeholders and clarifying the project’s boundaries.

How-related elements include drawing a rough solution (architecture and structure) and listing “problems that keep you up at night”—risks that can block progress. Typical examples are a boss overturning decisions (ちゃぶ台返し) and a competitor releasing first. Verbalizing these in advance enables calmer judgment when they occur.

“Determine the period” means sharing a feasible schedule not to lock a deadline but to align realistic expectations. “What is needed and how much” means identifying required budget, team composition, and skills.

The Inception Deck’s value lies more in the all-team discussion process than in the artifact itself: it aligns viewpoints and later makes decisions much faster. It is not one-and-done; projects are living things and must be continually revised as the environment changes. Whether that review continues often decides whether agile project operations succeed.

QCDS (Quality, Cost, Delivery, Scope) is tuned with a trade-off slider that visually shows high vs. low priority and makes clear what to emphasize and what to adjust. That removes hesitation in decisions, raises speed, increases field autonomy, reduces wasteful conflict, and lets the team focus on delivering essential value.
A trade-off slider (トレードオフスライダー) visualizes QCDS priorities: Quality (品質), Cost (コスト), Delivery (スケジュール), and Scope (スコープ), each adjustable between MAX and MIN.
QCDS settings should be decided through discussion with the team and stakeholders, but the product owner (プロダクト責任者) holds final decision-making authority and responsibility.
Do not impose decisions with “everyone decided, so follow.” Treat QCDS as an agreement people genuinely buy into (腹落ちさせる).
Even when there is disagreement, the product owner’s role includes enabling the team to move forward with a disagree-and-commit (ディスアグリー＆コミット) spirit.
Section 5-3 covers role division among PM, Scrum team, Product Owner (PO), and Scrum Master—an area where field confusion is common.
Scrum is a development methodology for agile product development that builds the product by repeating fixed-period cycles.
Common Scrum-adoption failures include roles that exist but do not function, ambiguous accountability, and exhaustion over “who decides what.” These issues can determine whether Scrum succeeds.
Role-division problems arise largely because the scope of PO responsibilities in Scrum differs from the responsibilities a PM is expected to take on.
Some organizations use the title “PO” in ways that do not match Scrum’s definition of Product Owner, contributing to confusion about who owns which decisions.

The term PO is sometimes used outside the Scrum context to mean 'the person responsible for the product,' but this is a very confusing expression. Globally, the common understanding is that the role with general product responsibility is called PM.
PM is a role represented by the Product Management Triangle: it requires proficiency in development, customers, and business, and involves doing whatever is necessary for business growth.
In a product development organization, the person who manages the execution of development is not the PM.

The PM grasps the market and customers, defines value, sets priorities, continuously updates strategy, and makes decisions to win as a business. Responsibility for business results ultimately concentrates on this role.

The Product Management Triangle (cited from productlogic.org) maps activities across The Business, The Product, Users, and Developers, including areas such as Business Model Development, Monetization, Strategic Partnerships, Market Sizing, Product Roadmap, User Research, Design, SEO, Web Analytics, and more.

The PO in a Scrum team is responsible for maximizing the value of the product the Scrum team is developing. Within the Scrum Guide, the main focus is on managing the product backlog, assigning priorities, and ensuring the optimal product is built.
In recent years, delivery-oriented thinking and additional responsibilities have also been incorporated into the PO role beyond the original Scrum Guide scope.

The Scrum Guide does not clearly prescribe who should perform product discovery or define value. A Product Owner (PO) may execute discovery themselves, or external stakeholders may discover value while the PO communicates that work and reflects it in the backlog. Thus the PO can be a discovery executor, but this is not a fixed mandatory requirement of the role.

A Product Manager (PM), by contrast, cannot avoid value exploration and business-outcome accountability. This difference between Scrum’s flexible PO stance on discovery and the PM’s unavoidable ownership of value and outcomes is a primary source of role-division confusion.
In many organizations the PM concurrently serves as PO: a PM close to the Scrum team also owns the product backlog. That dual role is a natural structure, but it is not universal.

PM roles are hierarchical. Besides team-adjacent PMs, there are heads of the whole product-development organization, directors who manage multiple PMs, and CPO / VP of Product roles that are not tied to a single Scrum team. Those more senior PMs may not directly hold PO responsibilities.

PM and PO therefore do not always coincide; how far they overlap depends on organizational structure. That ambiguity makes field-level understanding harder, so organizations should intentionally design which accountabilities stay with PM and which are delegated to the PO for team-level operation.

From a product-responsibility viewpoint, engineering management also falls within the relevant job scope. An Engineering Manager (EM) typically owns people management of the team or organization and growth/enablement work that faces people rather than purely technical delivery.

When a Tech Lead exists, architecture design, code review, and other technical leadership usually sit with the Tech Lead, allowing the EM to concentrate on people and organization. When no Tech Lead is present, those technical-lead duties tend to fall onto the EM as well (content continues onto the next page).
EM (Engineering Manager) and Scrum Master responsibilities can partially overlap when the goal is keeping the team in a good state, but they are not the same role.
A Scrum Master is neither a people manager nor a progress manager. Their role is to support Scrum functioning correctly, with responsibility for process, communication, and removing obstacles.
An important Scrum Master duty is mediating friction not only inside the team but also with external stakeholders and other teams.

An EM may personally perform Scrum Master functions, or may deliberately leave those functions to the team and observe from outside. EM and Scrum Master need not be the same person; separation is sometimes preferable.

A Scrum Master is sometimes described as having the goal of eventually 'firing themselves': the ideal is a state where every Scrum team member understands Scrum and can support and execute it, making a dedicated Scrum Master unnecessary.
Engineers can behave in Scrum Master-like ways, and even a PO can understand that way of thinking.

Unlike a Scrum Master, an EM has duties such as evaluation and organizational design that a self-contained team cannot fully carry. Therefore, even if a Scrum Master can become unnecessary, an EM disappearing by 'firing themselves' is unlikely.
Like PO and Scrum Master, PM and EM should be peers with distinct scenes of excellence but equal expertise, able to trust each other's backs.

Growing the business sometimes requires hard work and strong commitment; that push tends to be the PM's domain. Stopping overwork for team health and sustainable working styles is where the EM's perspective is needed.
Business promotion and sustainability should function as two complementary wheels (事業推進と持続可能性の両輪).

When PM and EM positions are both correct, teams face a dilemma over which to prioritize and can feel torn; it is therefore important that PM and EM can debate from their respective stances. These two wheels are necessary, and occasional conflict and discussion keep the organization healthy. A product owner who understands both viewpoints then makes the final decision. A structure that does not run from decision-making is what moves the team forward.
The value of a Scrum team lies in the team being involved across the entire process and delivering results cross-functionally.

A prior challenge in Scrum teams composed of QA (Quality Assurance), designers, and engineers was that specialist walls biased discussion: designers found it hard to step into QA viewpoints and QA found it hard to enter design viewpoints. Despite claiming to be cross-functional, decisions tended to lean toward specialist domains.

AI expands the range of work that can cross role boundaries. For example, in a sprint focused on iOS improvements, Android engineers previously might have been sent to exploration unrelated to the sprint goal; with AI, everyone can contribute in a way that supports the sprint goal. Scrum teams can thus become truly cross-functional in a stronger sense.

Fixed-length sprints may become more problematic as AI shortens work that used to take a week into a day or even a few hours. Fixed sprint length may no longer be optimal, and sprint-goal definition, sprint planning, and backlog refinement themselves may need to evolve to a next phase.

As AI makes more things producible, backlog items can explode. Items still require preparation to enter the backlog, and refinement takes time, creating a dilemma in which time spent on backlog refinement can exceed time spent on essential development.

Role division in Scrum teams is not mere title cleanup; it is the design of decision-making and operations that makes development execution work as a tactic in the AI era, while competitors may already be shipping implementations at high speed with AI.

When PM, project manager, and Scrum PO roles mix, decision-making slows, accountability becomes unclear, and both outcomes and quality decline. This pattern occurs almost without exception regardless of organization size or product phase.

A product is managed from birth to death of that product. A project is a time-boxed initiative with a deadline. Keeping this shared distinction is a prerequisite for using PM / project manager / PO lines in real product development.

Project management is a core skill for every role (PM, project manager, and Scrum PO). Executing strategy requires planning, coordination, decision-making, and risk management—not only schedule control. QCDS trade-offs and stakeholder relationship building are part of that execution capability, which sits in front of product management.

Author’s working definition of PM skill level 1 (aligned with M3 CPO Satoshi Yamazaki): as Scrum PO, create a state in which the Scrum team functions as a fully capable unit, i.e., run development project management end-to-end by oneself.
Project management and Product Owner (PO) roles are not subordinate concepts of Product Manager (PM); they are distinct.

Manager leveling (as in some tech-company frameworks) is synonymous with how PM/PO impact is assessed; at higher levels (2, 3+), evaluation shifts from execution to the scale of business results (e.g., how many hundreds of millions of yen of profit a product generates).
Being able to manage a development project as a Scrum Product Owner is only the entry point, not the destination.

After that entry point there are two main career routes: (1) strengthen the business-growth perspective and become a PM accountable for business outcomes; (2) deepen project-management expertise and continue supporting execution as a senior project manager.
Globally, Product Manager and Project Manager are parallel professions, not a hierarchy. Both may be assigned to the same project and divide roles while driving the team.
In global practice, project management is often called program management; its scope is broader than the typical Japanese image of “building what you were told, on schedule.”

Excellent PMs tend to have first experienced high-difficulty execution before they start formulating strategy. Strategy that cannot be executed becomes empty pie-in-the-sky thinking; the real risk is mass-producing decisions the person themselves cannot carry out.

Therefore it is healthier for both the organization and the individual to hire PM candidates first as project managers, let them master project-management practices, and only then let them choose among product management, specializing further in project/program management, or another professional path, rather than hiring junior PMs from day one.
When a business or organization grows and development scale expands, the product owner who supported the launch phase almost always hits capacity limits.
A typical anti-pattern at that point is hiring a junior product owner: education costs rise and the original person's workload usually increases further.

Two recommended options instead: (1) hire an experienced project manager and delegate on-the-ground execution so the product owner can focus on strategy and the business; (2) delegate authority inside the Scrum team and distribute project-management work (e.g., to Scrum Masters or developers) to raise overall organizational autonomy.
The essential mindset is not 'hire a junior product owner because we are busy' but 'transfer/delegate authority from the project-management side.'
Exception: a multi-product strategy. Growing several products at once requires a senior PM for each product; this is a high-difficulty management decision that needs a real commitment of resources.

Common failures: pursuing a multi-product strategy without being able to hire senior PMs, or placing junior PMs on some products. Coordination and education costs then spike and every product ends up half-finished.
If adopting a multi-product strategy, first raise the attractiveness of the products and the organization's ability to hire PMs so the strategy is adequately resourced.
プロダクトとプロジェクトの線引きは組織規模・フェーズ（10人未満、30人、100人、200人など）によって変わる。チームが分かれたときのPMとプロジェクトマネージャーの配置は、プロダクト戦略・事業戦略と直結する組織設計の問題である。
プロダクト責任者は、戦略に合わせて役割の線引きを設計し続ける責任を負う。
本章のまとめとして、プロジェクトマネジメントとアジャイルの失敗パターンが7つ紹介される。
失敗パターン1「計画倒れ」：問題は計画を立てること自体ではなく、計画を固定化し、前提が変わっても更新しないことにある。
多くのプロジェクトでは初期計画が守るべき約束（聖域）になり、市場環境・技術的制約・チーム構成・顧客の反応が変化しても計画だけが更新されない。
計画の聖域化が現場に生む歪み：(1) 無理なスケジュール遵守による品質低下とチームの疲弊、(2) 現場の工夫や学習の余白がなく抑圧される、(3) 計画変更＝失敗という空気が生まれる。
A plan is originally a hypothesis for decision-making and should be updated according to the situation. When protecting the plan itself becomes the goal, the project loses its ability to learn.

Trying to satisfy all of QCDS (Quality, Cost, Delivery, Scope) at the same time is closely related to plans collapsing. Decision-making that tries to maximize every QCDS element simultaneously is the most irresponsible choice.

When priorities are not made explicit, teams cannot answer what may be sacrificed, where they should hold firm, or where they should compromise. Judgment criteria then diverge among members, producing conflict and exhaustion.
The moment someone says “everything is important,” the project has effectively abandoned decision-making.
Common misunderstandings of Agile include: Agile equals no planning; Scrum equals holding events; simply running sprints will produce value. These misconceptions appear repeatedly in the field.
Agile is a structure for treating plans as having preconditions and continuously updating them through learning. Scrum events are means, not ends.
If sprint planning, review, and retrospective become hollow rituals, Agile itself becomes mere ceremony.

Especially dangerous is using Agile as a free pass: “quality can be low because we are Agile” or “we need not take responsibility for mid-course changes because we are Agile.” That usage is the opposite of Agile philosophy.

A disconnect between strategy and execution occurs when strategy remains abstract when it reaches the field. Symptoms include not knowing why a feature is being built, success criteria not being shared, and priorities changing daily without the background being communicated.

To put strategy into execution, verbalization, structuring, and visualization of the strategy are indispensable; projects that cannot do this will not keep producing results no matter how excellent the members gathered.
It is not necessarily vital that every team member feels fully convinced; some things cannot be understood until one reaches the leader’s vantage point.

Members with a lower viewpoint demanding that the leader ‘explain it so I am satisfied’ is misplaced; pushing one’s own inability to understand (due to lower skill/level) onto the leader is also wrong.

Information asymmetry is inevitable: some facts are known only to executives or cannot yet be shared. Teams must still move first. Raising dissatisfaction solely because ‘I am not personally convinced’ shows a lack of understanding of company structure and is self-centered.

A core job of the product owner/product lead is to accumulate daily trust so that members can still say: ‘I don’t understand, but I understand there are things you cannot explain, so I will trust you and proceed.’

When roles of PM, project manager, business owner, PO, Scrum Master, and EM are vague, decision-making slows: no one knows who has final say, judgments become consensus-based and delayed, and responsibility floats when failure occurs.
Role division exists to raise decision speed; if roles remain ambiguous, even excellent frameworks will not function.

Human-side project failure patterns include over-personalization (属人化) so the work cannot run without specific people, unsustainable work becoming the norm and causing burnout, and lack of psychological safety so problems never surface.
Death-march projects can look successful in the short term but reliably erode long-term organizational productivity; the most capable people leave first, after which both quality and speed decline.
Organizational learning failure causes the same mistakes to be repeated: retrospectives produce no improvement, failure is blamed rather than learned from, and knowledge is not accumulated.
The essence of Agile is learning speed; many planning collapses and Agile misunderstandings come from organizational designs that do not assume learning will occur.

Failure patterns commonly reduce to: no design that connects strategy to execution, priorities not made explicit, decision-making being abandoned, and prioritizing avoidance of responsibility over learning.
These root causes are problems of how an organization relates to project management and Agile.
「なんちゃってアジャイル」（形だけの偽アジャイル）からチームを救うには、スプリント計画やレトロスペクティブなどの各セレモニーが「なぜ必要なのか」を実践的に理解し、正しい実行基盤として再構築することが重要である。
プロダクト責任者は、現場の開発が「終わらないタスクの消化試合」になっていないか、デイリースクラムが単なる進捗報告会になっていないかを点検するチェックリストとしてセレモニーを使うべきである。
アジャイルはIT現場のバズワードではなく、変化の激しいビジネス環境に適応するための組織論である。経営・事業側（CFOやBizDev）には、ウォーターフォールではなくアジャイルで進める理由として「不確実性のコントロール」という事業上のメリットを論理的に説明できる必要がある。
開発プロセスがどれほど美しくても、作るべき価値（Discovery）が間違っていれば意味がない。「無駄なものを最速で作る」という悲劇を避けることが本質である。
不確実な顧客課題を手探りで突き止め、それをアジャイルな開発プロセスへ接続する「仮説検証のサイクル」を回すことが、正しいものを正しくつくるための中核である。

関連学習書：『SCRUM BOOT CAMP THE BOOK』（西村直人・永瀬美穂・吉羽龍太郎、翔泳社、2020年）はセレモニーの必要性を実践的に解説する入門書。『アジャイル開発とスクラム 第2版』（平鍋健児・野中郁次郎・及部敬雄、翔泳社、2021年）はスクラムの理論的背景と組織論としてアジャイルを位置づける。『正しいものを正しくつくる』（市谷聡啓、ビー・エヌ・エヌ新社、2019年）はDiscoveryと仮説検証を開発プロセスへ接続する枠組みを示す。

Align the basic viewpoint of product management (PM) by returning to first principles; many PM books assume prior knowledge, whereas a rare approach explains product management from a perspective even a middle-schooler can understand, using no difficult jargon while still capturing the essence. People who have already studied project management or Agile especially benefit from this reset.
Book: 『ゼロから始めるプロダクトマネジメント』 (Tanno Mizuki, Gijutsu-Hyoronsha, 2020) — product management explained simply without missing core ideas.

Large-scale system development and projects routinely overrun budget and miss deadlines because of human cognitive biases, especially optimism bias, which breaks plans. A counter-principle is “Think slow, act fast” (遅く考え、速く動く): slow down thinking/planning to confront bias, then execute quickly.

Book: 『BIG THINGS』 (Bent Flyvbjerg and Dan Gardner, Japanese translation by Sakurai Yuko, Sunmark Publishing, 2024) — documents how optimism bias and related cognitive biases cause planning failure in megaprojects.

Management methods should be switched according to the level of uncertainty (high vs. low). Short-term delivery results and long-term team growth/autonomy are not inherently a trade-off; both can be pursued together if methods match uncertainty.

Book: 『両利きのプロジェクトマネジメント』 (Yoneyama Tomohiro, Shoeisha, 2025) — “ambidextrous” project management: balancing short-term outcomes with sustainable Agile/Scrum so teams deliver without burnout and gain agency. Useful for people who want to keep Agile/Scrum running in a maintainable form.
Chapter context: Chapter 5, Project Management and Agile.
Chapter 6 covers technology and engineering for product leaders, with the theme of understanding technology and using it as a weapon (技術を理解し武器にする).
Technology means the new technologies overflowing in the world; engineering means implementing those technologies yourself and embedding them into working systems and mechanisms.
The foundation of product leadership is understanding both technology and engineering.
Product owners/PMs have often come from engineering backgrounds, but non-engineers increasingly take the role: consultants, marketers, and customer-success professionals who bring domain knowledge.
That diversification is healthy and natural because product management is a role that binds together multiple specialties.
The main barrier for non-engineer PMs is keeping up with rapidly evolving technology and having the engineering experience to turn it into concrete systems.

The chapter organizes (1) the minimum technology and engineering understanding a product leader should have, including non-engineers, and (2) the problems that tend to occur when that understanding is missing.
Core premise: product value resides in working software (プロダクトの価値は動くソフトウェアに宿る).
A product is not a specification document or a proposal document; it is working software delivered to users.

AI has made prototyping and simple product development accessible even to non-engineers, but a large technical gap remains between vibe coding (instructing AI in natural language for intuitive development) / PoC (validating feasibility of a new idea) and products that actually run continuously in production.

Production products must continuously confront security requirements, availability, scalability, sustainable architecture, and technical debt; a strategy that does not understand these constraints will necessarily fail at the execution stage.

Technical understanding does not mean being able to write production code (code that runs in the live environment) yourself. It also differs in essence from traditional SI-style skills such as estimating person-hours or writing simple specifications.

The essence of technical understanding is whether one can make decisions. Product quality, speed, and cost are ultimately determined by technical constraints; without technical understanding, judgments on these are dragged by wishes and gut feeling.

Typical failures from insufficient technical understanding: making baseless judgments such as 'it looks easy' or 'it can be done immediately'; deciding without considering data structures or dependencies; estimates always missing due to optimism bias; misidentifying technical debt as a motivation or effort problem; systems holding back the business during growth; inability to build trust with engineers, leading to an adversarial structure.
These failures result from underestimating both understanding of technology as new tech and the engineering practice of implementing it oneself.
The minimum line of technical understanding required of a product owner is discussed in the context of (high-level) production code and related competencies.

Responsible persons (product/tech leaders) do not need to write code themselves, but in the era of vibe coding it is possible to build and release a product alone in a single day off; never having done so even once is no longer a knowledge-hurdle problem but an attitude/posture problem.
Minimum technical understanding required of those in charge consists of four points (shown as a hierarchy in Figure 6-1).
1. Overall architecture: understand the structure of infrastructure, server-side, and frontend plus language characteristics, and be able to grasp the overall design.
2. Data flow: understand how user-behavior data is processed and stored; without this, one cannot grasp what is happening during incidents/failures.
3. Places where bottlenecks tend to arise: grasp points that become business risks, such as old vs. new technology, maturity of frameworks/libraries, and licenses.
4. Distinguishing high-change-cost vs. low-change-cost areas: the ability to see what can be changed later, what must be decided from the start, and which changes require downtime.

Figure 6-1 presents these four items as the hierarchy of technical understanding demanded of a responsible person, stacked as: overall architecture → data flow → bottleneck-prone areas → distinguishing high vs. low change-cost regions.
The purpose of technical understanding is not to use specialist jargon accurately, but to abstract technical discussion and translate it into business decisions.
A large language and culture gap exists between engineers and executives; PMs and product owners serve as translators between them.
Technical understanding is the foundation that keeps technical debates from turning into emotional arguments.
As AI lowers implementation cost, the quality of decision-making becomes more important than the ability to build.
The relevant questions become 'what to build' and 'when to discard,' not merely 'can we build it.'
The more technology is democratized, the more important design judgment becomes.
Both overvaluing and undervaluing AI come from shallow technical understanding.
AI is essentially a technology that substantially changes cost structure.
LLM usage cost, accuracy, model selection, and ease of switching models are explicitly management decisions.
In an era when AI writes code, leaders still need judgment on architecture, security, and authentication.
Delegating to AI without understanding the difference between prototype and production code is dangerous.
Technical understanding builds trust with engineers, improves estimate accuracy and plan realism, and creates buy-in for prioritization.
The result is the ability to balance development speed and quality so that the product and the business can choose when to accelerate and when to brake.
Technology is both a means and the greatest weapon; understanding it is part of leadership, not a specialist skill, and is now a required competency.
Organizations that keep technology inward-looking and closed will eventually become unsustainable.
For product owners, how they engage with R&D is inseparable from their role.
R&D creates future options and does not directly tie to short-term revenue or KPIs.
R&D is an extremely important investment area because it expands future product and business options 3, 5, or 10 years later, even when it does not contribute immediately.

A common organizational misconception is treating R&D as something done only when there is spare capacity or after a product is already stable; in practice, starting R&D only after a product enters its growth phase often means technical options have already narrowed.
R&D work must be clearly separated from production code; technologies and prototype code verified with R&D spend should not be brought directly into production environments.
The purpose of R&D is not to produce working software but to verify technical possibilities, identify future options, and reduce uncertainty.
R&D should be treated as providing the basis for decision-making, including when (or whether) to incorporate a technology into the product and when to decide not to incorporate it this time.

Organizations that neglect R&D typically show these signs: technology selection that is always ad-hoc; inability to keep up with competitors’ technical evolution; inability to take on new challenges and instead only extending existing products; and being unable to accelerate when desired because of technical constraints.
Appropriate investment in technical understanding and R&D both strengthens trust with engineers and greatly increases freedom of management decision-making.
A core role of the product owner is to create a state in which the organization can choose by its own will where to attack, where to defend, when to rebuild, and when to discard.
R&D is an investment in the future. Increasingly, technology decisions are tightly coupled with accounting: LLM spend, cloud costs, and SaaS fees all require joint tech-and-finance judgment.
Typical decision scenes include: how much model-usage cost to tolerate; whether to build in-house or use an external service; and how to fold cloud-cost volatility into the business plan.

Without understanding costs, decisions cannot be made correctly; without a finance perspective they tend toward over-investment or under-investment. R&D and technology investment are management decisions the product owner must understand, not work to leave solely to engineers.
Product owners do not need deep mastery of every technical domain. Engineers themselves typically cover a necessary range at a working level and then specialize in particular languages or areas.

Being able to write code and being able to make technology judgments are different skills. Implementation experience without understanding the underlying structure and constraints does not constitute technology judgment.

Technology selection requires understanding current tech trends and the characteristics of languages/platforms, not merely coding in one language. This maps to the distinction between a programmer (focused on writing code) and an architect (who designs overall structure).

An architect’s role is not implementation itself but selecting technologies based on architecture and constraints and setting direction. Product owners need at least enough understanding to discuss technical decisions with architects.
Product owners need not decide every technical detail themselves, but they must grasp structure and constraints well enough to participate in those decisions.
Section 6-2 framing: at minimum, get a working overview of architecture, data flow, the cost stack, and AI.
Understanding architecture means grasping the division of roles among frontend, backend, infrastructure, and the data layer, starting with the basic mechanisms of the internet and web services.
What should be processed on the frontend versus the backend depends on the service's characteristics and processing content; this in turn determines which languages and frameworks are appropriate.
Technical selection must be based on understanding each language/framework's characteristics, engineer population, popularity, trends, and maturity—not just technical fit.

Tech selection is inseparable from hiring difficulty and organizational strategy: too-new technology makes talent hard to attract; overly mature ('枯れた') technology fails to attract ambitious engineers. Tech choices shape the organization itself.

Key architectural design judgments include monolith (all functions integrated into one system) versus microservices (independent small functions that cooperate), and synchronous versus asynchronous processing.

Those design choices affect the whole tech stack, including batch processing (processing large accumulated data in bulk), event-driven architecture (triggered by specific operations or state changes), and API integration.
A product/tech leader must be able to explain 'why this architecture now' and 'where bottlenecks tend to occur,' and hold technical conversations with engineers.
Organizations that do not understand data flow will inevitably get stuck. One must be able to explain the full path from user action through data acquisition, storage, and utilization.
Diagramming the flow from frontend to database rapidly deepens understanding. Log collection, analysis platforms, and connections to BI tools should also be grasped.
Early-stage organizations often lack analysis infrastructure, which prevents quantitative decision-making; the product owner must therefore take ownership of data-platform understanding.
Data design is characteristically hard to change later: data flow is the foundation of architecture, and changing it incurs large costs.
Insufficient logging and monitoring prevent tracing root causes during incidents, delay recovery, badly damage user experience, and directly erode trust.
Technology stack selection is a management decision, not a matter of personal preference or trends; early choices lock in future strategy and cannot be easily reversed.
A stack shapes organizational structure, the hiring market, and development speed. Evaluate not only current optimality but whether the choice can endure for about three years.
Leaving stack choice to an individual engineer’s favorite languages or frameworks is equivalent to handing mid- to long-term management decisions to a single member.
Stack decisions affect hiring market, development velocity, learning cost, and future extensibility. Judge whether future hires—not only current staff—can maintain and extend the system.
Identify bottleneck-prone areas in advance: data design, external API dependencies, infrastructure, security, and authentication/authorization.
When to invest in security is itself a management decision. “No problem now” can be valid, but the call must still weigh future risk.
Intentional technical debt is often taken to prioritize business speed. What matters is recognizing the debt in the decision and planning when it will be repaid.
Technical debt is not inherently evil; mistimed repayment turns it into a constraint on the business. Architecture and product phase are tightly coupled.

Different company phases (seed stage, around product-market fit, and growth stage) each require different technical compositions and architectures; blindly applying a fixed formula can lead to organizational or technical failure.
Section 6-3 addresses how to define the roles of CTO, tech lead, and data talent and how to design their working relationships so they can jointly advance the organization.

The CTO should be understood as a member of the executive team (alongside CEO, CPO, CFO, etc.) who owns the technology domain: technology is treated as a management decision within the larger questions of how the company will grow and how operations as a whole should be optimized.
A CTO does not necessarily need to write production code themselves.

In practice, prior technology and engineering experience sharpens decision-making, raises the resolution of communication to others, and thereby improves the quality of judgments; this is why many CTOs come from engineering backgrounds.
The essential work of the CTO is connecting technical strategy to management strategy and to business strategy.

CTO responsibilities include: formulating a mid- to long-term technology roadmap; final decision-making accountability for technology selection (the CTO need not personally make every choice but does bear responsibility); treating technical debt as a management issue rather than a purely engineering concern; technology-stack decisions that take the hiring market into account, plus final responsibility for architecture selection; final responsibility for security, reliability, and availability; distinguishing R&D investment from production work; acting as a technology translator for the rest of the executive team and for non-technical officers; and defining role boundaries and collaboration with the product owner or CPO.

In many companies the product owner (product responsibility) role is filled by the CTO, so product owner = CTO is a valid organizational model; when a CTO is absent or is a figurehead, those decisions often fail and a CPO, VPoE, or other executive may cover, so product owner and CPO can be different people.

CTO expectations and role weight change with company phase: early startups often have a few founders sharing CEO/CTO/CFO hats and acting as CxOs; as the company scales, technical difficulty, investment size, technical-debt paydown, availability, and security requirements all rise, so technology-management difficulty grows with the business.

A common dilemma is that a founding CTO’s capability no longer matches a later organizational phase; a later-hired VPoE or product owner may be the better fit. Removing the founding CTO is not always correct—the product owner may instead support and raise that CTO’s perspective—but it is also common for the founding CTO to step aside or hire someone who becomes their boss so a phase-appropriate CTO can operate.

A tech lead is the on-the-ground technical decision-maker: daily design judgments, code quality, technical consistency, and protecting architecture at the implementation level. The role is often combined with architect. Duties go beyond being technically knowledgeable: proposing technology choices, owning implementation, and being the person who raises the team’s technical standard.

Tech Lead roles typically include: daily design decisions and guaranteeing code quality; forming a review culture and raising overall technical standards; detecting technical debt and proposing repayment from a field (on-the-ground) perspective; serving as the center for performance, observability, and incident response; and mentoring and developing junior engineers.
Although some companies have Engineering Managers (EM) concurrently perform Tech Lead duties, the general distinction is that the Tech Lead looks at technology while the EM looks at people.

A Tech Lead is often placed one per team or product, so multiple Tech Leads exist inside a company. When connecting to shared platforms (cross-cutting initiatives, data platforms, authentication/authorization platforms), Tech Leads must align with each other and sometimes collide while reducing friction.

A common Tech Lead burnout pattern: the entire day is consumed by reviews, consultations about technical issues outside production code concentrate on them, and as a result the Tech Lead themselves lose time writing code and touching quality.

If the company's evaluation system only has a management track for raising salary, Tech Leads who originally want to face technology may be assigned as EMs against their wishes and drift away from technology.
A Tech Lead is the on-site technical responsible person; organizations should understand that defined roles and division of labor are necessary to sustain the role.
Data talent is split across multiple job types. Representative examples are Data Engineer, Data Analyst, and Data Scientist.

A Data Engineer is the engineer who builds the data analysis platform: connecting the data warehouse to data sources, transforming data, and connecting it to tools so that Data Analysts, Data Scientists, and PMs can more easily make decisions.
Data engineers (データのインフラ屋) build the analysis platform and data infrastructure that others use.

Data analysts use a prepared analysis foundation to analyze data and visualize its meaning. They are not necessarily from an engineering background; many come from marketing or the business side. What matters is presenting interpretations that can stand up to decision-making.

Data scientist is a broadly used term. Some companies treat it as a mix of data analyst plus LLM/ML work. The decisive difference is that they can own building models (including AI and LLMs) and connecting those models to the business—for example creating a recommendation model and handing it to engineers to embed in the product.
In recent years data science work has often been specialized further into machine learning engineers, LLM engineers, R&D roles, etc. This book treats the whole area as “data talent” for convenience.

Do not isolate data talent as a mere analysis department. If product owners do not understand this, the role is never created and the organization falls into “so-called analysis”: just collecting whatever metrics and logs already exist. Data collection should start from the information actually needed for decisions.

Without data visualization, teams cannot track before/after of each measure, KPIs can only be designed from what is currently visible, and the absence of essential data causes decision-making to drift off target.
Excellent data talent can guarantee data quality, reproducibility, and reliability. Because data preparation is a prerequisite for AI use, the value of data talent has increased further.
There is risk in adding data talent late: existing data structures may already be too late to salvage, and it can be faster to rebuild the analysis platform from scratch.

Strong data talent communicate well with marketers and business teams, can themselves hear what the business wants to see and then build it. That lets the work run without constant involvement from PMs or product owners, and data talent can become a bridge between the product-development organization and the business side.
CTO, tech lead, and data talent have different natures, so the product owner must design communication so that all three functions work together rather than treating roles as cleanly separated.
In practice, roles overlap: a CTO may also serve as tech lead, a CTO may come from a data background, or a tech lead may be strong on data infrastructure. Coverage therefore varies by person.
The product owner should assess each person's strengths and weaknesses and build relationships with an intent to fill gaps where needed.

Clarify who decides what and who holds responsibility. Visualize the decision process (e.g., with a RACI chart) so it is never ambiguous who is consulted vs. who decides, who has execution responsibility, and where final accountability sits. This directly affects speed and quality.

Relationships among CTO, tech lead, and data talent change as the organization scales. As phases advance, new roles appear and specialization increases. Do not freeze roles once decided; accept role changes by organizational phase.

The product owner is also responsible for designing an environment in which technical leaders can conflict healthily: mechanisms so technical debate does not become personal, management that does not isolate people, and ensuring debate is translated into on-the-ground implementation.

If technology, data, and product become siloed, decision-making slows, learning stops, and the organization wears down. When the three mesh, decision speed and quality rise a level, and product development starts functioning as a management weapon.
Section 6-4 argues against the impression that the product owner must understand, judge, and carry everything: architecture/design and monitoring should be left to engineers.

図表6-2 compares three roles—CTO, Tech Lead (テックリード), and Data Talent (データ人材)—across positioning, perspective, duties, engineering background, coding frequency, organizational phase, collaborators, role boundaries, and risks.

CTO positioning: a member of the management layer (経営層／マネジメント). Tech Lead: technical decision-maker at the team/field level. Data talent: specialist group that builds the infrastructure for decision-making.

Central perspective of the CTO: connecting management/business strategy with technology, and mid-to-long-term technology strategy. Tech Lead: technical consistency at the design and implementation level in the field. Data talent: supporting decisions with data and providing the connection layer between product and business.
