CTO main duties: formulating the mid-to-long-term technology roadmap; final responsibility for technology selection and architecture; treating technical debt and security as management issues; translating technology for non-technical executives.

Tech Lead main duties: daily design judgments and guaranteeing code quality; fostering a review culture and raising the technical level of the team; detecting technical debt from a field perspective and proposing repayment; mentoring and developing juniors.

Data talent main duties (by subtype): DE—building a data environment that makes decisions easy; DA—analysis and visualization that give data meaning; DS—building AI/ML models and connecting them to the business; plus guaranteeing data quality and reliability.

Engineer experience: not strictly required for CTO, but experience raises decision quality so many CTOs come from engineering. Required for Tech Lead (must be technically deep and raise field standards). For data talent it depends: DE and DS require it; DA often comes from business/marketing.

Code-writing frequency: CTO is generally not the person who writes the most code and need not write production code. Tech Lead is the implementation owner and still writes code, but overload can make writing impossible. Data talent: DE/DS involve implementation; DA centers on analysis tools.

Organizational phase: CTO expectations and weight change with company stage—founding period is CxO-like for everyone, but technology-management difficulty rises with growth; a founding CTO can become mismatched and be replaced. Tech Lead is typically one per team/product, with multiple in the company who must coordinate on cross-cutting work. Data talent subdivides into DE (infrastructure), DA (analysis/visualization), and DS (model building); late involvement risks data structures becoming unrecoverable.

Main collaborators: CTO works with CEO, CPO, CFO, product-development organization heads, and non-technical executives. Tech Lead works with Engineering Managers (EM) and other Tech Leads. Data talent works with Product Managers (PM), product-organization heads, marketers, and business teams.

Role boundaries: CTO may concurrently head the product-development organization; CPO or VPoE may cover parts of the role. Tech Lead “looks at technology” while EM “looks at people,” and may also serve as architect. Data talent is not merely an “analyst shop”; excellent data people communicate directly with the business side.

Key risks: founding CTO capability may no longer match the company’s growth phase. Tech Lead can burn out from concentrated reviews and consultations, or be assigned against their will as EM. Data talent may inherit data structures that are already too late, forcing a rebuild from the foundation.
Product owners should deliberately leave detailed design and day-to-day monitoring/operations to engineers rather than treating them as the product owner's own daily work.
When delegating, explicitly clarify three things: why you are delegating, how far you will delegate, and how you will delegate.
Many PMs and EMs take on too many detailed design judgments and daily operational tasks, causing them to neglect the roles they should actually fulfill.
If the line between what to delegate and what not to delegate remains vague, the organization will inevitably become distorted.
Work that should be delegated is work that requires on-the-ground, field-level decision-making.

Delegatable areas include: daily system health checks (e.g., whether there was unexpected access or CPU load at certain times even if no errors or restarts occurred); incident detection and first response (detecting unauthorized access or temporary load spikes, identifying causes, and recovering); implementation-level detailed design (the How based on Why and What—specific database structure, where code should be written, choice of frameworks); and concrete design of operational flows (communication design based on specs, review rules, document storage locations and writing methods, timing).
Engineers, especially tech leads who work with the system every day, make these decisions faster and at higher quality.
If the product owner retains control of these areas, problems arise (the organization becomes slower and decisions become lower quality).

When judgment and decision-making are concentrated at the top, decisions are delayed, people judge with shallow technical understanding (creating bottlenecks), and mixed lines of responsibility make incidents unmanageable.
Therefore, create conditions so that on-site responsible people (現場の責任者) can make decisions about problems that arise in the development field.
Clarify the boundary between areas the product owner must hold (握るべき領域) and areas to delegate (任せるべき領域).

Product owner must hold architecture basic principles: monolith vs. microservices; modern/challenging tech vs. proven/mature tech. Share the underlying basic principles, which are shaped by business situation and hiring strategy.

Product owner must hold non-functional requirements (SLO, security, availability, etc.): target SLA/SLO, security standards, and desired availability, examined and shared based on use cases and scaling possibilities.

Product owner must hold the policy for technical debt: gradual repayment in daily work vs. a dedicated period for re-architecture. This is not a purely technical decision; it must consider business scale timing and be made by a person with deep understanding of both business and technology.

Product owner must hold technology-investment policy: investments such as LLM or new technologies should be examined from a mid-to-long-term strategy—whether the tech is a passing trend or will become general-purpose, or whether to ride the current trend on the premise of changing later. This varies by domain.

Areas that should be delegated to the field (rather than centrally controlled) include: per-project concrete design patterns, implementation policy and library selection, detailed test strategy, and practical operational procedures.

On design patterns: after teaching the underlying design philosophy, which specific pattern to choose should be left to members who better understand the actual code and the team, because they can pick what fits better.

On implementation policy and library selection: field-usable implementation policies and libraries are often better known by on-site tech leads, who catch up in more detail and have higher sensitivity; that kind of person is who a tech lead should be.

On test strategy details: after the team agrees on QCDS (Quality, Cost, Delivery, Scope) trade-offs, the methods that actually fit should be chosen by on-site QA and the team—things that are familiar and compatible—because that is one way to reduce uncertainty.

On operational practice: after sharing the escalation flow, error-detection methods and response methods needed to realize it should be decided by the team. Because engineers differ in domain knowledge and understanding of implementation locations, some personalization (属人化) is unavoidable in emergencies from the standpoint of response speed and accuracy.
Leaders need not intervene in detailed design itself, but should keep a state in which they can explain what decisions were made. Architecture Decision Records (ADR) are effective for this.

ADR (Architecture Decision Record) lets you guarantee accountability and transparency of decisions without intervening in design details. When QCDS priorities drift, ADRs also become important clues for retrospectives of where and what happened.

Delegation requires operational standardization: do not create a state where 'only that person understands it.' Leaving design to the field is most rational, but it is not an exemption from responsibility (免責ではない).

Deploy procedure documents should eliminate personalization in which only a specific ace engineer can release. They should clearly define procedures so that whoever is assigned can safely and reliably update the system, or roll it back to the previous state when a problem occurs.

Automated dashboards provide visualization so the entire team can continuously grasp system health and key business metrics in real time against the same standards, eliminating manual report creation.

Alert rules must be clarified in advance: define what truly constitutes danger, and who responds how (initial Playbook) when a given alert fires, to prevent alert fatigue (crying wolf) and missed incidents.
Non-functional requirements—especially availability and security—are business requirements, not purely technical ones. Service reliability directly affects revenue, churn rate, and brand value.
The responsible person owns the target (e.g., which SLO to aim for); the field owns how to achieve it. This division of labor is essential. The same applies to monitoring.
Monitoring is not merely for operations; it supplies material for investment decisions and priority setting.
The three pillars of monitoring are metrics, logs, and traces.
Metrics are numerical data on system health (CPU utilization, response time, error rate, etc.) used to detect at a glance whether something is currently abnormal.
Logs are detailed textual records of events inside the system, used to determine when, where, and what happened and to drill down to root causes of errors.
Traces follow a request’s path across multiple systems or microservices to pinpoint where in an end-to-end flow a bottleneck, delay, or error occurred.
Together these three give an understanding of what is happening right now. Tool selection, alert design, and day-to-day response should be left to the field.
Monitoring scope must include user experience, not only internal system state. Insufficient monitoring surfaces as management risk, not merely a technical problem.

Problems from weak operational foundations include delayed failure detection and prolonged recovery, inability to explain root causes so decisions become intuitive/sensory, failure to meet customer accountability, and accumulation of technical debt that later explodes.

Even with a robust technical foundation, zero incidents is impossible in product operations; therefore define SLOs (Service Level Objectives) in advance and prepare escalation mechanisms for unexpected events.
Abandon the illusion of 100% system uptime: even cloud providers do not guarantee 100% availability, so services built on them cannot either.

Rather than slowing development speed to chase 100% availability, explicitly define an SLO for how much downtime or error is tolerable and agree in advance on: (1) up to what severity the on-site team may handle autonomously, (2) at what point to escalate (hand over incident response) to a responsible person, and (3) the priority between incident response and feature development.
Triage thinking is effective: switch response and escalation paths according to incident severity, thereby reducing on-site judgment load while still enabling appropriate control.
Ideally, operations should be entrusted to senior engineers who possess design skill, explanation skill, judgment skill, and a sense of responsibility.
When such senior talent is scarce, realistic alternatives include external support, introduction of design reviews, and gradual delegation of authority.
Evaluation of the chosen approach is itself an important closing step.

Delegating detailed design and operations should be evaluated by whether it actually works: escalation response speed, decision-making speed, quality vs. operational load, incident frequency, recovery time, and the learning cycle.
Operational and monitoring maturity should be continuously verified through dashboards, SLOs, alerts, and retrospectives.
Delegating design and monitoring is not abdication of responsibility; it exists so the accountable person can focus on the decisions they must own.

Product owners should personally understand minimum security domains: authentication/authorization, secrets management, and vulnerability response. Final responsibility always remains with the product owner.
In incidents, the product owner’s role includes translating technical facts into language that executives and customers can act on, rather than repeating raw technical detail.
Failure pattern 1 (technology/engineering): treating technical debt as inherently evil and denying its existence. Technical debt is a result of decisions; the goal is not zero debt.
Blaming people for having created technical debt (instead of treating it as a decision outcome) produces a culture that rapidly damages the organization.

A common failure pattern is reframing technical debt as a motivation or skill-shortage problem. Even when the debt was a deliberate management or product-strategy decision, treating it as a purely on-the-ground issue prevents correct improvement.
Another failure is being unable to distinguish unintentionally incurred debt from strategically taken debt. Treating all debt as equally evil makes prioritization of what to fix unclear.
When debt is not distinguished or prioritized, organizations reach a state where no one can explain the amount of technical debt, where it lives, or its impact on the business and quality.
Typical failures include accumulating debt with no repayment plan, and not revisiting debt priorities when the business phase changes.
Repeated speed-first decisions can produce a reversal: development velocity actually falls because of the resulting debt.
Technical debt’s impact on UX and quality is often underestimated, so repayment is postponed indefinitely as something to do “when there is spare capacity.”
If that continues, teams may not even notice that estimation accuracy has collapsed because of technical debt.
The common outcome of underestimating and continually postponing technical debt is a inverted situation: when the business wants to accelerate, it cannot.
A clear hiring-related failure is choosing technology based on one person’s preferred language or hobby rather than organizational needs.
Deciding a tech stack without considering the hiring market makes later organizational scaling extremely difficult.

Making “being modern” an end in itself is a dangerous selection criterion. Too-new technology can impose high learning cost and instability; overly mature/stale technology can make the company unattractive to engineers who want challenge.

Frequent related problems: tech selection disconnected from organization and hiring strategy; the stack becoming a black box so outsiders cannot be brought in; missing documentation and ADRs so onboarding takes abnormally long.
Leaving a technology that only one person in the company can touch, and selecting a stack without estimating future technology-migration cost, are similarly fatal.

Failure patterns in technology stack selection often occur when the choice is not treated as a judgment about the future, but instead as uncritical acceptance of current conditions or advisor opinions, combined with insufficient understanding of the chosen technology's properties; this knowledge gap frequently leads to unexpected large-scale rewrites or rebuilds.

A more serious anti-pattern is treating technology selection as a purely operational/field-level matter and detaching it from management decision-making; this commonly results in tech-stack changes becoming practically impossible and unclear accountability for technical decisions.

When a real CTO is absent or the CTO role is in name only, typical problems include inability to explain the rationale behind technology choices, successors who cannot inherit those judgments, technology that fails to follow shifts in business strategy, and business plans made without understanding technical constraints.

Technical debt can drive hiring difficulties and rising turnover, exhausting the organization if leadership fails to notice the connection; the root cause is the absence of people on the team who both understand technology and can make judgments about it—at minimum, bring in talent (even as advisors) who can own these decisions.
Product owners must treat technology selection and the handling of technical debt as management decision-making itself.
Core principle: technical debt is the result of management decisions.
Core principle: technology selection locks in (fixes) both business strategy and organizational strategy.
Core principle: technology failures are almost without exception failures of decision-making.
Core principle: the problem is not the technology itself, but who decided what, when, and based on what criteria.

Building a strong technical organization requires a management career path that covers the walls excellent individual-contributor engineers face when moving from player to tech lead, engineering manager (EM), and CTO, and how to overcome those walls.

Product owners can treat evaluation systems and role definitions as a design blueprint for hiring and developing technical management layers and for scaling the structure of the development organization.
The myth that “if you put more people on it, it will finish faster” is false; adding engineers because development is late can lower productivity (Brooks’s law).
True development speed is raised not by mere resource addition but by eliminating person-dependency (属人化) and by improving architecture.
Product owners sometimes must act as coaches so the development team notices problems itself and can run an improvement process.
Accompanying (伴走型) leadership includes drawing out autonomy from teams that wait for instructions and facilitating retrospectives so they do not become hollow rituals.

Recommended resources for these ideas include Camille Fournier’s The Manager’s Path (『エンジニアのためのマネジメントキャリアパス』), Kurahira Yoshito’s 『人が増えても速くならない』, and Rachel Davies & Liz Sedley’s Agile Coaching (『アジャイルコーチング』).
AI should be treated not as a mere convenient tool or automation method, but as something that fundamentally transforms all activities.
The book AI Agents: Machines that Collaborate with Humanity (AI エージェント 人類と協働する機械) by Daichi Hiroki (広木大地), Ric Telecom, 2025, explains why this view of AI is essential.
The book discusses how AI can participate in decision-making, execution, and learning, and how human roles must be redefined as a result.
AI is not a passing trend; it must be understood from a medium- to long-term perspective as a lasting presence.
For product owners/managers (プロダクト責任者), the critical question is how AI changes the division of roles: who is responsible for what, and to what extent.
Without understanding that new responsibility split, one cannot read the future P/L of the business.
In the AI era, implementation cost falls while the importance of design judgment, technology selection, and knowing when to abandon work actually rises.
The book supplies a thinking foundation for organizational design, decision-making, and responsibility boundaries (責任分界) that assume AI is already present.
Core theme of the discussed material: redefining the domains that humans themselves should still own (人間が担うべき領域を再定義する).

Product leaders often focus inward on the development organization, internal politics, schedules, and resource allocation, but the essence of product work is understanding and solving customer problems. If that premise collapses, even advanced technology and sophisticated organizational design cannot save product value.
Customer understanding is the highest-priority responsibility of a product owner and must never be abandoned or fully handed off.

Specialist roles that face customers (marketers, customer success, UX researchers) are healthy, but growth often creates an implicit division of labor in which customer understanding is treated as someone else’s job.
Org design, management, hiring, and evaluation get forced calendar time via 1-on-1s and meetings; customer understanding does not, so it only happens if the product owner acts proactively.
The resulting pattern—postponing customer contact because one is busy, or believing documents equal understanding—is the trap of division of labor.
Information gathering and analysis can be delegated to specialists, but delegating customer understanding itself causes the product owner to lose the axis of decision-making.

Customer understanding requires the self-awareness that you understand customers better than anyone else. Perfection is not required, but you must be able to say that customer matters can be left to you.
Without that awareness, you cannot correct team members when their judgments drift, and you cannot present a reliable judgment axis in emergencies.
Customer understanding is not an output; it is a prerequisite for decision-making and is itself the judgment axis.
Treating customer understanding as research or report-writing work misses its essence. It is the infrastructure of decision-making, not a deliverable.
Product vision, roadmap, prioritization, and decisions about what to discard all fail without the latest, deep customer understanding.

Decisions made after losing customer understanding lose the junction of technology, organization, and strategy and create large distortions—for example, roadmaps aimed at personas different from actual customers, technical optimization that sacrifices customer experience, and resulting mismatched organizational structure.
Customer understanding is often wrongly equated with implementing customer requests as-is. What customers say and what they truly need do not coincide.

Customer understanding is not taking customers’ words at face value; it is discovering insights even customers themselves have not noticed, by going into the motivations, constraints, and context behind surface requests.
Product owners need empathy plus interpretation and editing skill: they use customer voices as raw material and translate them into business and product terms.

Only primary information leads to customer understanding: actual customer words, silences, hesitations, tone of voice, facial expressions, and the atmosphere of the setting. These cannot be obtained from secondary information such as documents and dashboards.
Secondary information is efficient but has already been edited, so it cannot substitute for primary information.

Processed or second-hand information, especially survey results and external research reports, often has the most important noise and context stripped away for customer understanding; arbitrary editing to make results look better is also common.
Quantitative data shows what is happening but not why it is happening. Behavioral logs and KPIs are materials for forming hypotheses, not answers themselves.

Only qualitative customer understanding enables deep exploration of why things are the way they are. Repeated hypothesis validation and narrowing to high-quality actions depend on customer understanding.
Nothing is more dangerous than treating someone else's summarized customer framework as fact without verification.
The ideal for customer understanding is conducting user interviews yourself. For B2B products this can be hard, so start by sitting in on sales meetings or customer-success (CS) meetings.
Hearing customers yourself matters because information filtered through sales or CS inevitably carries unconscious filters due to internal interests and politics.
Customer understanding cannot be sustained by individual effort alone. Product organizations must build a culture in which the question 'which customer is this decision for?' arises naturally.

When engineers, designers, and QA can refer to specific prior interview cases (e.g., 'this matches the case of so-and-so we interviewed'), that is evidence that customer understanding is rooted in the organization. Creating that atmosphere is part of the product owner's job.

Experience design is not done by sensation or personal taste alone. Terms such as 'good experience' and 'bad experience' sound clear but, when used subjectively, discussions collapse because criteria for good vs. bad differ by each person's position and experience, and both sides can claim a degree of correctness.

Section 7-2 covers progressing discovery from the idea stage through to concretizing experience design (customer journey through service blueprint), i.e., the process immediately before building a product from scratch.

Experience design (体験設計) must be treated as a tool for consensus-building and decision-making and must always proceed in a structured way using frameworks; unstructured, ad-hoc approaches turn discussions into clashes of preferences and values with no resolution, consuming time—especially when executives or product owners hold strong preconceptions.
Organizing facts with the correct framework is of primary importance so that debates do not become answerless arguments such as “that may not be right” or “this could also be considered.”

Before entering experience design, use an Inception Deck to verbalize the project’s overall picture: why the project exists, what value it aims to create, what constraints apply, and what must not happen.

Many internal coordination issues can be resolved by returning to the Inception Deck; if the deck remains vague, debates such as “is this the right way to proceed?” or “who decides?” continue indefinitely and physically steal time that should be spent facing customers.
Next use a Customer Journey Map to visualize the customer’s actions, thoughts, and emotional changes along a time axis.

When creating a new business or product, the essential question is not “what features should we build?” but “how do we support the customer’s experience.” Proceeding only from the provider’s ideas (“this feature is needed,” “this product should sell”) produces a self-centered, product-out offering that may have no real customers or that must be forced onto the market.

A customer journey map (カスタマージャーニーマップ) is not a finished deliverable but a map for deepening understanding of the customer. It is a tool for posing questions such as: where customers feel value, where they stumble, what emotions they hold, where the real pain that the product can solve lies, and what dissatisfaction remains even after using existing alternatives.

Do not treat a customer journey map as a one-time artifact. First draw it as a hypothesis, then verify it through customer interviews and similar research, and redraw it repeatedly. Through this iterative process, the resolution (解像度) of the customer journey increases.

Customer journey maps also surface organizational fragmentation in the customer experience. Although the experience is continuous from the customer's perspective, internally it is often split across sales, customer success (CS), and support, with fragmented ownership and information.
A typical symptom of this organizational split is that a customer using multiple products does not know whom to contact when they have a problem.
Experience design (体験設計) is an act that reaches beyond the product itself into organizational design.

A simplified customer journey map example typically covers stages such as: 認知・発見 (awareness/discovery: SNS, word of mouth, noticing, interest, expanding awareness); 検索・検討 (search/consideration: search/compare, comparing, considering, differentiation); 意思決定・購入 (decision/purchase: EC store, buying, conviction, purchase simplification); 利用・体験 (use/experience: arrival, guidance, starting to use, experience, onboarding); and 評価・共有 (evaluation/share: review, share, telling others, recommendation, becoming a fan). Layers often include 接点 (touchpoints), 顧客行動 (customer behavior), 思考感情 (thoughts and emotions), and 課題機会 (challenges and opportunities).
When drawing a Customer Journey Map, competitors, alternatives, and overall market structure inevitably become a concern; the Business Model Canvas is effective for surveying that market structure.

A Customer Journey Map captures customer movements, while a Business Model Canvas captures market and business structure; combining the two makes it possible to think about customer experience and business structure at the same time.
Multiple frameworks can be combined according to the situation (e.g., Value Proposition Canvas, SWOT analysis) so that necessary information is gathered without excess or deficiency.

What matters is creating a state in which all outputs remain and continue to be updated; preparing a place to return to when one is lost or has forgotten something is the foundation for continuously advancing experience design.
After customer experience and business structure have been drawn, the service structure that realizes them is considered using a Service Blueprint.
A Service Blueprint is a framework that visualizes the front-stage experience visible to the user together with the systems and operational processes that support it behind the scenes.
Framework usage by purpose (Figure 7-2): Service Blueprint — detailing how the service is provided, movements of backstage staff and systems, service quality management, identifying bottlenecks.
Framework usage by purpose: Business Model Canvas — defining the nine building blocks, overall picture of the business model, verification of profitability.
Framework usage by purpose: Customer Journey Map — visualizing customer processes, grasping emotional movements, identifying issues (pains), touchpoint analysis.
Framework usage by purpose: Persona — defining target customers, making characteristics concrete, building shared understanding within the team.
User Story Mapping is another complementary framework used alongside these for experience and communication design.

With the development of AI, mockups and prototypes can be created at high speed; once frameworks have raised the resolution of experience design, immediately giving it form is becoming the new common sense.
Documents have not become unnecessary; documents are logs of decision-making.

Visual or summarized outputs still require complementary explanation of why choices were made; the role of filling in background and constraints that appearance alone cannot convey remains indispensable.
Have your own organization methods (整理手法). Frameworks are excellent tools (武器), but using them without matching them to purpose causes confusion rather than clarity.

Match framework to purpose and clearly separate ends from means: Inception Deck to align project premises; Customer Journey Map to understand customer experience; User Story Mapping to organize issue priorities.

Like Doraemon pulling out the right tool for Nobita’s situation, keep many frameworks as a personal toolkit and use them fit-for-purpose rather than assembling a unique way of thinking from scratch every time.
With thinking tools in place, attention can focus on accumulating facts (ファクト) and hypotheses (仮説) rather than on inventing the thinking method itself.
Periodically review whether a tool still fits the current situation and has not become outdated; this raises the accuracy of experience design (体験設計).

All outputs organized so far are nothing more than hypotheses. The essence of experience design is a fine-grained back-and-forth: organize with a framework, meet customers, verify, then organize again.
Running frameworks only at the desk produces products nobody uses. Meeting customers without organizing the findings fails to involve stakeholders and cannot form consensus.
Desk work and field work must keep circulating like the two wheels of a bicycle. That cycle is the only path to truly understanding customer experience and creating valuable products.

Section 7-3: Collaboration with designers and UX researchers starts from the premise that final responsibility for customer understanding cannot be delegated, no matter how excellent the designer or UX researcher is.
Ultimate product responsibility always rests with the product owner (プロダクト責任者). Relinquishing it inevitably creates contradictions between the product vision and mid-to-long-term direction.

A product vision built on shallow customer understanding becomes a mere slogan: it looks correct and no one objects, but no concrete picture of the experience emerges. Even with the same framework, members interpret it differently, so unified experience design never happens.

When no one owns decisions that resolve those contradictions, the product owner's own intent disappears from the product. Therefore, continuously holding high-resolution customer understanding that is linked to intent is an indispensable duty of the final responsible person.

When developing from customer understanding, one must keep defining 'which customers, and what change we want to cause in them.' This is not a UX tactic; it is the act of defining the product's reason for existence (存在意義).

After release, measure whether that intended change actually occurred (qualitatively and quantitatively) and reflect. Check original goals, KPIs/OKRs, and whether the product is approaching its vision. The product owner must never hand off measurement and reflection.

Few people can translate UX quality into business results and strategic context. Converting 'UX improved / experience improved' into management language ('so what actually changed?'), sharing it with executives, and fulfilling accountability is a core role of the product owner.

The product owner holds final decision-making responsibility that integrates qualitative and quantitative insight, and must keep judging how to connect customer understanding to the product roadmap (priority of value delivery plus timeline toward the product's goal).
Decision-making based on customer understanding cannot be delegated. As customer understanding deepens, issues and needs that were not originally anticipated emerge.
Product managers (プロダクト責任者) own decisions about whether customer requests belong on the product roadmap, whether to postpone them, and when to address them.

When UX improvements trade off against business KPIs, the product manager must decide what to prioritize, what not to do, and in what order; those choices create consistency across the whole product roadmap.

Customer requests often fall into local optima (局所最適). Product managers must keep a bird’s-eye view and not accept UX research results or customer voice at face value; they have a duty to question and reframe them.
When customer voice contradicts management judgment, the product manager should stand between the two and translate so that UX can be explained in terms of outcomes.
Converting UX work into business results and explaining that conversion remains the product manager’s ongoing responsibility.
After owning those decisions, actual UX execution should be left to specialists.

Specialist UX work spans discovery through delivery: research design, method selection and execution, interview design, usability testing, personas and customer journeys, information architecture and UI design, and iterative prototyping and validation.

In the launch phase a product manager may do some of this work themselves, but deeper work requires higher resolution; collaborating with specialists yields more effective and efficient experience design.

Collaboration easily blurs boundaries: whether to implement customer voice as-is or interpret and elevate it, and who decides the ‘right’ UX. Those calls should be made as a team, always against product-vision alignment.
The ideal is to entrust UX judgment to specialists, but that only works if those specialists understand the business and the vision.
When research findings conflict with business judgment, the final decision maker is usually the product manager.

Teams should maintain a productive tension: designers and UX researchers going too far into business strategy (and conversely, product managers over-controlling craft) can undermine user-centered outcomes.

There is an inherent tension in product organizations: product value can be damaged when UX is neglected, but product owners who become too involved in UX details can reduce their contribution to the business. Healthy debate should proceed on the assumption of this tension.

Good UX does not automatically equal sales or growth. Organizations must agree in advance on how to define ROI of UX improvements, how to evaluate outputs, and on KPI design and management policy. Neglecting this leaves the UX function as an internal support or advisory unit that loses ownership, producing dumping of work, indifference, person-dependent UX, and a shortage of people who can discuss UX.

Successful collaboration with designers and UX researchers requires these designed premises: (1) pre-sharing of purpose, constraints, and decision criteria; (2) forums for jointly interpreting UX research results; (3) not turning design reviews into decision-making meetings; (4) structures that prevent experts' decision fatigue; (5) clear delegation of authority and assignment of final responsibility; (6) treating UX outputs as a decision log. Only then does a healthy relationship of 'delegating without abandoning' hold.

Frameworks (personas, customer journey maps, user story mapping, service blueprints, etc.) do not create value by themselves. Value appears only when the understanding gained through them is connected to the right decisions.

Who uses a framework and who bears responsibility need not be the same person. Confusing the two easily breaks experience design. Therefore: leave framework usage to specialists, but keep a firm grip on customer understanding and final responsibility.

Figure 7-3 maps the flow of framework use and where responsibility sits. Story Mapping is used to organize user stories, plan releases, identify an MVP, and set priorities. Customer Journey Maps visualize the customer process, capture emotional shifts, identify pain points, and analyze touchpoints. The Inception Deck is used to share vision, clarify goals, grasp risks, and define scope.

Using a framework and owning responsibility for it should be treated as separate roles. Designers and UX researchers typically have the deepest knowledge of which framework fits which situation and how to combine them; they should therefore be the ones who actually apply the tools. The product owner does not need to run every framework personally.

The product owner remains accountable for purpose and decisions: what the team is trying to achieve, what decisions the framework is meant to support, and who owns those decisions. They must be able to explain why a given framework is being used and what will be decided as a result.

When designers or UX researchers produce framework outputs, the product owner still holds final responsibility for that content. Evaluation should not be based on personal taste or gut feel (e.g., 'it doesn't match my intuition' or 'it doesn't sit right'). Discussion should center on whether the output contributes to the stated purpose.
If an expert's approach differs from the product owner's original assumption but is still rational and purpose-aligned, the product owner should be willing to defer and let the expert's method stand.
Once a product owner makes a judgment based on an output, they must accept result-responsibility for decisions made from that output.

Output responsibility requires never giving up access to primary information: raw customer voices, facial expressions, pauses, hesitation, and contradictions. Without that contact, the validity of an output cannot be judged.
Receiving only processed output without primary information always leads to mistaken judgment, and those mistakes cannot be undone later.
Framework outputs (from workshops or organizing sessions) are not finished products. They are intermediate artifacts for verification and hypotheses that should always remain updatable.

A neatly completed workshop output often creates a false sense of completion. A polished artifact is not necessarily a good sign; a rough artifact that deepens customer understanding is more valuable.
Continuously re-ask “who is defined as the customer.” The moment that question stops, experience design begins to drift.
A common trap is assuming “I already know the customer” from founding-era or new-venture research and then making decisions for months or a year on that outdated customer image.
The required stance of a product owner is to keep breaking the “I think I know” mindset and to keep doubting their own understanding, because this trap is especially easy to fall into.
Using multiple frameworks will inevitably produce contradictions between outputs and fluctuations in interpretation (e.g., UX research that does not match product vision or business strategy).

Do not leave ambiguous who sets the discussion, who facilitates, and who makes the final call. Final responsibility sits with the product owner, but they need not personally make every individual output decision.
Even with a tightly structured framework, poor-quality questions produce low-quality answers; the critical step is how well the questions have been honed before the framework is applied.

Questions are refined only by continually touching primary information and steadily raising the resolution of customer understanding; over-reliance on frameworks yields only generic outputs and pursuit of non-existent personas, resulting in products nobody uses or markets that prove extremely narrow.
A valid operating model is to leave judgment to domain experts while remaining accountable for the outcome.
Misalignment between customer understanding and business strategy must never be left unaddressed; once the gap appears the product quietly stalls.

Typical signs of customer-understanding / business-strategy misalignment: (1) taking a subset of customers’ strong voices at face value, (2) over-emphasizing UX so that originally monetizable value is given away free, (3) prioritizing fit with existing customer workflows and thereby stopping the product from driving transformation.

These failure modes all stem from hugging the customer’s current state too closely; the value a product should deliver lies half a step or one step ahead. Experience design pulled by status-quo bias therefore diverges from business strategy.
Chapter summary (section 7-5) introduces six failure patterns of experience design and communication design.
A common UX failure is reducing UX to visual appearance: whether the screen looks pretty, the UI is modern, or animations feel good. This collapses discussion of the whole experience.
When UX is treated as looks, design reviews become debates of taste ('this looks cooler', 'this feels current') instead of who the product is for and in what context it is used.
The root cause is confusing UX with UI. The same feature needs different expression, font size, and interaction depending on whether the user is a child, in their 20s, or in their 80s.
Skipping user and context and treating 'the most modern, cool UI' as the answer turns the work into an interface discussion rather than an experience discussion.

Another pitfall is treating production of artifacts as success: finishing a Figma mockup or prototype creates a false sense that 'UX improvement was done,' after which discussion stalls or never ships into the product.
Over-investing in design systems and guidelines without understanding real customer experience produces process without improved outcomes.
Hypothesis tests and usability tests can fail the same way: the fact of having run them is rewarded, but no one can explain how findings changed the product or what experience actually changed.
When no one can describe UX Before/After, UX work stays disconnected from the product roadmap and is treated as something to do only when there is spare time.
A common failure pattern is making decisions without the customer present: relying on secondhand accounts of customer talk and never touching primary information.

Related cases include looking only at quantitative data while abandoning qualitative understanding, and deciding for reasons unrelated to customers—organizational convenience, schedule, or internal politics (e.g., “it takes too much effort, so let’s not”).
Another case is justifying degradation of customer experience in the name of KPI achievement.

A typical error is mistaking a loud minority of customers for representative customers and interpreting their voice in a self-serving way, so that only the latest voices or most recent requests get priority and the team no longer shares a common answer to “who is the customer?”
A dangerous sign is when “customer understanding” becomes synonymous with reading old interview documents.
Framework dependence is another failure: using a framework creates the illusion of understanding; personas and customer journeys are created once and then left untouched.

Contradictions between frameworks go unaddressed, updates stop, and workshops become mere events. Using the framework itself becomes the evaluation target, and customer data is distorted to fit the frame.

In that state, hypothesis and fact become indistinguishable, and people fall into the illusion that “the output looks clean, therefore it is correct.” Even after involving many people, the question “does this work even matter?” arises and the practice becomes hollow.
When learning from frameworks is not reflected in the product, or the framework work itself is what gets evaluated, that is putting the cart before the horse.

A fifth failure is damaging the relationship with UX specialists: dumping UX entirely on experts so research results are not used in decisions; the UX organization becomes like an internal consultancy and loses a sense of ownership.

When UX ownership is unclear, designers and UX researchers suffer decision fatigue and it becomes unknown who has final responsibility for UX. If the relationship between UX and business KPIs cannot be explained, UX improvement is not discussed in management meetings; even excellent UX specialists then have only limited impact on the business and product. Design importance fails to permeate the organization, and talent often leaves.

Failure pattern 6 (caused by the product owner): the product owner claims to have “delegated” customer understanding, stops touching primary information, and is dragged by past success. Overconfidence (“I already understand the customer”) appears; internal explanations are prioritized over customers. UX is treated as an implementation topic rather than strategy, UX discussion is postponed, and time to update customer understanding is not intentionally reserved. Experience then does not improve; the team moves further from customer understanding. A product owner who creates this state can be said to have lost qualification for the role.

When these failures accumulate, typical outcomes include: unused features being mass-produced; UX work that produces no results; loss of product consistency; growing distance from customers year by year; ambiguity inside the team about who the product is for; and the word “UX” itself losing credibility.
To avoid creating an organization that develops aversion to UX and experience design, the principles discussed in the preceding material should be adopted.
Chapter 7 is titled Experience Design and Communication Design (体験設計とコミュニケーション設計).
The greatest failure of UX research is conducting it but not using the results; research must be connected directly to management decision-making.
UX research does not produce answers. It supplies material that raises the quality of decisions; final judgment remains a human responsibility.
Key utilization processes for UX research include how to interpret findings, how far to trust them, and which decisions they should inform.
A practical challenge is connecting UX research to product vision and business strategy (from 『UXリサーチの活かし方』 by 瀧本はろか, 翔泳社, 2024).
Gameful design implements mechanisms that make people absorbed in order to raise continuation/retention rates; it is not limited to badges and points.

Motivation design examines why people continue and become absorbed, covering the risks of relying on extrinsic motivation, how to design intrinsic motivation, and the distinction between short-term behavior and long-term habits.
These principles apply to B2B products and work tools as well as B2C: the goal is an experience that is not merely used but continuously used (from 『ゲームフルデザイン』 by 伊藤真人, 翔泳社, 2025).
Chapter context: Chapter 7 covers 体験設計とコミュニケーション設計 (experience design and communication design).
GTM (Go-To-Market) strategy is the execution plan for how to deliver a product to the market and acquire customers.

How you cut segments determines product success and growth: even an excellent product will not have its value correctly delivered if segmentation is wrong; conversely, appropriate segmentation lets you draw a winning path even with limited resources.
Broad (wide-sense) marketing is the overall set of activities that deliver value to customers and create a system that sells.
Segmentation and positioning are the core of translating marketing activities into concrete strategy; in practice they are often confused and treated as equivalent.
Segmentation means dividing the market (deciding who to target). Positioning means taking a stance within that divided market (how to differentiate from competitors).
Positioning cannot be established if the segment is vague. Claims such as 'I want to be number one' or 'I want to be a distinctive presence' are not valid positioning without a clear segment.
Market selection (which battlefield to enter) is a prior, larger decision; within the chosen market, segmentation and positioning define how you actually compete.

It is dangerous when theory alone precedes strategy and the target segment to win in is undefined. Speaking only of standing position without a target segment looks like branding but is empty self-assertion. Position is always taken inside a market; refined segmentation is indispensable for good positioning. First divide the market into segments, then decide where to stand—do not reverse this order.

Segmentation should be cut by customer problems (課題で切る), not by attributes. A common organizational pitfall is dividing by industry, company size, or age. These attributes are easy to understand but fail to capture individuals’ actual challenges, contexts, and diversity.

Especially for B2B products, the age of the person in charge or the company’s size does not necessarily determine the problems they face. Even within the same industry and same company size, challenges differ greatly depending on business phase and situation. Conversely, companies in different industries or of different sizes can share extremely similar problems.

Therefore segmentation should be performed on the axis of ‘what kind of problem they have, in what kind of context,’ not on attributes. Attributes do not directly represent the issues. The proper axes for cutting segments are situation, problems/challenges, and constraint conditions.
Segmentation means ‘dividing the market’; positioning means ‘taking a standing position’ within that divided market (Figure 8-1).

The same offering can belong to a different segment when its context changes: a change of department changes the scope of responsibility and the problems to be solved; a change of assigned work changes the solutions that are needed. Touchpoints (every contact point between customer and company/service) should therefore be viewed in terms of situation, not person.

When opening a new segment, people often claim there are no competitors. No such segment exists. What is usually true is only that an identical product form does not exist; substitutes and the status quo remain powerful competitors. A seemingly competitor-free segment may simply have weak need or failed monetization; one must ask whether competitors are truly absent and why.

Segment granularity matters. Segments that are too fine have too few target customers for sales and marketing to act. Segments that are too coarse cannot support decisions and collapse into a collection of one-off responses. The quality of a segment is judged not by theoretical correctness but by whether the organization can actually move on it.

How segments are cut is directly tied to organization design. Targeting SMB (mid-size firms with relatively fast decisions and low adoption hurdles), enterprise (large organizations with complex requirements and high unit price), or domains that require deep specialized knowledge each demands very different talent. Hiring and skill-set priorities follow from segment choice. Organization design that is misaligned with the market creates internal friction and leaves even strong people unable to perform.

Touchpoints must be chosen decisively when considering segments. Touchpoint selection is itself a survival strategy. Targeting every segment looks ambitious but is equivalent to having no target. Marketing executed with vague touchpoints becomes mere noise.

Marketing measures only become meaningful once it is clear who to reach, what to deliver, and why. Vague ideas such as “just try hitting a wide audience” or “let’s run a commercial” are empty without this clarity.
Touchpoint setting is a prerequisite for every marketing action, no matter how small. If you cannot choose and commit to specific touchpoints, you cannot win at any of them.
A core pre-marketing decision is to identify the segment where you can actually win and then decide how to fill that touchpoint with measures—segmenting before product development.
TAM (Total Addressable Market) is the maximum market size if everyone in the world became a customer.
SAM (Serviceable Available Market) is the portion of TAM narrowed to the company’s target segment that it can actually approach.
SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market) is the realistically obtainable share of SAM after accounting for the company’s own capabilities and the competitive situation.
TAM > SAM > SOM form a nested structure: TAM is the largest possible market, SAM is the approachable subset, and SOM is the realistically winnable subset.
Treating TAM/SAM/SOM as mere number-fitting is dangerous; companies often define the market too broadly so the figures look convenient rather than truthful.

Arbitrarily expanding segment definitions for investor materials or internal explanations may feel easy in the short term, but it creates a gap versus actual segment size and significantly degrades decision quality.
TAM, SAM, and SOM should not be used as explanatory materials for others; they should be used as a framework for deciding where to win first.
SOM in particular is a concept for making explicit the battlefield where you first win completely; if this remains vague, neither sales nor marketing can function.
Targeting a niche market is often misread as fleeing to a small market; the greatest value of a niche is high learning speed and high win rate.
A product that cannot even become number one in a small market has an extremely low chance of winning in a large market.
A realistic, highly reproducible modern winning path is to first take an overwhelming position in a limited market, then expand horizontally.
It is essential to judge whether a chosen niche can expand in the future or will become a dead end.
Touchpoint selection and product strategy cannot be separated: recutting the segment necessarily changes product requirements.
There is a limit to continuously changing only the product without changing the segment.
However excellent a product is, it will not be used and monetization will not work if the need does not exist.
Setting touchpoints can be said to define the product roadmap.
When defining touchpoints, apply Jobs-to-be-Done: do not ask whether the product fits the segment, but what job the customer is trying to get done.
Competitors are not necessarily similar products; every means that solves the same job is a competitor—including other IT products, human BPO, Excel/spreadsheets, or the status quo of doing nothing.
This jobs view is a way to break out of feature-versus-feature competition.
Redefine market segments by job (Jobs to be Done), starting from what the customer is trying to accomplish rather than traditional demographic or firmographic cuts.
Winning-customer definition: reverse-engineer the target segment from people who will buy now, not from a future ideal customer profile.
Burning need (product-development term): a state of desperate, immediate need—the customer wants the solution so badly they would ‘reach for it with both hands.’
Do not start with a visionary future customer; first define the customer you can actually win with today.

Early adopters vs. early majority: early adopters invest and experiment before many public success stories exist; early majority wait until they see those stories. Target early adopters first. Mixing them up produces a ‘looks sellable but nobody buys now’ market.

Positioning goal: be named in the customer’s comparison set (‘for cheapness it’s X, for quality it’s Y, for changing how we work it’s Z’). Positioning is a relative evaluation formed in the customer’s mind, not a company declaration.
You do not need to be #1; a clear, defensible position is the foundation for brand (covered in a later chapter). The subject of positioning is the customer, not the company.
Functional advantages are copied and become obsolete. Establish positioning at the meaning layer—value, stance, and how the product is used—not at the feature layer.
Be able to explain, in the customer’s own words, why the function is needed and why it is chosen.
Competitors are not only products in the same category: people-intensive workarounds, Excel, manual processes, and the status quo itself are all competitors.
Correct positioning is impossible without understanding what is included in the customer's decision set (the set of alternatives they consider).
Trying to serve every direction (全方位対応) destroys positioning. It is essential to clearly define what you will not do and which customers you are not suited for.
Whether the sales team can refuse customers is a key indicator of whether positioning is actually functioning.
Positioning cannot be changed easily. Brand awareness accumulates over time and cannot be reset. Changing positioning requires understanding both the reason and the cost.
A Product Marketing Manager (PMM) is the role that joins product and market. It requires simultaneous product understanding and market understanding, making it an extremely high-difficulty position.

In many organizations, during early product development the PM also performs product-marketing work: designing who to tell, what to tell, and how to tell it, and delivering the product's value to the market.
That combined PM + product-marketing model works when the market is single and customer segments are limited.
Once a product achieves PMF and must simultaneously pursue multiple customer segments and touchpoints, one PM can no longer cover both product and market.
Example: enterprise, mid-market, and small-business segments each have different resonating value, messages to emphasize, and decision-making processes.
As the number of targeted segments grows and the product scales, a PMM is hired as the translator between product and market.
Organizations that need a PMM are those that become multi-product (or otherwise need to address multiple segments/touchpoints at once).

PMM (Product Marketing Manager) is the person responsible for defining who to communicate to and how. Their role is not limited to correctly explaining product features; they must verbalize value and context.
PMM stands between the PM, the market, sales, and customer success, translating each party's perspective so that the product's value is correctly understood in the market.

If a PMM's hypotheses or judgments are wrong, even an excellent product will fail to have its value reach the market. As a result, the PM's outcomes are not properly evaluated and the organization falls into a state of not knowing why the product does not sell.

A marketer is the specialist who creates a state of being continuously chosen. Even for digital products, the essence of marketing is largely the same as for consumer goods or manufacturers: acquire awareness, get onto the comparison stage, and ultimately be selected. The marketer designs, executes, and continuously improves this entire flow.
Concrete marketer responsibilities include designing channel strategy (web ads, events, PR, SNS, SEO, etc.), executing and operating initiatives, and building improvement cycles.
Being chosen by AI (LLMO / AI Search optimization) has recently entered the marketer's scope, in addition to search engines.
Marketers use data to visualize market reactions, determine which initiatives are working, and identify where improvement is needed; a data-analyst perspective is therefore essential.
PMM and marketers are translators to each other. They are not in a hierarchical relationship, nor is it the case that the PMM solely thinks strategy while the marketer solely executes.

PMM (Product Marketing Manager), marketer, and PM (Product Manager) are complementary specialists rather than a simple division of labor: they respectively address how value is delivered to the market and how the market perceives it. PMM rarely handles ad operations; marketers do not typically lead product strategy.

Core responsibilities: PMM is accountable for making the product's value succeed in the market; the marketer is accountable for delivering it to the market and keeping it chosen; the PM is accountable for creating product value.

Effective collaboration among the three requires shared agreement on segments and positioning, plus: a loop that iterates message hypotheses and market validation; mechanisms that feed marketing-campaign results back into the product; a culture that treats campaign reviews as learning rather than blame; and regular forums that share market changes.
The product leader must neither dump work entirely onto PMM/marketers nor micromanage every detail. Ultimate ownership of segments and positioning remains with the product leader.

Role evolution by stage: in the launch phase the PM typically concurrently holds these roles; in the growth phase a dedicated PMM becomes necessary; in the expansion phase division of labor with marketers advances; multi-product organizations further layer the roles. Continuously design the organizational structure so that these roles keep functioning.
Section 8-3 principle: the product leader tightly holds target (segment) selection and delegates tactics/execution.

Target selection is a committed decision, not merely an analysis. Even after gathering data and refining hypotheses, what remains is a human act of will: 'where do we bet?' Selecting one option from a list requires no special skill; possessing the resolve to accept every resulting consequence does.

That resolve is work only a business or product leader can carry. Segment choice is a 'decision' (ketsudan), not a 'judgment': it means proceeding even while residual doubt remains. No market exists with 100 % certainty. Therefore segment selection is something anyone can perform yet must not be delegated to just anyone.

Choosing a target segment is an act of intentionally discarding possibilities in order to maximize the probability of winning. It also means defining customers you will not serve, problems you will not address, and revenue you will not pursue for now.
Segment-choice decisions carry a heavy psychological burden because many leaders feel that going after everything prevents missed opportunities. That feeling is an illusion.

Choosing not to narrow the market produces products and messages that do not deeply penetrate any market. Without this recognition, stacking marketing tactics yields scattered, disconnected activities rather than a coherent line.

To raise the value of marketing initiatives, place a hypothesis before executing: define in advance roughly how likely the initiative is to succeed and roughly how much result it should produce, then verify the accuracy of that hypothesis.
The meaning of a result differs completely depending on the prior hypothesis: a campaign expected to score 60 that scored 50 is not the same as a campaign expected to score 100 that scored 50.
Being able to explain why a given initiative was run turns campaigns from mere tasks into learning.
Treat marketing initiatives as sensors for understanding markets and customers. Connect campaign results to the product roadmap so selling is not the end of the design.
Product owners must be able to tell which layer of discussion they are in: market strategy, product marketing, or individual tactics.

Segment selection and campaign-level decisions sit at different hierarchical levels. Segment selection is a higher-order concept that affects product, roadmap, pricing, messaging, channels, and organizational design; once chosen, subsequent decisions are pulled toward it.
Marketing campaigns are trial-and-error conducted on top of the premises of segment selection, assuming failure and iterating at high speed.

Do not confuse market hypotheses (市場仮説) with tactic/measure hypotheses (施策仮説). A typical error is the shortsighted judgment that 'if measures don't hit, the market is bad.' Often the communication method or channel choice is wrong while the market hypothesis itself is still valid.

Running tactics at high speed while the market hypothesis remains vague is also dangerous: the team merely celebrates or mourns hits and misses, no learning accumulates, people burn out, and trust in marketing itself is lost.
Keep the market hypothesis unchanged in the short term and change tactic hypotheses rapidly. Only this separation lets marketing function as a learning system.

Continuously running measures without fixing the segment makes it impossible to tell what went wrong. Frequently changing segment selection because tactics failed prevents deeper understanding of the segment.

To conclude that the market hypothesis was wrong, define conditions in advance: 'If this segment choice is correct, at least this level of response should appear.' Only if that expectation is not met over a defined period should the market hypothesis be questioned. That order matters.

What the product owner must hold (vs. what to delegate to specialists) are the decisions about who to target and how to differentiate from competitors. Relinquishing those decisions makes individual tactics look optimized while the overall effort keeps drifting.

Delegating is not abandoning. Preconditions must be shared: why this segment was chosen, which hypothesis is being bet on, and what is being verified. These must be verbalized into a common understanding.

The product owner's degree of involvement changes by phase: in the launch/startup phase the owner deeply engages in both segment selection and tactics while exploring; in the growth phase the owner holds segment selection and begins to delegate tactics.

In later phases, the product owner retains only the judgment on market expansion and fully delegates tactics/measures; however, across every phase, responsibility for segment selection must never be relinquished.
The product owner’s required role is to understand the overall marketing picture and know what is happening at which layer.

Product owners should retain: segment definition (cuts depend deeply on customer situation, so the person who best understands customer experience must strongly influence it); ideal-customer and jobs-to-be-done context (the person closest to customers can identify the ideal customer and the jobs they perform); the high-level positioning (standing within the segment is informed by competitors and industry trends, so the person who best understands the whole market should keep it); and explicit definition of customers/segments not to serve (positioning is a declaration that everything else is deprioritized; exclusion is paired with segmentation).

Specialists should own: channel selection (optimal approach given the decided positioning is best set by professionals who know many methods); messaging expression (choosing the best message for channel × positioning requires a large repertoire of expressions); measure prioritization and execution (people who have run many campaigns can estimate outcomes within the chosen direction; share goals then incorporate expert input); and operational improvement/optimization (daily reaction-driven PDCA and accurate follow-up actions are the experts’ strength).

Final responsibility for segmentation and positioning belongs to the business owner and product owner, not the marketer. Specialists can be assigned verification and execution, but forming hypotheses and deciding direction cannot be delegated. That judgment is the starting point for the product roadmap, organizational design, and all messaging.

GTM strategy and marketing failure pattern 1: becoming lost in the market (市場迷子). This is the biggest marketing failure and almost always surfaces as tactic-dependency. When market selection is vague, tactics such as ads, events, content, SEO, and SNS are piled on one after another; if results do not appear, the team switches to another tactic. Organizations in this loop repeat exhaustion rather than learning.
A worse form of being lost in the market is the next failure: tactic-first thinking (施策ファースト).

GTM strategy and marketing failure pattern 2: starting from tactics rather than from strategy. Examples that look proactive but fail: “let’s just run ads,” “competitors are doing events so we should too,” “SNS is growing so let’s push X,” “SEO is important so let’s write articles.” Tactics executed without defining who to reach, in what context, and why almost certainly fail.
The core problem of tactic-first marketing is that it reduces marketing to an execution problem, instead of treating it as a strategic choice of market, context, and reason to communicate.
GTM/marketing is the act of first understanding the market and customers, then choosing optimal means on that premise. If that order is reversed, measures lose their purpose.

Measure-first organizations often learn incorrectly from campaign results: ads that miss → 'ads are meaningless'; weak event turnout → 'events are not a fit'; unread content → 'publishing is useless.'
Most such failures are not problems with the measure itself, but with wrong segment selection and messaging.

Executing measures on a vague market hypothesis means failure has no diagnosable cause. Only the crude conclusion 'we tried and it didn't work' remains before jumping to the next tactic. That is not learning; it is 'measure gacha' (施策ガチャ).
A market that looks like a blue ocean can have zero demand. The slogan 'no competitors means opportunity' is a trap if you do not investigate why competitors are absent.
Absence of competitors usually means either the problem is overwhelmingly hard and no one has succeeded, or demand does not exist. Zero-demand blue oceans are the most dangerous.
Zero-demand blue oceans are often sold with phrases such as 'a market no one has noticed yet,' 'it will definitely come,' and 'no competitors so we get first-mover advantage.'
In reality, 'no competitors' often means customers are not seriously in pain, not that a hidden market exists.
Where customers truly struggle, some alternative always exists: Excel, manual work, outsourcing, or status quo. Those substitutes are real competitors.
If even those substitutes do not exist, the issue is typically 'not worth solving' or 'customers are not hurting enough to pay.'
Running tactics in a zero-demand market produces no ad response, unread content, and sales conversations that end with “not now.”
A tactics-first organization misdiagnoses this as bad messaging, insufficient awareness, or a need for more tactics—when the real problem is that the market itself does not exist.
Adding more tactics when the market is not viable is equivalent to pouring water into a leaking bucket.

Failure patterns form a closed loop: ambiguous segment selection → tactics-first execution → no results → judging the market as bad → searching for a new “competitor-free market” → applying tactics again.
In that loop the organization endlessly hunts for the “correct” market; the actual problem is confusing segment selection with the hierarchy of tactics.
The root cause of these failures converges on one thing: no one is accountable for segment selection.

Tactics and deepening market understanding can be delegated; deciding which market to target, which demand to bet on, and which customers to abandon must remain the resolve and responsibility of the business owner or product owner.
Holding that accountability turns marketing from a war of attrition into learning and growth.
Segment selection is a higher-level decision than marketing tactics or campaigns.
Do not confuse the failure of a tactic with the failure of segment selection.
Avoid being tactic-first; think market-hypothesis-first.
Markets with 'no competitors' should raise suspicion about whether demand actually exists.
Marketing tactics function as sensors for deepening market understanding.
These points appear as takeaways in a chapter on GTM (Go-To-Market) strategy and marketing.
SaaS should not be treated as a mere product model; it is a management system in which market, product, sales, customer success (CS), and organization design are tightly interdependent.

SaaS growth cannot be reduced to the simple story that a good product will automatically grow. Segment choice in SaaS cascades into LTV, CAC, churn rate, onboarding design, pricing model, and sales organization.
Segment selection is not a marketing decision that comes later; it is an act that determines the business structure itself.
There is no single correct SaaS playbook. The right SaaS model changes with the market, so product leaders must abandon ‘because it is SaaS, this method is correct’ thinking.
Book: 『All For SaaS』 (Miyata Yoshitaka, Shoeisha, 2021) frames SaaS growth as this interlocking operating system and ties it to concrete KPIs and organization design.

Strategy should be freed from a binary win/lose frame. Segment choice and positioning do not have 100% correct answers, yet people still ask ‘will this segment hit?’ or ‘will this initiative succeed?’
Strategy is the act of maximizing expected value under uncertainty. Every market has risk and every strategy has uncertainty.
Useful strategic questions are: which option has the highest probability of success, and which choice still leaves learning even if it fails.

Book: 『確率思考の戦略論 ― USJでも実証された数学マーケティングの力』 (Morioka Tsuyoshi and Imanishi Kiyotaka, Kadokawa, 2016) and the related 『確率思考の戦略論 ― どうすれば売上は増えるのか』 (Diamond, 2025) present this mathematical, expected-value approach to marketing and strategy.

Strategy is framed as continually asking “what if,” rather than oscillating with the short-term success or failure of individual marketing tactics. Organizations that treat a campaign miss as a reason to abandon the segment choice itself are especially likely to miss this point.

『確率思考の戦略論―どうすれば売上は増えるのか』 extends probabilistic thinking into why people fail to think rationally. Failures in segment choice and marketing strategy more often come from bias, emotion, and organizational pressure than from missing theory.

Decision-making is quietly distorted by past success experiences, obedience to authority, conformity pressure (同調圧力), and responsibility avoidance. The book’s claim: strategy failure is a problem of the decision environment, not of individual capability.
Product owners, as final decision-makers, absorb these distortions most strongly; the book is presented as a mirror for doubting one’s own judgment.

『LOVED』(Martina Lauchengco, Japanese ed. 2023) treats a product being chosen in the market as a structural condition, not an emotional branding story. The core is designing the relationship with the market.
Positioning is defined as creating a state in which the product’s name comes up in comparison. The book decomposes how that state is formed and maintained.
Product strategy, marketing strategy, and organizational culture must interlock; the book is described as a highly useful PMM (product marketing) textbook for that linkage.
The surrounding section frames GTM as: once something is built, how it is made known to the market and sold (作ったものを、どう市場に認知させて、売るか).

In this book, sales is defined not merely as the technique of selling a product, but as the activity of proposing the product as a solution to the customer's problems and converting that value into confirmed revenue.
Many B2B companies unconsciously draw a line that sales is the sales organization's job and not something the product owner (product lead) should directly engage with.
Core premise to recognize: creating a product that can sell, and the fact that if the person who understands the product best cannot sell it, nobody can sell it.
Exploring whether a product will sell before building it has itself become a prerequisite for product development.
If a product owner distances themselves by saying selling is not their role, that product cannot be considered a good product in the first place.
A product that cannot sell cannot exist; this harsh reality must be faced before collaborating with sales or thinking on the same plane as sales.
The text introduces two patterns of unsellable products that must be confronted (details begin on this page but are cut off).
A good product is not defined merely by doing something technically new (the discussion of what constitutes a good product begins here).

Technical completeness and excellent UX are components of product quality, but they are completely separate from whether customers will pay. Even a highly refined product creates no business value unless it is tied to a problem customers will pay to solve.
Unsellable products typically fall into two patterns. The first is product-out: building something nobody asked for, disconnected from customer problems, so no one pays.

The second unsellable pattern is going too far ahead of the customer's problem. The product requires a large replacement of the customer's workflow or operational structure, and the customer's understanding or readiness has not caught up. The result is judgments like 'it seems valuable but we cannot buy it now' or 'it is still too early,' and a market does not form.

Important distinction: 'does not sell' is not the same as 'has no value.' Separate whether value is not yet established from whether discovery or communication of value has failed. In either case, do not look away from the fact that customer value is not currently established.

Products that cannot exist as a business also fall into two typical patterns. The first is that sales scale cannot cover costs: the upper bound of TAM (number of users in the market times unit price) is clearly insufficient relative to development, operations, and sales costs. Even an excellent product cannot stand as a business.

The second non-viable-business pattern is 'would use if free, but will not pay.' The product is convenient, but free substitutes already exist, or the customer can handle it in-house with some extra effort. There is no economic rationale to pay. Analogous to tools like Word or Excel that already exist as taken-for-granted instruments.
Sales is not a downstream process after product completion; it is part of the product itself. Considerations about how a product will be sold must happen before the product is finished, not after.
