Sales is a design problem, not merely a matter of salespeople's effort. The way a product sells is itself a product requirement and a part of service design. Who will buy it, why, and how should be designed before the product is built.

A common corporate misconception is that if a product is technically novel and has refined UX but still does not sell, the cause is insufficient sales effort. From the standpoint of salespeople who are forced to push something that will not sell, that demand is unreasonable.

To design who buys, why, and how, the purchasing entity must be decomposed. In BtoC, the decision-maker, user, and champion are often the same person and decisions tend to be immediate. In BtoB, the decision-maker and user are typically separate, and among users both champions (promoters) and non-champions coexist.

For a given product, identify: Who is the decision-maker? Who is the user? Who is the champion/promoter? Then design what value each receives, what anxieties must be removed, and how the product and sales process will supply information that makes it easy for the champion to explain the product to the decision-maker. That entire chain is the design of how the product sells.

It is extremely dangerous to dump onto sales the full responsibility for designing purchase reasons and introduction triggers and for visualizing the decision process and emotional dynamics. Sales is specialized and each member sees only a partial view of customers, so explanations tend toward local optima.

The product owner must integrate the fragmentary facts held by individual sales members and abstract them into a coherent, explainable account of why this product is chosen. That work affects hiring, organizational motivation, and roadmap design.
A product does not sell because its features are good. It sells only when people understand in what scene and what problem it solves.
Sales first-hand (primary) information is invaluable because meeting minutes cannot capture customer facial expressions, hesitation, enthusiasm/temperature, or internal company circumstances.
Even a single word such as 'want' (ほしい) can have completely different backgrounds; rejection reasons, concerns, and internal politics are information that rarely remains in text.
When product and sales are siloed, this primary information is not used. When they collaborate, sellable vs. unsellable can be judged with reproducibility rather than luck.
One-off accidental wins do not scale. Selling conditions must be structured so that anyone selling has a certain probability of success.
New products always have a period of not selling. The key is treating that period as hypothesis verification rather than neglecting it.
Do not romanticize or beautify not selling. Do not use technology, UX, or philosophy/ideology as excuses. Keep facing the market.
The product owner is responsible for having a judgment axis of whether to improve or withdraw.
Judge calmly by separating emotion from rationality: look for signs of continued positive consideration at multiple companies versus continued clear rejection.
Many 'living dead products' (リビングデッドプロダクト) exist that were never withdrawn. Opening that Pandora's box is also the product owner's role.

The cycle 'selling hypothesis → verification → sales organization' (売れる仮説→検証→セールス組織化) is not a one-time process but a continuously looping part of the product development process (before sales, during sales, and in ongoing operations).
図表9-1 describes a circular cycle from a sellable hypothesis (売れる仮説) through sales (セールス), organization (組織化), and verification (検証), then back to the sellable hypothesis.

A sellable hypothesis is part of the product hypothesis, not a separate afterthought. Whether something will sell should be treated in discovery as a hypothesis on the same level as functional hypotheses and UX hypotheses.
Functional hypothesis (機能仮説) defines what problem the customer wants to solve.
UX hypothesis (UX仮説) designs how that solution will be provided as an experience.
Sellable hypothesis (売れる仮説) defines who will buy it, in what context, at what timing, and at what price.
Functional, UX, and sellable hypotheses are not independent; they strongly depend on each other.

Sellable hypotheses require five elements. Element 1 is the purchasing-subject hypothesis (購買主体の仮説): in B2B products, the decision-maker, promoter, and user are usually different people. You must define each party's position, the value each expects, and at what company size this structure holds. If this remains vague, sales cannot explain who the product actually resonates with.

導入トリガーの仮説: customers will not pay for a future that will be obvious in 10 years or for improvements that might someday be needed. A hypothesis must articulate a reason to introduce the product at this exact moment, such as regulatory/institutional change, a shift in business phase, organizational expansion, or the materialization of risk.

競合・代替手段・現状維持との比較軸: competitors are not limited to products in the same category. Excel, spreadsheets, manual work, human services such as RPO/BPO, and the status quo of doing nothing are all competitors. Customers decide after comparing against these alternatives.

却下理由や不安要素の仮説: anxieties such as high price, operational difficulty, hard internal rollout, and heavy personal responsibility if the project fails always exist. Entering sales without hypothesizing these is like going into battle blindfolded.

価格・契約形態・導入コストへの耐性仮説: whether the offering is subscription, usage-based, or includes an initial fee, and which form this customer would accept and pay, itself defines the relationship between market and product.

仮説検証装置: early-stage sales should be redefined as a hypothesis-verification apparatus before it is an order-taking apparatus. A lost deal is not failure but a disconfirmed hypothesis (learning). A won deal must still be examined for whether it was reproducible under the hypothesis or merely coincidental. The metric is not sold/not-sold but which hypotheses hit and which missed, expressed in language.

Early sales attitude required: go hear reasons for lost deals, dissect reasons for won deals, and feed that information back to the product organization. Convert sales activity from personal hero stories into organizational learning.
Do not assume functional split (field sales / inside sales / customer success) in the early stage, because what sells, to whom it sells, and why it does not sell are not yet clear.
Dividing sales labor is equivalent to leaving product-hypothesis verification to others; in the launch phase the product owner must sell personally.

Startup saying: a product the manager cannot sell themselves cannot be sold by anyone. The same structure applies beyond founding—to new businesses and new products. Even in a mature company, as long as the product is in its launch phase the product owner must sell it.
Selling is not mere sales activity; it is the act of verifying the product hypothesis in the real market.

Whether something sells is not a matter of sales-talk skill but of whether the product hypothesis is true. Information that can only be verified by the product owner selling in person exists while the product is still at the hypothesis stage.

Initial sales should not be expected to close deals immediately. The priority is first-hand customer reactions received with one's own senses: clearly positive; interested but withholding judgment; understood but not leading to adoption; or judged not even worth listening to.

Initial sales also tests these hypotheses: differences between customers who buy and those who do not; patterns in rejection reasons; tolerance for price and contract form; and the presence or absence of an adoption trigger.
Product owners should personally observe the moments when customers lean in versus cool off, in order to discover a sellable structure rather than scaling sales blindly.

Increasing sales headcount or handing the product to an existing sales organization without a visible winning path (勝ち筋) is dangerous: if even the people who understand the product best cannot sell it, others will not be able to sell it either.
When the product owner sells firsthand, unsellability can no longer be blamed on external factors such as high price, a bad market, or a weak sales team.

Where customer reactions change, which explanations fail to land, which contexts raise interest, and whether the product itself is structured in a way that is hard to explain, cannot be learned from sales reports—only by facing customers and trying to sell.
Personal selling experience makes it harder to dump ‘just go sell it’ on sales and then hold them accountable only for results, because failure can be understood as a structural problem.

Selling yourself reveals the gap between the language customers actually use and internal company jargon; specialist terms that feel obvious inside the company often fail to communicate at all. That gap is a communication-design problem that only the product owner can fix immediately.
Sales is the practice of presenting the value the customer truly needs and getting them to pay for that value.
Customers do not buy features; they buy how their work will change and what outcomes they will get.
If the outcomes the product delivers are urgent for the customer, they will listen even if the explanation is somewhat unskilled.
Customers often want improvement of the entire workflow; continuing to explain features without understanding that gap will not produce sales.

Only a product owner who personally sold the product through during the launch phase can confidently hand it over to sales in the growth phase; knowing the pain of selling prevents unreasonable demands and enables healthy relationships among sales, CS, and marketing.
Being able to discuss what sells and does not sell in terms of structure rather than gut feeling is proof of taking responsibility for both the product and the business.
Selling the product yourself in the launch phase requires no special skill—it is simply a matter of doing it or not—and is a prerequisite imposed on the product owner, not an optional choice.

A state ready to hand over to sales (which cannot be organized without selling yourself) includes: winning patterns and losing patterns being verbalized; customers who should not be sold to being clearly defined; validity of pricing, contract forms, and onboarding processes being verified; and the value to be explained being organized by context rather than by features.
Hold market selection and customer definition yourself while delegating sales execution, improvement, and operations; clearly separate decision rights from scope of responsibility.

Product-owner involvement by phase: launch—stand on the front line yourself; growth—run alongside while structuring; expansion—focus on supervising market hypotheses and handling exceptions; maturity—engage only with important customers and new markets.
In the launch phase, sales may be personalized/ad-hoc; the top priority is that a single person (founder, PM, or business owner) appears who can sell independently.
To move sales toward organization, structure why deals were won: winning patterns, losing patterns, rejection reasons, and the decisive moment. Abstract these so others can reproduce them.

Sales organization is not adding headcount; it is designing reproducibility. It is not forcing people to memorize talk scripts, but sharing judgment criteria: which customers, in what order, what to communicate, and where to pull back. Sharing those branching points is the essence of organization.
Sales enablement assets (materials, case studies, demos, comparison tables) should not be left to individual salespeople. The product owner should design them from a flat, unbiased perspective.
Making a product easier to sell is different from exaggerating it. Deciding not to sell to unfit customers is an important decision that protects product value.
Success stories of selling to customers who were a poor fit tend to produce later cancellations, churn, and distortion of the product.

A reproducible sales organization strengthens the product: sales feedback returns to the product, product improvements help the next sale, and the cycle starts turning. Product and sales must not be siloed; they should understand and respect each other's constraints rather than looking down on each other.
The loop of sellable hypothesis → verification → organization must be continuously updated as markets, competitors, and the product evolve. The product owner stands at the center of that cycle.

Field-sales deals and closing alone are not enough for a product to keep selling, keep being used, and grow as a business. Collaboration with inside sales and customer success (as in frameworks such as THE MODEL) is required.
IS, FS, CS, and marketing are all collaboration partners and should not be treated as siloed, disconnected functions.
A core question for product leaders is whether they can design a structure that does not end at the sale but continuously circulates value provision.
IS and CS must not be treated as mere post-order or post-implementation support departments; separating them that way is dangerous.

THE MODEL is often misread as a waterfall-style division of labor; it is actually meant as a circulating structure in which roles move back and forth to deepen customer understanding and value delivery.

When IS, FS, and CS are strictly separated by department, information degrades like a telephone game: primary information thins, context is lost, and customers are forced to repeat the same explanations at every phase change.

Typical failures of siloed handoffs include: customer expectations not being inherited, sales-time promises becoming uncollectible by CS, and rich customer context being reduced to mere attribute data—all of which damage customer experience and trust.
Department-level KPI optimization frequently destroys overall value and customer experience; local optima accumulate into a broken journey.

Product managers must intentionally connect the functions so that selling, onboarding, usage, and outcome creation are designed as one consistent customer experience rather than the company’s fragmented internal workflow.
“Sell,” “get them to use,” and “produce results” form an inseparable continuum; they cannot be treated as independent stages.
On the customer side, decision-makers, approvers, and actual users are often different people, which readily produces fruitless friction such as “I said / I didn’t say” or “I never heard that.”
To prevent that friction, the vendor side must deliberately maintain relationships that span phases rather than resetting at each handoff.

IS (Inside Sales) must be redefined away from mechanical appointment-setting after lead acquisition; emails, DMs, and phone calls all interrupt the recipient’s work and are therefore inherently unpleasant unless the communication is still received favorably and its necessity is understood.
The essence of IS is pursuing interruption-based communication that the other party nevertheless accepts positively and whose necessity they understand.

IS functions as an initial hypothesis-verification device for customer problems: hypotheses formed in pre-product discovery can be tested in a more realistic context, and the ability to make concrete proposals even before development greatly expands what can be verified.
IS also tests door-knocking communication itself—which wording resonates and which value-proposition axes generate responses.
A critical IS role is visualizing the customer’s temperature (interest level), context, and adoption triggers; this is not a mere toss-up (handoff) to Field Sales (FS).

IS must pass along not just a lead but a hypothesis about what the customer is currently trying to do and where they are stuck; that information should be shared company-wide, including with product owners, not only with FS.

CS (Customer Success) is not an inquiry-handling or churn-prevention department; its essential role is to verify whether the assumed customer value is actually being delivered and to drive that value to results.

CS sits on the front line of verifying whether customer value is being realized; it structures usage reality, adoption obstacles, and expectation gaps and shares them with product owners and other roles, acting as a transmitter that continuously improves the customer experience.
Primary information obtained by CS is useful for both product improvement and sales improvement; when CS is reduced to a mere support function, this valuable information is not utilized.
The “sellable hypothesis” and the “CS hypothesis” lie on the same continuum: even if a product can be sold, the hypothesis is meaningless if the product is not actually used.

In products where the adoption decision-maker and the actual user differ, it is common for the product to be introduced but then unused. This is a state of not making the customer happy. The gap between customers who buy and customers who continue using must be identified.

Connect the initial sales hypothesis with the onboarding hypothesis to pinpoint bottlenecks. Having an LTV-based customer definition from the start is essential. CS work is experience design and execution that looks beyond one-time orders toward continued use and subsequent proposals.

Handover documents alone have limits for transferring customer understanding. Information that should be abstracted differs from information that should be shared as specific atmosphere or feel. Sharing via recordings or joint attendance is sometimes necessary. Customer understanding should be an organizational asset, not a personal one; design is needed to share information that has been siloed in IS or CS across the organization.

When IS-CS collaboration advances, reasons for selling become clear, customers who should not be sold to become visible, product-improvement priorities become clear, and the whole organization can converse about customers. This is the form of an organization that does not stop at selling but circulates value delivery.

Common customer definition and success definition are indispensable for this collaboration. Clarify responsibility scope and decision rights by phase, create a culture of visualizing what hypotheses IS and CS are testing, and treat reviews as learning rather than blame.

The product owner must hold overall consistency of the customer experience: alignment of how the product is sold versus how it is used, meaning-making of information gathered by IS/CS, and final mediation when departments contradict each other. Practical operations and improvements can be delegated, but customer understanding and success definition must not be let go. KPI design should not be left to the field because an overall-optimization perspective is required.

In IS-CS collaboration, responsibility boundaries must be clearly drawn: do not relinquish customer understanding and success definition, because these are core to the product and the responsible person must keep high-resolution understanding; do not relinquish KPI design, because goals must be set from an overall-optimization perspective rather than field-level local optimization.

Delegate practical operations, execution, and improvement work, because these sit inside the already-defined success-definition and KPI framework and consist of concrete execution plus daily PDCA cycles.
Chapter summary presents five failure patterns of sales and stakeholder management.

Failure pattern 1: Aggressive selling. Occurs when only revenue targets are emphasized and there is no definition of whom to sell to, whom not to sell to, or what happens after the sale; the field then sells aggressively on the rational logic of 'do whatever if it sells.' This is usually treated as an individual character or attitude problem, but most cases are actually problems of organizational design and decision-making structure produced by ambiguous strategy plus incomplete responsibility boundaries imposed on the field.

Failure pattern 2: Easily acceding to customer requests. A subtype of aggressive selling in which customizations that ignore the product roadmap are promised. Sales routinely receives requests of the form 'if we had this feature the deal would close' or 'can you change this a little?'

Immediately agreeing to custom requests without checking the product roadmap or strategy is harmful: product priorities get dragged by individual deals, core customer problems are postponed, the development organization is exhausted by exception handling, product consistency is lost, and explanation costs skyrocket.

When a product is shaped by one-off exceptions, it becomes unclear whose product it is. This also harms the requesting customer, because they themselves become disconnected from the maintenance and evolution of features that were built as exceptions.

Evaluating sales solely on short-term top-line results makes destructive behaviors look rational: selling to customers who are a poor product fit, maximizing only the initial contract amount, and signing contracts that ignore post-implementation operations and support load.
Those short-term-sales behaviors destroy LTV. Revenue may appear temporarily, but churn, extra development work, and customer-success exhaustion steadily weaken the business.
In B2B products especially, sales that ignore LTV act as a time bomb. The damage typically surfaces six months to a year later as overloaded CS teams and stalled product development.

Unjustified discretionary discounts often accompany aggressive selling. Discounting itself is not inherently bad; the problem is discounts made only to hit this month’s numbers, to avoid losing to a competitor, or just to get a customer to start using the product.
Price is a signal of product value to the customer. Unjustified discounts plant the belief that the product’s value can be negotiated downward.

If the team cannot articulate why a discount is being given now and what will be learned from it, the discount is an escape. The result is that renewal negotiations, upsells, and cross-sells all become harder.
Strategically valid discounts exist and can be summarized into a limited set of cases (the page introduces this distinction but does not list the cases).

Discounts or special offers should only be used when they have a clear purpose (verification, acquiring case studies, or removing adoption barriers), a limited period and conditions, a design for future recovery or LTV improvement, and organizationally agreed rules.

A common failure pattern is expanding beyond the target segment as an extension of aggressive sales. Reasons such as 'it looks sellable,' 'there is demand,' or 'it will hit the numbers' cause the product to rapidly lose its outline.

Consequences of expanding beyond target include: it becomes unclear whose problem is being solved; messaging becomes vague; sales talk becomes dependent on individuals; development priorities cannot be decided. The result is a product that 'can do anything but is chosen by no one.'

Typical failure structures are: an ambiguous market segment; no definition of customers who should not be sold to; sales methods not connected to how the product is actually used; and unclear ownership of responsibility.
Those structures produce a chain of shortsighted decisions: sell because it sells, promise because a promise can be made, and discount because discounting closes the deal.

What a product owner must hold: definition of customers who may be sold to vs. must not be sold to; alignment between the product roadmap and sales promises; discount rules and their purpose; a success definition premised on LTV; and final arbitration when departments conflict.
Aggressive sales is not runaway behavior by the field. It is an organizational failure that occurs inevitably when leadership lets go of the things that should be held with resolve.

THE MODEL (Fukuda Yasutaka, 2019) models the SaaS process from customer acquisition through retention as a relay across four departments. Product owners who understand the business pipeline (lead acquisition → order → continuation) can avoid unproductive 'dev vs. sales' conflict and design feature development and data integration that improve metrics at each phase.

Sales should be treated as a reproducible science rather than a personal art (Sales is, Imai Akiya, 2021). Product owners need to know how salespeople translate and communicate product value to customers so they can provide effective sales enablement (sales materials, demo environments).

Listening skill is essential for customer understanding and user insight. The book on interviewer technique (Miyamoto Eriko, 2021) distills 88 hints from interviewing more than 25,000 people on how to draw out stakeholders’ and customers’ hidden true feelings rather than interrogating them.

In conversations (especially user hearings), avoid 'why?' / 'how come?' questions as much as possible. Instead react with empathy or surprise to the other person's words so the conversation rolls forward naturally.

Digging too deep with Why can make the other person feel interrogated and pressured; therefore avoid direct reason-asking questions and use talk-friendly reactions such as nodding (aizuchi), parroting/repeating their words (oumugaeshi), and showing interest in specific points, in order to draw out their true feelings (honne).

This listening approach connects to user-hearing tips from Chapter 7: drawing out the counterpart's true intentions and latent needs through keicho (active listening) is the foundation of quality product development and customer-relationship building.

Product-Led Organization (Todd Olson; Japanese ed. 2021): a practical guide to aligning the whole company—sales, marketing, CS, org design and strategy—around the product. Break silos; the product owner acts as hub so every stakeholder orients toward maximizing customer value through the product.

The Law of Minimizing Sales, Maximizing Profit (Kinoshita Katsuhisa, 2021): warns SaaS firms against the trap of chasing large-customer custom requests that inflate development cost and destroy profit. Look beyond top-line growth to LTV and contribution-margin ratio; stop thin-margin, high-volume feature work and build a lean product-and-org structure that continuously generates profit.

Brand is not something a company itself defines; it is established by how customers, users, and society see and recognize the company. It is a collection of expectations that exist in the customer's mind.
Visual and surface elements such as logos, visuals, copy, and tone & manner are only a small part of a brand, not the brand itself.
No matter how much a company describes its ideal image, if that image is not recognized and accepted by others, it is not a brand.
The true identity of a brand is the history of how consistently the company has met expectations and how much it has accumulated without betraying those expectations.

A company must still clearly define how it wants to be seen and how it wants to exist, then honestly and continuously face that stance; that process itself becomes the image perceived by customers and users.
What is communicated through unspoken aspects and unintended behaviors often exceeds what is deliberately stated.
A brand is a promise made to customers; it is formed as the accumulation of sustainable trust created by continuously keeping that promise.
広報PR combines 広報 (widely disseminating the company's own information) with PR/Public Relations (building good relationships with stakeholders).
Inconsistency example: a product that claims sophisticated design while the corporate website and members' communications appear messy undermines the brand.
Inconsistency between a claimed brand personality and actual customer support (e.g., outdated support despite a modern image) makes customers feel disjointed and damages credibility.
Companies like Apple demonstrate consistent decision-making across product, store experience, events, presentations, and copy; that consistency itself becomes the brand.
A brand can be understood as the external manifestation of company culture.
Branding and PR are tightly connected: PR is the work of building relationships so that an organization continues to be trusted.
Public Relations is not limited to customers or users; it includes business partners, investors, employees, and even employees' families.
The goal of PR and branding is to create states such as 'this company is trustworthy,' 'I want to keep choosing this company's products,' and 'I can be proud of the people who work here.'

Short-term ads and events can generate momentary awareness, but people forget; therefore one must ask how the accumulation of short-term tactics produces residual, medium-to-long-term effects (brand equity).
A brand is the sum of expectations.
Brand trust is asymmetric: exceeding expectations accumulates trust, but betrayal can collapse it all at once—the same dynamic as personal trust.
Even if product leaders speak impressively, insincere behavior by sales or support damages the brand; the gap between words and actions is among the fastest ways to destroy a brand.
Product, UX, pricing, sales, onboarding, and customer success are all brand experiences, not separate functions.
Beautiful UI or copy cannot compensate for a cumbersome actual experience or lack of felt results; trust is lost.
Post-contract (after-sale) experience is remembered more strongly than the pre-sale experience.
The 'caught fish, no more bait' pattern—neglecting customers after they buy—is one of the most damaging brand behaviors.
Consistent experience design is required from before the sale through after use; the product itself is the most eloquent form of PR.
Choosing short-term exception handling for immediate results while understanding the risk to long-term brand is very different from doing so unconsciously; that difference matters a great deal.

A brand is not only a relationship with customers; it is the relationship with society itself. Trust is generated by a consistent stance on why the business exists, what problems it confronts, and where it takes responsibility.

Brand building requires the resolve to keep the same values and the same judgments over a long period (1, 3, 5, 10 years). PR initiatives that are not premised on accumulating along that time axis will spin their wheels and fail.

Brand cannot be controlled, but it can be designed. Customer cognition and evaluation cannot be manipulated; what is possible is understanding points that are easily misunderstood or hard to convey, and designing so that experience and communication stay consistent.
Aligning product, public relations, personal communication, and organizational culture is the work required of a product owner/manager.
Whether the company name, the product name, or executives/star players become the 'face' is a branding-strategy decision, not merely a publicity or exposure tactic. Each option has meaning and risk.

The key is not short-term exposure efficiency but intentionally deciding where trust will be accumulated. That decision cannot be easily switched later; it is analogous to market selection in product development.
Once a direction is set, it grows stronger through accumulation; if it wavers midway, customer cognition becomes confused. Therefore the structure must be decided first.

Putting something without cognitive assets (認知資産) in front as the face will not function immediately. A people-forward strategy works when the audience already wants to work with that person or to use what that person creates.

When customers already feel 'I want to use something from this person,' that existing emotion is a major asset. The same applies to company names and product names: if an image is already formed in the customer's mind, it becomes a powerful weapon. Putting unknown companies, unknown products, or unknown executives front and center takes much longer.

Before deciding 'who to put forward,' define the intersection of the company's uniqueness and customer needs. Clarify what the company's uniqueness is, and whether that uniqueness actually overlaps with the value customers truly seek. Only after this alignment is clear does it become possible to see which axis (person, company, or product) should be featured.
Brand architecture is the decision of how to structure the relationship among the company (house brand), products, and individuals. This structural judgment comes one step before PR tactics.

Many companies reverse the order and start with tactics first—'just attend events,' 'just write a blog,' 'just start SNS.' This is analogous to building product features without first deciding the market. It may succeed by chance but has no reproducibility.
Correct sequence: first decide the structure (brand architecture), then stack measures along that structure, so that customer awareness forms as a result. Keep this order.

A company-name-as-face strategy works when corporate philosophy, culture, and thought are the source of value and decision-making is consistent. Even if products change, the state 'I can trust this company' holds. Trust then accumulates in the company's personality rather than in a product, which benefits recruiting, PR, and business expansion.

If philosophy and vision are too abstract, they do not resonate with customers. Phrases such as 'become world number one' or 'become industry No. 1' are company-side wishes and do not help customers imagine value, so the brand gets buried.
To make the company name the face of the brand, the philosophy must be reflected in daily decision-making, and customers must be able to experience it.
A product-name-as-face branding strategy requires the readiness that failures and controversies will also reflect on the entire company.

Putting the product name forward as the brand face works when use cases and problem-solving are clear and growth is product-driven; it is especially powerful when the offering hits the center of what customers want and signs of PMF (product-market fit) are visible.
In that case, customer touchpoints concentrate on the product experience. Leading with the value the product solves, customer voices, and before/after change generates understanding and empathy.
For hiring, a product-first face makes it clear what someone can accomplish by working on that product.

A key risk is that the product name becomes known while the company name does not; the product name can be put first, but the connection to the company behind it must be gradually recovered by design.

Company and product play different messaging roles to society: the company should speak Why (why this business exists and which social issues it takes responsibility for—philosophy and mission). That Why is the core for social empathy, recruiting, investor appeal, and mid-to-long-term corporate brand.

The product should speak What and How: what it is and how it solves the concrete problem in front of the customer (practical benefit). Customers mainly want to know how the tool will make their work easier.
Example of the split: company Why = “free all working people from routine work”; product What/How = “AI-based automatic input (What) that halves monthly accounting work (How).”
Making this Why vs What/How division explicit keeps PR, speaking, and media-exposure design from drifting.
Personal vs corporate communication also needs a careful split: if they diverge, brand consistency is lost; if corporate messaging is too detached from personal thought, it becomes unnatural.
A brand is judged not by what is said but by what seeps out; that premise must not be forgotten.

The public 'face' a business should put forward differs by business model (BtoB / BtoC / SaaS) and by growth phase; this must be switched intentionally, because an unplanned shift collapses the brand.
BtoB: company name and the representative’s credibility strongly drive decisions. Deal size and failure risk are high, so buyers emphasize who will take responsibility.
BtoC: individual experience is the center of decision-making. Awareness often starts with the product, so the product name tends to become the public face.
SaaS sits between BtoB and BtoC: both corporate trust and conviction from product experience are required, so hybrid design of company name plus product name is common.
Startup phase face: founder / person in charge. Reason: little track record and the company is unknown. Role: lead with personal passion, vision, and philosophy to win the first trust.
Growth phase face: the product. Reason: the product is accepted by the market and growing. Role: the product that embodies solving the customer’s problem becomes the center of trust.

Expansion phase face: the company name. Reason: the business diversifies/expands and becomes a social presence. Role: recover and accumulate trust earned by the product as the personality of the company as a whole.
PR and brand-building specialists should be grown rather than merely assigned; work with people who jointly own PR and inner branding rather than treating PR talent as a slot to fill.

In product and organizational PR, the decisive capability is not merely executing tactics, but deeply understanding company culture, recasting its strengths in one's own words, turning that into strategy, and keeping the overall design consistent.
The first PR hire should understand the intent of the organization, product, field/site, and market, and translate that both internally and externally.

Words and assumptions that are taken for granted inside the company often do not work outside. There is a temperature gap and perception mismatch between the world seen internally and the world seen by customers, media, and job candidates.
A core PR skill is interpreting those gaps, adjusting language differences, switching between the context media wants and the context customers feel, and connecting them.
The ideal first PR person is not primarily a writer of articles but a translator of structure.
Context-understanding ability is the key competency; tactic-level execution talent is abundant, but people who can draw strategy or judge what should be said are rarer.
Mid-career PR hires are not automatically immediately effective. Job descriptions should be designed carefully and the relationship should assume development and training.

Internal engineers and product people increasingly move into PR (e.g. DevRel). In product-centric companies, industry understanding, product understanding, engineering literacy, and cultural understanding determine PR quality.
Experience at a major PR agency does not necessarily translate into results in this domain.
PR experience matters less than context-understanding ability: talent who can grasp in which context the company should be spoken about will create long-term value.
PR talent must proactively go looking for internal and external attractiveness rather than waiting for it to be handed to them.
PRの質は現場への接触量によって決まる。会議室の中だけで議論して生まれるPRには明確な限界がある。開発現場・セールス現場・CS現場などの一次情報にどれだけ触れているかによって、「今、何を語るべきか」「何が求められているか」の解像度が変わる。
採用PRであれば実際に採用イベントに足を運び候補者と話すこと、顧客向けPRであれば顧客の現場に同席することが、一次情報に触れる具体例である。
PRとインナーブランディングは切り離せない。外部発信と内部実態の乖離は必ず破綻を生む。
採用広報で良い面だけを発信し続けると、入社後のギャップに苦しむ人が増え、早期離職が起き、かえってブランドを毀損する。
社内で合意されていないメッセージを外部に出すことも同様に危険である。「キラキラした会社」という印象で人を集めても、実態が伴わなければ失望を生むだけである。
ミッション・ビジョン・バリューを掲げることは容易だが、それが日常の意思決定・評価・採用・行動に反映されているかは別問題である。掲示物となった瞬間に形骸化する。
日々の小さな意思決定や評価がどの価値観に基づいて行われているかが、やがて社外ににじみ出てパブリックイメージとして統合されていく。
こうしたPRは、会社の文化解像度が高い人ほど貢献できる領域である。初期はどうしても個人依存になるが、そこから組織分散へと移行する設計が必要である。
PR担当が抜けた瞬間にすべての発信が止まってしまう企業は少なくない。防ぐには、社内全体で共有される最低限の共通言語が必要である。
登壇・執筆・発信を支援する仕組みや評価制度も重要である。なぜその行動が自分に返ってくるのかを理解できる動機付けも欠かせない。情報の共有が将来の仲間を増やし、自分の負荷を下げることにつながるという実感を持てれば、行動は変わる。

PR talent development accumulates learning when judgment criteria are verbalized (who decides up to what point, and from where to escalate) and when the background of go/no-go decisions on communications is carefully shared.

PR outcomes, like branding, cannot be measured in the short term. Metrics such as event placements and volume of exposure are only self-referential indicators; contribution to trust formation becomes visible only later.
Evaluating outcomes rather than outputs requires a mid-to-long-term perspective. Quarterly evaluation cycles are not always a good fit.

Even when quarterly reviews do not fit, the product owner must design KPIs around changes in the trust balance and around talent-development goals, and must keep those KPIs aligned with the formal evaluation system.
The product owner must clearly define the responsibility boundary in branding and PR: who decides what, and who executes how.

PR roles differ: some people excel at execution, some at planning, some at both. Delivery models also vary (in-house, external PR agency or freelancer, or in-house execution with external accompaniment). These choices must be made explicit.
It is essential to verbalize from the outset who decides what and who executes how, and to treat that as shared common understanding.

A frequent failure is conflating direction with means. Typical symptoms: later applying the brakes with “that went too far,” or completing strategy discussions together but then leaving execution half-done so that ownership of the work is left floating.
Those failures occur when responsibility boundaries and the location of decision rights remain ambiguous when work begins.

Before starting, clarify what is a consultation matter versus what is within someone’s discretion, and where final decision authority sits. Grasp the direction yourself and leave tactics/measures to the specialists.

A product owner must hold two non-delegable things: (1) consistency of market selection, customer definition, and value proposition; (2) the line between themes to talk about and themes not to talk about (including tone and expressions to avoid).

If the market/customer/value-proposition axis wavers, even excellent later tactics produce overall off-target communication. This is the same principle as in product development itself, not only PR and branding.
Which themes to discuss, which to avoid, which tone to use, and which expressions to avoid constitute brand stance itself and ideology; therefore the product owner keeps final judgment.
The product owner must also own reputation risk: backlash (炎上) from inappropriate communications and loss of corporate social credibility.

Owned media (blogs, podcasts, etc.) are powerful weapons but inherently contain reputation risk. Excessive review lowers posting frequency and makes content bland; no review lets unintended risks surface.
Designing final fact-check and value judgment—what is correct information for the product, and which communications become risks—is the product owner’s job, not the PR person’s.

The person who most deeply understands the product’s philosophy and where risks sit should delegate verbalization while holding the judgment axis of the line that must be defended. Only this split makes PR a powerful product weapon.
That same split determines whether the other party becomes a partner or merely an outsourcer.
Reviewing execution results by only saying ‘good/bad’ about output is insufficient. Feedback should include process and thinking, with a stance of building culture together.
Evaluating expert proposals requires at least enough understanding of world trends and of what information the company’s own customers use to make decisions.
To prevent becoming a “measure factory” (施策工場化), keep asking: what outcome this measure is targeting, and what business impact is expected relative to cost.
Timing judgment is required: whether a measure should be done now, based on alignment with management announcements, product releases, and the overall annual schedule.

Leave flexible domains to specialists: measure design under an agreed overall strategy, choice of expression methods, channel/media selection, optimization of presentation to media characteristics, and improving execution speed and operations.
Specialists turn strategy from theory into real form; their value is breadth of options and high resolution, so have them explore the best choices within the strategy.

Do not treat specialists as a mere execution unit. If strategy is not shared, the range of measures narrows and the organization falls into strategy-less measure consumption: activity volume rises but results do not.

Shared understanding of outcome KPIs is essential. Do not stop at lead counts or exposure counts; share business outcomes beyond them (e.g., hiring or product adoption) as KPIs, with both internal members and external partners.
When working with agencies or freelancers, make explicit what the goal is and what results you are paying for.

Without shared strategy, partners tend to propose viral or flashy creatives that serve their own portfolios. Always check whether trendy or high-visibility measures diverge from company KPIs and whether they fit the intended purpose.
Authority-delegation design changes by organizational phase. In the launch phase, strengthen directional intensity, run alongside measures, and build the brand foundation.

In branding and PR, the product owner (プロダクト責任者) must hold the steering wheel: fix direction and delegate execution. In the growth/expansion phase they concentrate on exception judgments and overall supervision rather than day-to-day tactics.
Holding direction causes the brand to accumulate and creates reproducibility. Organizational decision-making wobble decreases, and specialists can keep performing at full strength.
The owner’s ultimate job is deciding ‘where to store trust’ (どこに信頼を貯めるのか). Decisions should be based on long-term trust recovery, not short-term exposure efficiency.
The person in charge determines structure; execution and improvement of individual measures are delegated. Clarifying that boundary is what first allows branding to stack up.
A brand is accumulation and another name for consistency. Deciding ‘who will be the face’ is the starting point of that consistency.
Chapter summary (10-5) lists nine typical failure patterns of publicity/PR and branding.

Failure pattern 1 — Starting from appearance (外見から入ってしまう): The most typical branding failure. Refreshing a logo, polishing copy, unifying website tone or SNS posts are important but do not themselves create a brand. Tidying only the outside when there is no substance will eventually collapse. A brand is not the image you want to show; it is the result actually experienced. Appearance is a promise; experience is proof that the promise was kept. The moment the two diverge, the brand loses trust.
Failure pattern 2 — Talking too much about the ideal image first (理想像を先に語りすぎてしまう): Describing a future desired state as if it has already been achieved.

Attractive corporate phrases such as customer-first, challenging organization, flat culture, and speedy decision-making become mere ideals if they are not backed by actual practice. Presenting ideals as if they were current facts causes customers and job candidates to notice the gap with lived experience, and that discomfort is remembered more strongly than expected.

Recruitment PR that overstates the ideal image and diverges from reality is a common failure pattern. Externally promoting a free, high-discretion organization and a culture that welcomes challenge, while internally decisions are slow, approval processes are numerous, and failure is punished, produces a gap that drives early post-hire turnover.

In hiring, brand-reality divergence is not merely a trust issue: it affects people's lives. Negative experiences spread together with strong impressions, resulting in a lasting reputation that 'the company says one thing and does another.'

Evaluating PR work by exposure counts or page-view numbers is a mistake. What matters is who was reached, how the message arrived, and what action it produced. A viral article that is inconsistent with the brand is worthless; events that generate large volumes of uninterested leads can actually damage the brand.

The metrics that should be pursued are lagging indicators such as whether activity led to purchases, whether the pool of hiring candidates grew, and whether people actually joined. Therefore short-term evaluation must be resisted.
An externally projected brand is also exposed when it is inconsistent with the actual product experience.

Marketing copy that claims a product is 'easy,' 'intuitive,' and delivers 'immediate results' can create a damaging expectation gap when onboarding is actually complex, setup takes time, and outcomes appear only after a long delay. Customers register this as a drop in expectations.

Customers evaluate a brand more strongly on whether expectations were betrayed than on the product's inherent quality. Even if the product has functional value, brand trust can be severely damaged when promises and reality diverge.

A common brand-design failure is when Sales/PR create expectations that Customer Success (CS) cannot fulfill. Sales may claim 'this product can do X,' but after implementation CS must say the request was not assumed or cannot currently be supported. This is not a CS effort problem; it is a mismatch between externally claimed value and internally deliverable value. Careful CS handling cannot restore trust in that state.

Brands rarely collapse from a single campaign, but they weaken through accumulated inconsistent messages: sometimes challenging, sometimes conservative; customer-first in one context and company-centric in another. Outsiders then see a company they 'don't know what to believe.' Inconsistency shows especially on SNS and owned media, e.g., when tone shifts with staff changes or when management decisions and field communications do not align.
Over-reliance on short-term KPIs (page views, follower counts, exposure, event attendance, etc.) can encourage a surface-only brand that looks good on metrics but lacks substance.

Metrics and numbers are convenient indicators, but they do not themselves represent brand value. Chasing numbers and sending messages that diverge from reality may look successful in the short term, but they damage trust over the medium to long term.
Failure pattern: branding without a responsible owner. Surface-only brands often arise when the product owner treats branding as PR work and detaches from it.

Market selection, customer definition, how you sell, and how you refuse are all brand decisions. If the product owner is not involved in those decisions, teams are forced into local optimization, producing a brand that looks plausible but has no matching substance.
The most important principle for avoiding these failures is to design the brand from reality: admit what you cannot yet do, and if you are still improving, include that context when you speak.
A brand is not fiction; it is the accumulation of honesty (誠実さの積み重ね).
Before any external messaging, confirm internal consistency. Product, sales, customer success, and recruiting must tell the same story; the owner must continually check that alignment.

Whether a company falls into a surface-only brand is ultimately a question of resolve: willingness to spend time stacking trust versus prioritizing short-term results. That choice determines brand strength.
A brand is not something you create; it is something that accumulates. Unless you confront the substance, stacking beautiful words and design cannot produce a true brand.
PRの基本構造は、プロダクト責任者が陥りがちな「新機能が出ました」という一方的なWhat（機能）の発信ではなく、「今、世の中にあるどんな社会課題を解決するのか」という社会文脈（Why）に翻訳し、メディアや世論を巻き込むことである。
科学的ブランディングの核心は、エモーショナルな「ブランド論」や「コアなファンを大切にすればブランドは成長する」という常識ではなく、プロダクトのUI・ネーミング・日々の発信を通じて顧客の脳内にメンタル・アベイラビリティ（購買時にパッと思い出される状態）を構築することである。『ブランディングの科学』（バイロン・シャープ）は、コアファン重視の常識を膨大なデータで覆した。
カテゴリー戦略とは、差別化が難しい成熟市場で新たな市場（カテゴリー）そのものを創造し、自社をそのカテゴリーの第一想起ブランドに仕立てる戦略である。競合との差異を訴える従来型マーケティングでは人の記憶に残るブランドはつくれず、「市場ではなく人の頭の中で戦え」というのが要点である。

Legal affairs and IP strategy is among the most specialized, high-difficulty topics in product/business work: unlike product development or org design, correct answers are rarely clear, and a single wrong judgment can threaten the business itself.
Few product-development or product-management books treat legal affairs head-on, yet from a risk-management standpoint legal is indispensable; 'I didn't know' is not an acceptable excuse.

Typical legal-domain disasters that can wipe out accumulated product assets or threaten company survival include: trademark infringement forcing a sudden service-name change and loss of brand recognition; open-source license violations forcing code disclosure and rewrite; and having to discard all accumulated data because it was obtained by improper means.
A practical difficulty is that the company often has no internal expert who can teach these risks, so the product owner must confront them personally.
Legal risk should be treated as insurance, not as a cost; the asymmetry between cheap prevention and enormous post-incident losses makes this obvious.
Small confirmations that could have prevented trouble later generate huge losses; such cases never cease.
Paradoxically, putting IP and contracts in order can sometimes increase business speed rather than slow it.
Organizations strong in legal affairs have clear decision criteria, consult early, and treat legal as an enabler ('legal that advances') rather than a blocker ('legal that stops').
Legal work is part of business and product design itself, not merely post-incident trouble handling. Treating legal staff only as a reaction team causes fatal risks to be missed.

Many disputes already have their seeds in contract wording, public-facing documents, display methods, contract timing, and word choice—before any problem materializes. Issues that could have been avoided at that stage later appear as large losses.
Product owners need a preventive legal viewpoint: catching and avoiding problems in contracts and disclosures before they surface.

Legal impact is especially large in the launch (0→1) phase because contracts and terms of service must be created without templates. Errors at this stage can produce not only unfavorable terms but irreversible legal violations.
In the launch phase, trusted relationships with in-house legal or outside counsel usually do not yet exist. Insufficient explanation of the business domain can lead counsel to miss risks.
A typical startup legal risk is structural: speed-to-market and implementation are prioritized, so legal review is postponed or incomplete.
Entering a new domain with no precedent is itself a risk; teams must proceed without established case law or guidelines.
In fields where statutes and guidelines change frequently, staying current cannot be left to individual effort; it requires organizational systems covering people, product, and contracts together.
Acting before a contract is signed, or allowing operations to diverge from the signed contract, creates compound (複合) legal risk and is described as extremely dangerous.
A signed contract is not merely a source of reassurance; it should be treated as a potential hotbed of risk because, as a rule, everything written in it is legally effective.
An organizational culture of not reading contracts should be corrected immediately.

AI-based contract review is useful but typically yields only generic comments and often fails to surface company-specific risks; special attention is required for low-probability but fatal clauses such as those that constrain future growth or that cap damages.

Neglect of intellectual property can be fatal to the business: open-source license violations and failure to obtain trademarks (creating later name-change risk) threaten continuity and must be understood by product owners, not only engineers.

Five representative legal risks that cannot be excused by 'I did not know': (1) Contract risk — requesting work beyond the scope of an outsourcing agreement or performing acts not defined in the contract; NDA (confidentiality) issues around retention periods and penalties for breach. (2) Intellectual-property risk — unintentional infringement of copyright, patents, trademarks or licenses; problems may surface only later as lawsuits or claims, so both protection of own IP and periodic checks against third-party rights are required. (3) Labor/HR risk — blurred boundary between outsourcing and employment, presence or absence of command-and-control, working-hours management; discrepancy between form and reality. (4) Personal-information and data-handling risk — acquisition, storage, third-party provision and anonymization; a leak produces both legal liability and severe loss of social trust. (5) Advertising/PR legal risk — insufficient labeling of promotional content and expressions that mislead consumers.
It is impossible to avoid all legal and business risks. What matters is distinguishing risks that should be taken from those that should be avoided, and practicing intentional risk-taking.
Organizations that postpone legal affairs face severe consequences including business shutdown, damages claims, loss of trust, and negative effects on hiring and sales.

Legal affairs as a defensive shield function as infrastructure that supports offensive (growth) strategies. Establishing minimum legal defenses before scaling actually helps the business move forward.
Terms of Use (利用規約) and Privacy Policy (プライバシーポリシー) are not merely legal documents; they are part of the product specification itself.
Users actually see these documents, agree to them, and use the product on that basis, making them equivalent in importance to UI/UX, feature design, and data design.

Although Terms of Use and Privacy Policy are often placed in the footer, that does not mean they have low importance. Where they are displayed, at what timing consent is requested, and in what context they are presented constitute essential product specifications.

Particular attention must be paid to aspects closely tied to data design and UX: what personal information or equivalent data is collected, where it is stored, how it is used, and to what extent it is shared with external parties.
The actual implementation must remain within the scope promised in the Privacy Policy. The Privacy Policy is the document that guarantees this alignment.
Terms of Use are not documents to be consulted only when trouble arises; in principle they are presented to every user.
Legal requirements must be designed in from the beginning rather than treated as an afterthought, especially regarding data handling and user-facing consent flows.
Terms of service and privacy policies are a prerequisite for using a service and define where responsibility lies; only people who agree to this promise can use the service.

Data integration with third-party tools is now almost essential. When using analytics (e.g. Google Analytics), ad measurement tools, or external CRMs, it is mandatory to disclose which data goes to which third parties. Failure to do so is a privacy-policy deficiency and a personal-information-protection problem.
Whether merely checking a checkbox truly constitutes consent is being judged more strictly every year.

Design must rest on accountability and understandability; implementations for withdrawing consent and opting out, and the operational impact of consent management on the product, must not be underestimated.
If UI operations and the written contents of the terms of service or privacy policy do not match, the business operator can reasonably be held responsible.

Consent to terms of service is often a hollow formality: terms are updated without user re-consent, or they are not presented in an understandable form. Designing on the assumption that they will not be read is dangerous.
Dark patterns that make cancellation extremely difficult carry high legal risk and are also fatal to user experience.

Terms of service and privacy policies should not be assembled after the fact; they must be built in from the design stage. Because they are updated in response to laws, third-party tools, and new features, operational design must also cover notification methods, handling of re-consent, and management of revision history.

The central role of terms of service is to clarify the scope of responsibility: what is provided and what is not; where the service operator’s responsibility ends and the user’s begins; disclaimer clauses and caps on damages; and preparation for unexpected or abusive use.

Disclaimer clauses and caps on damages in terms of service are critical points that always become issues in worst-case scenarios. Whether the business or the user is responsible—for example if a user misuses the service in unexpected ways and commits fraud or legal violations—is decided by what the terms of service actually say, not by emotion.
If the business is found partly responsible, whether a cap on damages is stipulated changes risk dramatically. Without a cap, liability can theoretically be unlimited.

Drafting terms of service is not especially hard because every existing service publishes its terms. Studying the terms of services you use daily or of similar services shows typical structure and where attention is paid; company-specific issues can then be reviewed with a lawyer.

A privacy policy is a declaration to users of how the company handles data. It must explicitly state what information is collected and what is not, so users can check whether unwanted data is taken and whether it is processed appropriately.

The balance of specificity vs. abstraction in stated purposes of use is important: too specific and a slight change of purpose easily puts the company in non-compliance; too abstract and users cannot imagine what will be done with their data. Referencing established services is a practical way to strike this balance.
Third-party provision, outsourcing, and overseas transfer are essential topics. Even with strict in-house management, if the hosting data center is abroad, the applicable rules change.
Data retention periods and deletion policies matter: what happens after account withdrawal (physical vs. logical deletion) directly affects the impact scope if a leak occurs.
Therefore a privacy policy should be designed starting from the data flow.

User data handling must be mapped across five stages: acquisition (what data is collected from users and by what means), storage (where it is kept, e.g. domestic vs overseas servers, and how it is secured), use (only for stated purposes such as service delivery, marketing, or product improvement), third-party sharing (when and under what conditions data goes to SaaS tools or partners), and deletion (when and how data is made irrecoverable on account closure or end of retention).
Map the full data flow so it is clear who can touch the data at each point; include third-party SaaS terms of service and define responsibility boundaries.

In BtoB, the relationship between the contract and the terms of service is critical; in BtoC, consumer-protection requirements are stronger. Corporate contracts are not exempt when personal information is involved.

Enterprises and mega-ventures often have dedicated in-house legal and IP staff; startups typically use external lawyers and patent attorneys on retainer or spot contracts. How those professionals are briefed and engaged is itself a design choice that affects speed and risk tolerance.

Legal counsel, lawyers, and patent attorneys should be treated as design partners from the start, not only called after an incident. A purely reactive legal setup almost always increases risk because, once trouble has occurred, large volumes of information must be shared under severe time pressure.

Urgent legal judgment requires conveying four hard-to-transfer contexts: (1) the business premise structure—who pays whom, how money is received, and what value and data flows constitute the model; (2) the history of past decisions—why current system specs and terms of use exist, and which risks were weighed or compromised during development; (3) communication history with customers and partners—what was promised and how far things were explained in sales materials and support; (4) a clear split between confirmed objective facts (e.g., system logs) and subjective field speculation.

Even specialists find it extremely difficult to convey those contexts accurately under time pressure; therefore legal, lawyers, and patent attorneys should be treated as partners from an early stage rather than summoned only after a problem arises.

Even when no legal work is pending, maintain regular communication so that business and product updates are continuously inputted; that accumulation largely determines judgment quality when a crisis hits.

A common misconception is that lawyers are overly cautious or that legal ‘holds the business back.’ If legal lacks sufficient business understanding, the only rational move is to minimize risk, which often means stopping. Without knowing what the business wants to accelerate and where its competitive advantage lies, a halt is the safest default.
If legal is reduced to a brake, part of the responsibility lies with the business side for not sharing business context in ordinary times.

Legal that only enumerates risks has limited value. Build a relationship in which they can propose ‘how to proceed under conditions’ and ‘risk-controlled alternatives.’ That requires carefully sharing background, purpose, and constraints, and a culture of sharing reasons as well as conclusions.

When consulting legal experts, avoid asking vague questions such as “overall, how is it?” because answers become purely defensive. Law is a system that defines what must not be done more than what may be done.
Yes/No questions distort business judgment. Contracts and legal outcomes are almost always stacks of compromises; complete Yes and complete No rarely exist in practice.

Before consulting an expert, organize the issues as: (1) what constraints must absolutely be observed, (2) where there is remaining room within those constraints, and (3) what conditional forms could still work.
Vague whole-product questions are always answered with generalities. The business side should structure the issues in advance so discussion stays specific.

Generative AI can help surface related statutes and typical risks, but the goal is not to obtain a final answer. The goal is to enter expert discussion already knowing where judgment is likely to split.

Product owners need a minimum of legal literacy to discuss productively with experts. Three baselines: (1) issue-spotting rather than statute-memorization—e.g., sensing that a feature that acquires other companies’ data may raise copyright or terms-of-service issues, not reciting Personal Information Protection Act article numbers; (2) recognizing legal minefield patterns such as handling user payments/money, collecting sensitive data like health information, or letting users post content to one another; (3) being able to decide whether a matter is worth escalating to counsel rather than treating every question as a binary legal/illegal call.

The critical legal skill for business teams is not independently judging whether something is legal or illegal, but recognizing gray zones and correctly pausing to escalate to legal counsel or lawyers at the right time—before development work begins.
Legal role-sharing changes by business phase. A legally protected line exists, but the final decision-maker is always the operating company, not the lawyer.

Do not treat expert legal opinions as final. Adopt a posture of jointly considering alternatives: if a given judgment is too conservative/strict, what substitute options would still allow the business to proceed.

In the launch/startup phase, two engagement models should be used selectively: (1) spot consultation for one-off contract legal checks and generic document drafting, when the purpose is clear and you need a pinpoint yes/no on legality; (2) advisor (顧問) retainers for ongoing design support grounded in business understanding and iterative legal-risk wall-hitting, when you want to co-design the legality of a new business model and keep the venture moving.

As the business scales, both consultation frequency and decision speed become essential. An advisor retainer then functions as an investment that protects decision-making velocity rather than merely a cost.
At larger scale it becomes realistic to divide legal work by domain (contracts, IP, data, labor). Beyond a further size threshold, establishing an in-house legal contact/window should be considered.

Spot consultation is effective when the legal question is well-defined and you need a correct/incorrect confirmation. Advisor contracts are effective when the business model itself must be discussed for legality and the goal is to advance the venture together.

When selecting external experts (legal/IP), evaluate whether they seek high-resolution understanding of the company's unique business model and technical background instead of dismissing it as typical IT, and whether they catch up on their own.

Experts should not only state legal or terms-of-service prohibitions; they should also propose alternatives or workarounds, such as how to change product specs or flows so the business purpose can still be achieved legally and safely.

Experts need growth-phase tolerance: they should not impose large-enterprise perfect governance on an early-stage startup, but should accept a gradient of risk-taking matched to the company's growth speed and current capacity, and be willing to accompany the team.

Product owners must accept that legally gray judgments will never be reduced to zero. They must distinguish intentional, informed risk-taking from unconscious violations, take responsibility for decisions after considering expert input, and tie IP choices (what patents or trademarks to pursue, and when) to business strategy rather than treating IP solely as something to protect. This stance is the foundation of a healthy legal scheme.

Product leaders should organize which legal/IP areas they must understand themselves versus which they delegate to specialists. Legal/IP must not be treated as a black box; the attitude of 'I don't understand it so I'll just leave it to others' is extremely dangerous because legal functions structurally tend to lean defensive.

Insufficient legal understanding that leads to fully delegating everything to specialists delays decision-making and produces over-defensiveness. As a result, companies may fail to accelerate at the right moment, abandon viable alternatives, and halt business growth.

A product owner does not need to understand entire legal documents or memorize statutes. What is required is grasp of the key points: where the dangers and traps are, and which mistakes would have a fatal impact on the business.
The target state is being able to explain in one's own words why a given clause is problematic. This can be practiced through past court cases and other companies' trouble examples.

Even without full mastery of legal terminology, there is a recognizable boundary of 'this is a line that requires judgment.' Maintaining the ability to stay on the correct side of that line is the legal literacy expected of a product owner.
Legal work should be split into judgment (decision-making) that the product owner must retain versus operational tasks that can be delegated to specialists.

Judgment axes the product owner should keep: overall grasp of contract structure; understanding of the philosophy behind terms of use and privacy policy; types of intellectual property and their business impact; basic structure of labor, personal information, and data use; and types of legal risks that could stop the business.

Practical work that can be left to specialists: drafting and revising specific contract and terms language; patent/trademark search, filing, and registration; final confirmation of legal interpretation on individual matters; practical handling of litigation and disputes; and overseas regulation / cross-border data compliance.
Product managers must understand legal fundamentals themselves; without that understanding they cannot correctly evaluate explanations from specialists.

Product managers should personally grasp: overall contract structure; the underlying philosophy of terms of service and privacy policies; types of intellectual property and their impact on the business; basic structures of labor, personal information, and data use; and types of legal risks that can stop a business.

Work that should be clearly left to specialists (because it requires high expertise and experience) includes: concrete drafting and revision of contract/terms language; patent and trademark search, filing, and registration; final confirmation of legal interpretation in individual cases; practical handling of litigation and disputes; and overseas regulation and cross-border data issues.

Do not confuse judgment with execution. Judgment belongs to the product owner; execution belongs to specialists. What is outsourced is practical work, not decision-making. Deciding and writing are different things.
If the distinction between deciding and writing is blurred, decision-making is gradually handed to outsiders and business responsibility becomes hollow.
Judgment axes the product owner must hold include which risks to take and which risks to avoid.

Business leaders, not legal experts, own the balance of business speed vs. legal safety, the company's stance on gray zones, and the criteria for continuing vs. withdrawing. These are core business responsibilities.

Experts are advisors, not decision-makers. 'Legally cannot do it' and 'we will not do it as a business' are different judgments. Do not accept expert opinions uncritically; discuss how to interpret and use them, or experts become locked into a pure brake role.

Throwing every issue to experts and waiting for reviews leaves them too little time, so they default to the safest answers. This is typical over-conservatism produced by organizations that cannot decide themselves.
To raise both quality and speed of decisions, give experts regular, structured input: business background, product structure, why the action is wanted now, and constraints/priorities.

Delegation of legal/IP authority should shift by stage: founding—understand it yourself and delegate only the minimum; growth—fix the judgment axes and spread execution; expansion—concentrate on exception judgments and hand off routine work.
Final responsibility always stays with the business side. Do not hide behind legal opinions; take the resolve to own the decision.

Turn accumulated judgments into organizational knowledge via records and sharing of past decisions, explicit reasons for those decisions, and structures that stop the same consultations from being repeated.
Legal literacy speeds decisions, cuts wasted consultation cost, and raises the level of dialogue with specialists.
Use legal and IP offensively, not only defensively: IP for competitive advantage, contracts for scale resilience, and business design that assumes legal constraints from the start.
Chapter 11-5 frames ten typical failure patterns of legal and IP strategy as the chapter summary.

A common and fatal organizational pattern is treating the legal function as a post-incident consultation destination or cleanup crew after a crisis or scandal, which forces legal work to remain purely reactive.
Once contracts are already signed, terms of service published, and products launched, legal options are extremely limited; the typical outcome is that little can be done except minimize damage.
Legal should operate as a design function that eliminates risk before problems occur; treating it as a downstream/after-the-fact process discards its value.
Citing speed (especially in startups and new businesses) as a reason to skip legal review is not speed but gambling; omitting even the points that must be checked is a common failure mode.
In hindsight, many incidents could have been prevented by a 10-minute check or a single consultation; speed and sloppiness are different things.
Organizations that skip legal confirmation in the name of speed almost invariably later hit a major brake.
A culture of not reading contracts—assuming ‘legal will look at it’ or ‘experts already checked so it is fine’—is dangerous because what is written in a contract is in principle all valid.
Not having read or understood a contract is never a valid excuse.
Especially dangerous are clauses that cause no problem now but become binding after growth; by the time they are noticed they usually cannot be changed.
Watch for contract clauses that constrain future business expansion, termination and non-compete conditions, caps on damages liability, and attribution of intellectual property.

Leaving terms of use or a privacy policy unchanged while the product evolves (more features, more data collected, more integrations) is a time bomb: when trouble occurs, the gap between user experience and the written terms will be pointed out, and only the fact that you did things not written in the terms remains—intent and goodwill are not considered.

Do not treat a privacy policy as mere legal paperwork. Handling of personal information and data is tightly bound to UX, data design, and operations: how data is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, and when it is deleted are themselves product design. Paper compliance without matching reality is the most dangerous state.

Do not postpone IP strategy until after the business is profitable. Intellectual property often cannot be obtained later. Once a name is in use, a product is launched, or PR has started, being beaten to registration by someone else can force irreversible costs such as changing the service name, logo, or domain.

Do not outsource legal judgment entirely to specialists with the attitude that “experts are handling it so it is fine.” Experts do not substitute for your own decisions; unless premises and business intent are shared, they will naturally present only the safest options.

Typical results of dumping work on legal without sharing context: only reasons why something cannot be done are listed, constant braking occurs, and judgments become misaligned with actual business intent.

Startup-phase legal failures that can be prevented by thinking at the design stage include: copy-pasting template contracts without understanding them, producing context mismatch (example: a template forbids subcontracting, but the actual project requires partner collaboration, so the signed contract wrongly binds the company).

Reusing another company’s terms of service without understanding them can collapse premises (example: license terms of the frameworks actually used do not match the copied terms, required declarations are missing, and by the time the mismatch is pointed out it is too late to recover).

Do not reverse the sequence of implementation and legal documentation. Lawyers are busy with many clients; if the release date is already fixed and only a few days remain, expected turnaround is unlikely. Legal documents should be prepared in parallel once specifications are fixed (i.e., at the start of implementation) rather than postponed.

Leaving content that no longer matches reality until users point it out is the downstream result of all the preceding mismatches plus delayed countermeasures (customer notices and updates across multiple related documents get postponed).
